Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. ### PREFACE.

In the introduction to the story of the Forty-seven Rônins, I have said almost as much as is necessary by way of a preface to my stories.

Those of my readers who are most capable of pointing out the many shortcomings and faults of my work will also be the most indulgent toward me; for anyone who has been in Japan and studied Japanese knows the great difficulties with which the learner is faced.

For the illustrations, at least, I feel that I need make no apology. Drawn, in the first instance, by one Ôdaké, an artist in my employ, they were engraved on wood by a famous wood-engraver at Yedo, and are therefore genuine specimens of Japanese art. Messrs. Dalziel, on examining the woodblocks, pointed out to me, as an interesting fact, that the lines are cut with the grain of the wood, in the manner of Albert Dürer and some of the old German masters—a process which has been abandoned by modern European wood-engravers.

It will be noticed that very little reference is made in these tales to the Emperor and his Court. Although I

### PREFACE.

searched diligently, I was able to find no story in which they played a conspicuous part.

Another class to which no reference is made is that of the Gôshi. The Gôshi are a kind of yeomen, or "bonnet-lairds," as they would be called over the border, living on their own land and owing no allegiance to any feudal lord. Their rank is lower than that of the Samurai, or men of the military class, between whom and the peasantry they hold a middle place. Like the Samurai, they wear two swords and are, in many cases, prosperous and wealthy men, claiming a lineage more ancient than that of many of the feudal Princes. A large number of them are enrolled in the Emperor’s bodyguard; and these have played a prominent part in the recent political changes in Japan as the most conservative and anti-foreign element in the nation.

With these exceptions, I think that all classes are fairly represented in my stories.

The feudal system has passed away like a fading image before the eyes of those who have lived in Japan during the last few years. But when they first arrived there, it was in full force, and there is not an incident narrated in the following pages—however strange it may appear to Europeans—for whose possibility and probability those most competent to judge will not vouch. Nor, as many recent events can prove, have heroism, chivalry, and devotion left the land altogether. We may deplore and speak out against the <term>Yamato Damashi</term>, or Spirit of Old Japan, which still breathes in the soul of

# TALES OF OLD JAPAN.

## THE FORTY-SEVEN RÔNINS.

The books written in recent years about Japan have either been compiled from official records or have contained the sketchy impressions of passing travelers. The world at large knows very little about the inner life of the Japanese: their religion, their superstitions, their ways of thought, and the hidden motives that drive them—all these are still mysteries. Nor is this surprising. The first Westerners who came into contact with Japan—I am speaking not of the old Dutch and Portuguese traders and priests, but of the diplomats and merchants from eleven years ago—met with a cold reception. Above all, the native government placed obstacles in the way of any inquiry into their language, literature, and history. The fact was that the <term>Tycoon</term>’s government—the only one with which relations were maintained as long as the <term>Mikado</term> remained in seclusion in his sacred capital at <term>Kiôto</term>—knew that the imperial authority with which they sought to invest their leader must quickly fade before the strong sunlight that would be brought upon it as soon as there were European linguists capable of examining their books and records. No opportunity was missed to throw dust in the

<vocab>Japan, Rônins, Tycoon, Mikado, Kiôto, Western, Dutch, Portuguese, Imperial</vocab>

<summary>The author explains that Japan's inner culture remains largely unknown to the West because the Shogunate historically obstructed foreign research to protect its political legitimacy. This introduction provides the historical setting for the story of the Forty-Seven Rônins.</summary>
<keywords>Japan, Forty-Seven Rônins, Tycoon, Mikado, Kiôto, Western diplomacy, Shogunate history, cultural barriers</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author's preface, shifting from the historical obstacles faced by foreigners to the newfound openness following the Meiji Restoration and the author’s intent to preserve Japanese culture through its own stories.</meta>

# TALES OF OLD JAPAN.

...eyes of the newcomers, whom it was the official policy to lead astray, even in the most minor details. Now, however, there is no cause for concealment; the <term>Roi Fainéant</term> <note>A "Lazy King," referring to the Mikado's former state of seclusion.</note> has shaken off his sloth along with his <term>Maire du Palais</term> <note>A "Mayor of the Palace," referring to the Shogun who formerly held the real power.</note>, and the result is a transparent government that does not fear foreign scrutiny. Since the records of the country are nothing more than proofs of the Mikado’s title to power, there is no reason for maintaining any pretense of mystery. The path of inquiry is open to all; and although there is still much to be learned, some knowledge has been gained that may interest those at home to share.

The recent revolution in Japan has brought about social as well as political changes; and it may be that once railways and telegraphs have connected the main points of the Land of the Rising Sun—in addition to the progress already made—the "old Japanese," as he was and had been for centuries when we first encountered him eleven short years ago, will have become extinct. It has appeared to me that no better means could be chosen for preserving a record of a curious and rapidly disappearing civilization than the translation of some of the most interesting national legends and histories, along with other examples of literature on the same subject. In this way, the Japanese may tell their own story, with their translator only adding a few words of heading or a note at the end of a chapter where an explanation or further detail seems necessary. I fear that the long and difficult names will often make my stories tedious to read, but I believe that those who will persevere through the difficulty will learn more about the character of the Japanese people than by skimming over even the most brilliant descriptions of travel and adventure. The lord and his retainer, the warrior and the priest, the humble artisan and the despised <term>Eta</term> <note>A class of outcasts in feudal Japan who performed tasks considered "unclean."</note> or pariah, will each in turn become a leading character in my collection of stories; and it is from the mouths of these figures that I hope to present a fairly complete picture of Japanese society.

Having said this much by way of a preface, I ask my readers...

<summary>The author explains that Japan's recent political restoration has opened the country to inquiry, allowing him to translate national legends to preserve a record of their fading civilization. He aims to portray all levels of Japanese society, from lords to outcasts, through their own traditional stories.</summary>

# THE FORTY-SEVEN RÔNINS.

...to imagine themselves carried away to the shores of the Bay of Yedo—a beautiful, smiling landscape: gentle slopes, crowned by a dark fringe of pines and firs, lead down to the sea; the quaint eaves of many a temple and holy shrine peek out here and there from the groves; the bay itself is dotted with picturesque fishing boats, whose torches shine at night like glow-worms among the outlying forts; far away to the west loom the goblin-haunted heights of Oyama, and beyond the twin hills of the Hakoné Pass—Fuji-Yama, the Peerless Mountain, solitary and grand, stands in the center of the plain from which it erupted with flames twenty-one centuries ago.<note>According to Japanese tradition, in the fifth year of Emperor Kôrei (286 B.C.), the earth opened in the province of Omi, near Kyoto, and Lake Biwa—sixty miles long by about eighteen broad—was formed in the shape of a *Biwa*, or four-stringed lute, from which it takes its name. At the same time, to offset the sinking of the earth, but at a distance of over three hundred miles from the lake, Fuji-Yama rose; its last eruption was in the year 1707. The last great earthquake at Yedo took place about fifteen years ago. Twenty thousand people are said to have died in it, and the dead were carried away and buried by the cartload; many persons, trying to escape from their falling and burning houses, were caught in great cracks that suddenly opened in the earth and just as suddenly closed upon the victims, crushing them to death. For several days, heavy shocks continued to be felt, and the people camped outside, not daring to return to those houses that had been spared nor to rebuild those that lay in ruins.</note> For a hundred and sixty years the huge mountain has been at peace, but frequent earthquakes still suggest hidden fires, and no one can say when the red-hot stones and ashes may once more fall like rain over five provinces.

In the middle of a cluster of ancient trees in Takanawa, a suburb of Yedo, is hidden Sengakuji, or the Spring-hill Temple, famous throughout the entire country for its cemetery, which contains the graves of the Forty-seven Rônins,<note>The word *Rônin* literally means a "wave-man"—one who is tossed about here and there, like a wave of the sea. It is used to designate persons of noble birth, entitled to bear arms, who—having become separated from their feudal lords by their own act, by dismissal, or by fate—wander about the country as somewhat disreputable knights-errant, without any apparent means of support. In some cases, they offer themselves for hire to new masters; in others, they support themselves by robbery; or, falling a level in the social scale, they go into trade and become simple townsmen. On the left-hand side of the main court of the temple is a chapel in which, topped by a gilded figure of Kwanyin, the goddess of mercy, the images of the forty-seven men and of the master whom they loved so well are enshrined. The statues are carved in wood, the faces colored, and the dresses richly lacquered; as works of art, they have great merit—the action of the heroes, each armed with his favorite weapon, being wonderfully lifelike and spirited. Some are venerable men with thin, gray hair (one is seventy-seven years old); others are mere boys of sixteen. Close by the chapel, at the side of a path leading up the hill, is a little well of pure water, fenced in and adorned with a tiny fernery, over which is an inscription stating: "This is the well in which the head was washed; you must not wash your hands or your feet here." A little further on is a stall where a poor old man earns a pittance by selling books, pictures, and medals commemorating the loyalty of the Forty-seven; and higher up still, shaded by a grove of stately trees, is a neat enclosure, kept up, as a signboard announces, by voluntary contributions, around which are arranged forty-eight little tombstones, each decorated with evergreens, each with its tribute of water and incense for the comfort of the departed spirit. There were forty-seven Rônins; there are forty-eight tombstones, and the story of the forty-eighth is truly characteristic of Japanese ideas of honor. Almost touching the rail of the graveyard is a more imposing

<note>
It happens that for political reasons a man will become a Rônin so that his lord may not be implicated in some deed of blood in which he is about to engage. Sometimes, also, men become Rônins and leave their native place for a while until some trouble in which they have become entangled has blown over; after which they return to their former allegiance. Nowadays, it is not unusual for men to become Rônins for a time and engage themselves in the service of foreigners at the open ports, even in menial positions, in the hope that they may pick up something of the language and knowledge of Western people. I know instances of men of considerable position who have adopted this course in their zeal for education.
</note>

And now for the story.

At the beginning of the eighteenth century, there lived a daimyo called Asano Takumi no Kami, the Lord of the castle of Akô in the province of Harima. Now it happened that when an Imperial ambassador from the Court of the Mikado was sent to the Shogun<note>1. The full title of the Tycoon was Sei-i-tai-Shogun, "Barbarian-repressing Commander-in-chief." The title Tai Kun, or Great Prince, was borrowed to convey the idea of sovereignty to foreigners at the time the treaties were concluded. The envoys sent by the Mikado from Kyoto to communicate the will of his sovereign to the Shogun were received with Imperial honors, and the duty of entertaining them was entrusted to high-ranking nobles. The title Sei-i-tai-Shogun was first held by Minamoto no Yoritomo in the seventh month of the year 1192 A.D.</note> at Yedo, Takumi no Kami and another noble called Kamei Sama were appointed to receive and host the envoy. A high official named Kira Kôtsuké no Suké was appointed to teach them the proper ceremonies to be observed for the occasion. The two nobles were accordingly forced to go daily to the castle to listen to the instructions of Kôtsuké no Suké. But this Kôtsuké no Suké was a greedy man; and because he felt that the presents which the two daimyos had brought him—according to time-honored custom—in return for his instruction were meager and unworthy, he developed a great hatred for them. He took no pains in teaching them, but on the contrary, sought to make laughingstocks of them. Takumi no Kami, restrained by a stern sense of duty, bore his insults with patience; but Kamei Sama, who had less control over his temper, was violently enraged and determined to kill Kôtsuké no Suké.

One night, when his duties at the castle were ended, Kamei Sama returned to his own palace, and having summoned his councilors<note>2. Councilor, literally "elder." The councilors of daimyos were of two classes: the *Karô*, or "elder," an hereditary office held by members of the younger branches of the Prince's family, and the *Yônin*, or "man of business," who was selected based on his merits. These "councilors" play a significant role in Japanese history.</note> to a secret conference, said to them: "Kôtsuké

"Kôtsuké no Suké has insulted Takumi no Kami and me during our service in attendance on the Imperial envoy. This is against all decency, and I intended to kill him on the spot; but I reminded myself that if I did such a deed within the precincts of the castle, not only would my own life be forfeited, but my family and vassals would be ruined: so I held back. Still, the life of such a wretch is a misery to the people, and tomorrow when I go to Court I will kill him: my mind is made up, and I will listen to no protest." And as he spoke, his face became livid with rage.

Now one of Kamei Sama’s councillors was a man of great judgment, and when he saw from his lord’s manner that protest would be useless, he said: "Your lordship’s words are law; your servant will make all preparations accordingly; and tomorrow, when your lordship goes to Court, if this Kôtsuké no Suké should again be insolent, let him die." And his lord was pleased by this speech and waited with impatience for the day to break, so that he might return to Court and kill his enemy.

But the councillor went home and was deeply troubled, thinking anxiously about what his prince had said. As he reflected, it occurred to him that since Kôtsuké no Suké had the reputation of being a miser, he would certainly be open to a bribe, and that it was better to pay any sum, no matter how great, than for his lord and his house to be ruined. So he collected all the money he could and, giving it to his servants to carry, rode off in the night to Kôtsuké no Suké’s palace, and said to his retainers: "My master, who is now in attendance upon the Imperial envoy, owes much thanks to my Lord Kôtsuké no Suké, who has taken such great pains to teach him the proper ceremonies to be observed during the reception of the Imperial envoy. This is but a humble present which he has sent by me, but he hopes that his lordship will condescend to accept it, and commends himself to his lordship’s favor." And with these words, he produced a thousand ounces of silver for Kôtsuké no Suké, and a hundred ounces to be distributed among his retainers.

# THE FORTY-SEVEN RÔNINS.

When the retainers saw the money, their eyes sparkled with pleasure and they expressed their deep gratitude. Asking the councillor to wait a moment, they went and told their master of the magnificent gift that had arrived with a polite message from Kamei Sama. Kôtsuké no Suké, in eager delight, sent for the councillor to enter an inner chamber; after thanking him, he promised to carefully instruct his master the next day in all the different points of etiquette. So the councillor, seeing the miser’s delight, rejoiced at the success of his plan; having taken his leave, he returned home in high spirits. But Kamei Sama, having no idea how his official had appeased his enemy, lay brooding over his revenge, and on the following morning at daybreak, he went to Court in a formal procession.

When Kôtsuké no Suké met him, his manner had completely changed, and nothing could surpass his courtesy. “You have come early to Court this morning, my Lord Kamei,” he said. “I cannot admire your dedication enough. I shall have the honor of calling your attention to several points of etiquette today. I must beg your lordship to excuse my previous conduct, which must have seemed very rude; but I have a naturally irritable nature, so I pray you to forgive me.” As he continued to humble himself and offer flattering words, Kamei Sama’s heart was gradually softened, and he abandoned his intention of killing him. Thus, by the cleverness of his councillor, Kamei Sama and his entire house were saved from ruin.

Shortly after this, Takumi no Kami, who had sent no gift, arrived at the castle. Kôtsuké no Suké ridiculed him even more than before, provoking him with sneers and hidden insults; but Takumi no Kami pretended to ignore all this and submitted himself patiently to Kôtsuké no Suké’s orders.

This conduct, far from having a good effect, only made Kôtsuké no Suké despise him even more, until at last he said haughtily, “Here, my Lord of Takumi, the ribbon of my sock has come untied; be so good as to tie it for me.”

Takumi no Kami, although burning with rage at the insult, still thought that as he was on duty he was bound to obey, and he tied up the ribbon of the sock. Then Kôtsuké no Suké, turning from him, petulantly exclaimed: “Why, how clumsy you are! You cannot so much as tie up the ribbon of a sock properly! Anyone can see that you are a boor from the country and know nothing of the manners of Yedo.” And with a scornful laugh, he moved toward an inner room.

But the patience of Takumi no Kami was exhausted; this last insult was more than he could bear.

“Stop a moment, my lord,” he cried.

“Well, what is it?” replied the other. And, as he turned around, Takumi no Kami drew his dirk <note>a short dagger</note> and aimed a blow at his head; but because Kôtsuké no Suké was protected by the Court cap he wore, the wound was only a scratch, and so he ran away. Takumi no Kami, pursuing him, tried a second time to cut him down, but, missing his aim, struck his dirk into a pillar. At this moment an officer named Kajikawa Yosobei, seeing the fight, rushed up and, holding back the infuriated noble, gave Kôtsuké no Suké time to make his escape.

Then there arose a great uproar and confusion, and Takumi no Kami was arrested, disarmed, and confined in one of the apartments of the palace under the care of the censors <note>officials who oversaw the conduct of the samurai and lords</note>. A council was held, and the prisoner was given over to the custody of a <term>daimio</term> called Tamura Ukiyô no Daibu, who kept him in close confinement in his own house, to the great grief of his wife and his retainers. When the deliberations of the council were completed, it was decided that, as he had committed an outrage and attacked another man within the precincts of the palace, he must perform *hara kiri*—that is, commit suicide by disemboweling; his goods were to be confiscated, and his family ruined. Such was the law. So Takumi no Kami performed *hara kiri*, his castle of Akô was confiscated, and his retainers, having become *Rônins*, some of them took service with other <term>daimios</term>, and others became merchants.

# THE FORTY-SEVEN RÔNINS.

Now among these retainers was his principal councillor, a man called Oishi Kuranosuké, who, with forty-six other faithful dependants, formed a league to avenge their master’s death by killing Kôtsuké no Suké. This Oishi Kuranosuké was absent at the castle of Akô at the time of the conflict; had he been with his prince, it would never have occurred. Being a wise man, he would not have failed to win over Kôtsuké no Suké by sending him suitable presents; meanwhile, the councillor who was in attendance on the prince at Yedo was a fool who neglected this precaution, and so caused the death of his master and the ruin of his house.

So Oishi Kuranosuké and his forty-six companions began to lay their plans of vengeance against Kôtsuké no Suké. But the latter was so well guarded by a body of men lent to him by a <term>daimio</term> called Uyésugi Sama, whose daughter he had married, that they saw the only way of achieving their goal would be to throw their enemy off his guard. With this object, they separated and disguised themselves, some as carpenters or craftsmen, others as merchants. Their chief, Kuranosuké, went to Kiôto and built a house in the quarter called Yamashina, where he began frequenting houses of the worst reputation and gave himself up to drunkenness and debauchery, as if nothing were further from his mind than revenge.

Kôtsuké no Suké, in the meantime, suspecting that Takumi no Kami’s former retainers would be scheming against his life, secretly sent spies to Kiôto and ordered a faithful account to be kept of everything Kuranosuké did. The latter, however, determined to thoroughly delude the enemy into a false sense of security, continued leading a dissolute life with prostitutes and drunkards. One day, as he was returning home drunk from some seedy tavern, he fell down in the street and went to sleep, and all the passers-by mocked him. It happened that a man from Satsuma saw this and said:

One band, led by Oishi Kuranosuké, was to attack the front gate, and the other, under his son Oishi Chikara, was to attack the back gate of Kôtsuké no Suké's house; but as Chikara was only sixteen years of age, Yoshida Chiuzayémon was appointed to act as his guardian. Furthermore, it was arranged that a drum, beaten at the order of Kuranosuké, should be the signal for the simultaneous attack; and that if anyone killed Kôtsuké no Suké and cut off his head, he should blow a shrill whistle as a signal to his comrades, who would hurry to the spot and, having identified the head, carry it off to the temple called Sengakuji and lay it as an offering before the tomb of their dead lord. Then they must report their deed to the Government and await the sentence of death which would surely be passed upon them. To this the <term>Rônins</term> one and all pledged themselves. Midnight was fixed as the hour, and the forty-seven comrades, having made everything ready for the attack, shared a final farewell feast together, for the next day they must die. Then Oishi Kuranosuké addressed the band and said:

> “Tonight we shall attack our enemy in his palace; his retainers will certainly resist us, and we shall be obliged to kill them. But to kill old men, women, and children is a pitiful thing; therefore, I pray each of you to take great care lest you kill a single helpless person.”

His comrades all applauded this speech, and so they remained, waiting for the hour of midnight to arrive.

When the appointed hour came, the <term>Rônins</term> set forth. The wind howled furiously, and the driving snow beat in their faces; but they cared little for wind or snow as they hurried on their road, eager for revenge. At last they reached Kôtsuké no Suké's house and divided themselves into two bands; and Chikara, with twenty-three men, went

At last Kuranosuké, seeing that it was useless to urge him to die the death of a nobleman, forced him down and cut off his head with the same dagger with which Asano Takumi no Kami had killed himself. Then the forty-seven comrades, elated at having accomplished their goal, placed the head in a bucket and prepared to depart; but before leaving the house, they carefully extinguished all the lights and fires in the place, lest a fire should break out by accident and the neighbors suffer.

As they were on their way to Takanawa, the suburb where the temple called Sengakuji stands, day broke; and the people flocked out to see the forty-seven men, who, with their clothes and weapons all blood-stained, presented a terrible appearance; and everyone praised them, marvelling at their valor and faithfulness. But they expected at any moment that Kôtsuké no Suké’s father-in-law would attack them and carry off the head, and they prepared to die bravely, sword in hand. However, they reached Takanawa safely, for Matsudaira Aki no Kami—one of the eighteen chief <term>daimyos</term> of Japan, whose house Asano Takumi no Kami’s family was a branch of—had been highly pleased when he heard of the previous night’s work, and he had prepared to assist the Rônins in case they were attacked. So Kôtsuké no Suké’s father-in-law did not dare to pursue them.

At last, they were summoned to the Supreme Court, where the governors of <term>Yedo</term> and the public censors had assembled; and the sentence passed upon them was as follows: “Whereas, respecting neither the dignity of the city nor fearing the Government, and having banded yourselves together to slay your enemy, you violently broke into the house of <term>Kira Kotsuke no Suke</term> by night and murdered him, the sentence of the Court is that, for this audacious conduct, you perform *hara-kiri*.” When the sentence had been read, the forty-seven <term>Ronin</term> were divided into four parties and handed over to the safe keeping of four different <term>daimios</term>; and sheriffs were sent to the palaces of those <term>daimios</term>, in whose presence the <term>Ronin</term> were made to perform *hara-kiri*. And when the fame of this spread abroad, the people flocked to pray at the graves of these faithful men.

still remains to be seen along with those of the forty-seven comrades. This is the end of the story of the forty-seven <term>Ronin</term>.

It is a terrible picture of fierce heroism that is impossible not to admire. In the Japanese mind, this feeling of admiration is pure, and therefore the forty-seven <term>Ronin</term> receive almost divine honors. Devout hands still decorate their graves with green branches and burn incense upon them; the clothes and arms they wore are carefully preserved in a fireproof storehouse attached to the temple and displayed yearly to admiring crowds, who view them with perhaps only slightly less veneration than that given to the relics of <note>Aix-la-Chapelle is the French name for the city of Aachen in Germany, known for its religious relics.</note> Aix-la-Chapelle or <note>Trèves is the French name for the city of Trier, Germany, also famous for its cathedral relics.</note> Trèves. Once every sixty years, the monks of <term>Sengakuji</term> reap quite a harvest for the benefit of their temple by holding a commemorative fair or festival, which the people flock to for nearly two months.

A silver key once allowed me a private inspection of the relics. My friend and I were ushered into a back room of the spacious temple, overlooking one of those marvelous miniature gardens—skillfully decorated with rock gardens and dwarf trees—in which the Japanese delight. One by one, the chief priest brought out and opened boxes that were carefully labeled and indexed, containing the precious articles. What a curious collection of old rags and scraps of metal and wood! Handmade chain armor, composed of leather padding secured together by pieces of iron, bears witness to the secrecy with which the <term>Ronin</term> prepared for the fight. Buying armor would have attracted attention, so they made it with their own hands. There were old, moth-eaten surcoats, bits of helmets, three flutes, and a writing box that must have been very old even at the time of the tragedy and is now falling to pieces. There were tattered trousers made of what was once rich silk brocade, now completely unraveled and frayed; scraps of leather, part of an old gauntlet, crests and badges, bits of sword handles, spearheads, and dirks—the latter all red with rust, but with certain patches more deeply stained

The third manuscript is a paper which the forty-seven <term>Rônins</term> laid upon the tomb of their master, along with the head of Kira Kôtsuké no Suké:—

> “The 15th year of Genroku, the 12th month, and 15th day. We reverently announce this to the honored spirit of our late master. On the 14th day of the third month of last year, our honored master chose to attack Kira Kôtsuké no Suké, for reasons unknown to us. Our honored master took his own life, but Kira Kôtsuké no Suké lived. Although we fear that, following the decree issued by the Government, this plot of ours will be displeasing to our honored master, still we, who have eaten your food, could not without blushing repeat the verse, ‘You shall not live under the same heaven nor walk the same earth as the enemy of your father or lord,’ nor could we have dared to leave hell and present ourselves before you in paradise unless we had completed the vengeance which you began. Every day we waited seemed as long as three years to us. Truly, we have walked through the snow for one day, no, for two days, and have eaten only once. The old and frail, the sick and ailing, have come forward gladly to lay down their lives. People might laugh at us, as if we were grasshoppers trusting in the strength of our own arms, and thus bring shame to our honored lord; but we could not stop our act of vengeance. Having consulted together last night, we have escorted Lord Kôtsuké no Suké here to your tomb. This dagger, <note>The dagger with which Asano Takumi no Kami committed ritual suicide, and with which Oishi Kuranosuké cut off Kôtsuké no Suké’s head.</note> which our honored lord highly valued last year and entrusted to our care, we now bring back. If your noble spirit is now present before this tomb, we pray that you, as a sign, will take the dagger and, striking the head of your enemy with it a second time, dispel your hatred forever. This is the respectful statement of forty-seven men.”

# THE FORTY-SEVEN RÔNINS.

Page 113 contains an interesting paragraph summarizing the sage’s doctrine on the subject of revenge.

> “In the second book of the ‘Le Ke,’ there is the following passage:—‘A man must not live under the same heaven as the killer of his father; against the killer of his brother, a man must never have to go home to fetch a weapon; a man may not live in the same state as the killer of his friend.’ The <term>*lex talionis*</term> is laid down here in its fullest extent. The ‘Chow Le’ tells us of a provision made against the evil consequences of the principle by the appointment of a minister called ‘The Reconciler.’ This provision is far inferior to the cities of refuge that were set apart by Moses for a killer to flee to from the fury of the avenger. However, it existed as it was, and it is remarkable that Confucius, when consulted on the subject, took no notice of it, but instead affirmed the duty of blood-revenge in the strongest and most unrestricted terms. His disciple, Tsze Hea, asked him, ‘What course should be followed regarding the murder of a father or mother?’ He replied, ‘The son must sleep upon a grass mat with his shield for his pillow; he must refuse to hold office; he must not live under the same heaven as the killer. When he meets him in the marketplace or the court, he must have his weapon ready to strike him.’ ‘And what is the course for the murder of a brother?’ ‘The surviving brother must not hold office in the same state as the killer; yet, if he goes on his prince's service to the state where the killer is, even if he meets him, he must not fight with him.’ ‘And what is the course for the murder of an uncle or cousin?’ ‘In this case, the nephew or cousin is not the primary person. If the primary person, on whom the revenge falls, can take it, the nephew or cousin only has to stand behind with his weapon in his hand and support him.’”

I will add one anecdote to show the sanctity attached to the graves of the Forty-seven. In September 1868, a certain man came to pray before the grave of Oishi Chikara. After finishing his prayers, he deliberately performed <term>*hara kiri*</term>,<gloss>1</gloss> and, as the belly wound was not fatal, he killed himself by cutting his throat. # THE LOVES OF GOMPACHI AND KOMURASAKI.

Within about two miles of Yedo, and yet well away from the toil and noise of the great city, stands the village of Meguro. Once past the outskirts of the town, the road leading there is bordered on either side by woodlands rich in an endless variety of foliage, broken at intervals by the long, low line of villages and hamlets. As we draw near to Meguro, the scenery becomes more and more rustic and increases in beauty. Deep shady lanes, bordered by hedgerows as lush as any in England, lead down to a valley of rice fields bright with the emerald green of the young crops. To the right and to the left rise hills of fantastic shapes, crowned with an abundance of <term>Cryptomerias</term>, Scotch firs, and other cone-bearing trees, and fringed with thickets of feathery bamboos, bending their stems gracefully to the light summer breeze. Wherever there is a spot shadier and more pleasant to look upon than the rest, one can see the red gate of a shrine which the simple piety of the country folk has raised to Inari Sama, the patron god of farming, or to some other guardian deity of the place. At the eastern end of the valley, a strip of blue sea bounds the horizon; to the west are the distant mountains. In the foreground, in front of a snug-looking farmhouse with its roof of velvety-brown thatch, a group of sturdy children, sun-tanned and completely naked, are frolicking in the wildest play, all ignoring the scolding voice of the withered old grandmother who sits spinning and minding the house, while her son and his wife are away toiling at outdoor labor. Close at our feet runs a stream of pure water, in which a group of countrymen are

Not the least beauty of the scene consists in the wondrous clearness of an atmosphere so transparent that the most distant outlines are scarcely dimmed, while the details of the nearer ground stand out in sharp, bold relief, now lit by the rays of a vertical sun, now darkened under the flying shadows thrown by the fleecy clouds which sail across the sky. Under such a heaven, what painter could depict the lights and shades which flit over the woods, the pride of Japan, whether in late autumn, when the russets and yellows of our own trees are mixed with the deep crimson glow of the maples, or in springtime, when plum and cherry trees and wild camellias—giants, fifty feet high—are in full blossom?

All that we see is enchanting, but there is a strange stillness in the groves; rarely does the song of a bird break the silence; indeed, I know but one warbler whose note has any music in it, the *uguisu*, by some enthusiasts called the Japanese nightingale—at best, a king in the kingdom of the blind. The scarcity of animal life of all descriptions, man and mosquitoes alone excepted, is a standing wonder to the traveler; the sportsman must toil many a weary mile to get a shot at boar, or deer, or pheasant; and the plow of the farmer and the trap of the poacher, who works in and out of season, threaten to exterminate all wild creatures; unless, indeed, the Government should, as they threatened in the spring of 1869, put in force some adaptation of European game laws. But they are lukewarm in the matter; a little hawking on a duck pond satisfies the cravings of the modern Japanese sportsman, who knows that, game laws or no game laws, the wildfowl will never fail in winter; and the days are long past when my Lord the Shogun used to ride forth with a mighty company to the wild places about Mount Fuji, there camping out and hunting the boar, the deer, and the wolf, believing that in so doing he was fostering a manly and military spirit in the land.

It would seem natural, while writing of the Japanese countryside, to say a few words about the peasantry, their relationship to the lord of the soil, and their government. But I must reserve these for another place. For now, our dealings are with the pretty village of Meguro.

At the bottom of a little lane, close to the entrance of the village, stands an old shrine of the Shinto (the form of hero worship which existed in Japan before the introduction of Confucianism or of Buddhism), surrounded by tall *Cryptomerias*. The trees around a Shinto shrine are specifically under the protection of the god to whom the altar is dedicated; and, in connection with them, there is a kind of magic still respected by the superstitious, which recalls the wax dolls through which sorcerers of the Middle Ages in Europe—and indeed those of ancient Greece, as *Theocritus* tells us—claimed to kill the enemies of their clients. When the rest of the world is at rest at two in the morning—the hour symbolized by the ox—the woman rises. She puts on a white robe and high sandals or wooden clogs. Her headdress is a metal tripod into which three lit candles are placed; she hangs a mirror around her neck so that it rests upon her chest. In her left hand, she carries a small straw figure, an image of the lover who has abandoned her, and in her right, she grasps a hammer and nails, which she uses to fasten the figure to one of the sacred trees surrounding the shrine. There, she prays for the death of the traitor, vowing that if her prayer is answered, she will personally remove the nails that now offend the god by wounding the sacred tree. She returns to the shrine night after night, driving in two or more nails each time, believing that every nail will shorten her lover’s life; for the god, to save his tree, will surely strike him dead.

Meguro is one of many places around Yedo to which citizens flock for social or religious reasons—or both. Consequently, right alongside the old shrines and temples, you will find many charming tea-houses. Standing at their competing doors, Misses Sugar, Wave of the Sea, Flower, Seashore, and Chrysanthemum offer pressing invitations for you to enter and rest. These young women might not be considered beautiful by our standards, but the charm of Japanese women lies in their manners and dainty ways. The tea-house girl, acting as a professional lure, is an expert in the art of flirting—*all in good honor*, it should be remembered. She is not to be confused with the "frail beauties" of the Yoshiwara, nor even with her counterparts near the ports open to foreigners and their corrupting influence. For, strange as it seems, our contact throughout the East has a negative effect on the native people.

In the olden days, there was a priest called Jikaku, who at the age of forty—it being the autumn of the tenth year of the period called Tencho (A.D. 833)—was suffering from a disease of the eyes that had attacked him three years before. In order to be healed from this disease, he carved a figure of Yakushi Niurai, to which he used to offer his prayers. Five years later he went to China, taking with him the figure as his patron saint, and at a place called Kairetsu, it protected him from robbers, wild beasts, and other calamities. There he passed his time studying the sacred laws, both hidden and revealed, and after nine years set sail to return to Japan. When he was on the open sea, a storm arose, and a great fish attacked and tried to swamp the ship, so that the rudder and mast were broken; and as the nearest shore was a land inhabited by devils, to retreat or to advance was equally dangerous. Then the holy man prayed to the patron saint whose image he carried, and as he prayed, behold, the true Yakushi Niurai appeared in the center of the ship and said to him:

> "Truly, you have traveled far so that the sacred laws might be revealed for the salvation of many people; now, therefore, take my image, which you carry in your chest, and cast it into the sea, so that the wind may die down, and that you may be delivered from this land of devils."

The commands of the saints must be obeyed, so with tears in his eyes, the priest threw into the sea the sacred image which he loved. Then the wind died down, and the waves were stilled, and the ship went on her course as though she were being drawn by unseen hands until she reached a safe haven. In the tenth month of the same year, the priest again set sail, trusting in the power of his patron saint, and reached the harbor of Tsukushi without mishap. At this time there was an epidemic of smallpox in the village, so that men fell down and died in the street, and the holy man prayed to Fudô Sama that the plague might be stayed. Then the god appeared to him, and said:

“The saint Yakushi Niurai of the Cuttlefish, whose image you carry, desires to have his place in this village, and he will heal this plague. You shall, therefore, raise a temple to him here so that not only this smallpox, but other diseases for future generations, may be cured by his power.”

Hearing this, the priest shed tears of gratitude, and having chosen a piece of fine wood, carved a large figure of his patron saint of the cuttlefish, and placed the smaller image inside of the larger, and laid it in this temple, to which people still flock so that they may be healed of their diseases. Such is the story of the miracle, translated from a small, poorly printed pamphlet sold by the priests of the temple, all the decorations of which—even to a bronze lantern in the middle of the yard—are in the form of a cuttlefish, the sacred emblem of the place.

Jets of pure water springing from the rock are discharged through spouts carved in the shape of dragons into a stone basin enclosed by railings, within which a sign states that “no woman may enter.” If you are lucky, you may cool yourself by watching a devotee, naked except for his loincloth, performing the ceremony called *Suigiyô*; that is to say, praying under the waterfall so that his soul may be purified through his body. In winter it takes a great deal of courage to go through this penance, yet I have seen a penitent submit to it for more than a quarter of an hour on a bitterly cold day in January. In summer, on the other hand, the religious exercise called *Hiyakudo*, or “the hundred times,” which can also be seen here clearly, is a significant test of patience. It consists of walking back and forth a hundred times between two points within the sacred grounds, repeating a prayer each time. The count is kept either on the fingers or by placing a length of twisted straw each time the goal is reached. At this temple, the area designated for the ceremony is between a grotesque bronze figure of Tengu Sama (“the Dog of Heaven”)—the terror of children, a most hideous monster with a gigantic nose, which people believe is beneficial to rub with a finger and then touch to one’s own nose—and a large brown box inscribed with the characters *Hiyaku Do* in high relief, which can usually be seen full of straw tallies. It is no easy task to be a good Buddhist, for the gods are not easily appeased. Prayer and fasting, physical self-denial, and abstinence from wine, women, and favorite dishes are the only paths to advancement in office, prosperity in trade, recovery from sickness, or a happy marriage to a beloved maiden. Nor will faith alone be effective without action. A votive tablet of value equal to the favor requested, or a sum of money for the repairs of the shrine or temple, is necessary to win the favor of the gods. Poorer people will cut off the topknot (queue) of their hair and offer that up; and at Horinouchi, a very famous temple about eight or nine miles from Yedo, there is a rope about two and a half inches in diameter, and about six fathoms

Because the taking of life is displeasing to Buddha, outside many of the temples, old women and children earn a living by selling sparrows, small eels, carp, and tortoises, which the worshipper sets free in honor of the deity. Within the deity's territory, cocks, hens, and doves, tame and unharmed, perch on every ledge, frieze, buttress, and advantageous corner.

But of all the marvelous customs that I know of in connection with Japanese religious exercises, none appears to me so strange as that of spitting at the images of the gods, more especially at the statues of the <term>Ni-ô</term>, the two huge red or red and green statues which, like Gog and Magog, emblems of strength, stand as guardians of the chief Buddhist temples. The figures are protected by a network of iron wire, through which the devotees, praying all the while, spit pieces of paper which they had chewed into a pulp. If the pellet sticks to the statue, the omen is favorable; if it falls, the prayer is not accepted. The inside of the great bell at the <term>Tycoon</term>’s burial ground, and almost every holy statue throughout the country, are all covered with these spittings from pious mouths.<note>It will be readily understood that the customs and ceremonies to which I have alluded belong only to the gross superstitions with which ignorance has overlaid that pure Buddhism of which Professor Max Müller has pointed out the very real beauties.</note>

Through all this discourse about temples and tea-houses, I am gradually approaching the goal of our pilgrimage—two old stones, crumbling away in a rank, overgrown graveyard nearby, an ancient burial ground, forgotten by all except those who love to dig out the tales of the past. Setting it upright again, let us preserve it from decay for future generations, and let us write the following verse upon it: ‘These two birds, as beautiful as cherry blossoms, perished before their time, like flowers broken down by the wind before they have borne seed.’”

Under the first stone is the dust of Gompachi, a robber and murderer, mixed with that of his true love Komurasaki, who lies buried with him. Her sorrows and loyalty have hallowed the place, and devout people still come to burn incense and lay flowers before the grave. How she loved him even in death may be seen from the following old story.

About two hundred and thirty years ago, there lived in the service of a <term>daimio</term> of the province of Inaba a young man called Shirai Gompachi. When he was only sixteen years of age, he had already won a name for his personal beauty and courage, and for his skill in the use of arms. Now it happened that one day a dog belonging to him fought with another dog belonging to a fellow-clansman. The two masters, both being passionate youths, argued over whose dog had won the fight; they quarreled and came to blows, and Gompachi killed his opponent. As a consequence of this, he was forced to flee from his province and make his escape to <term>Yedo</term>.

And so Gompachi set out on his travels.

One night, weary and footsore, he entered what appeared to him to be a roadside inn, ordered some refreshment, and went to bed, little thinking of the danger that threatened him; for as luck would have it, this inn turned out to be the meeting place of a gang of robbers, into whose clutches he had thus unwittingly fallen. To be sure, Gompachi's purse was only poorly supplied, but his sword and dirk were worth about three hundred ounces of silver, and upon these the robbers (of whom there were ten) had cast envious eyes, and had determined to kill the owner for their sake; but he, completely unsuspicious, slept on in imagined security.

In the middle of the night, he was startled from his deep sleep by someone stealthily opening the sliding door that led into his room, and rousing himself with an effort, he saw a beautiful young girl, fifteen years of age, who, gesturing for him not to move, came up to his bedside and said to him in a whisper:

> “Sir, the master of this house is the chief of a gang of robbers who have been plotting to murder you tonight for the sake of your clothes and your sword. As for me, I am the daughter of a rich merchant in Mikawa; last year the robbers came to our house and carried off my father's treasure and myself. I beg you, sir, take me with you, and let us flee from this dreadful place.”

She wept as she spoke, and Gompachi was at first too startled to answer; but being a youth of great courage and a skilled fencer as well, he soon recovered his presence of mind and determined to kill the robbers and deliver the girl from their hands. So he replied:

> “Since you say so, I will kill these thieves and rescue you this very night; only, when I begin the fight, run outside the house so that you may be out of harm's way, and remain in hiding until I join you.”

So she wiped away her tears and smiled again when she heard him promise that he would soon return to her. Gompachi went on his way and, in due time, approached Yedo.

But his dangers were not yet over; for late one night, arriving at a place called Suzugamori in the neighborhood of Yedo, he encountered six highwaymen. They attacked him, thinking to make short work of killing and robbing him. Undaunted, he drew his sword and dispatched two of the six; but, being weary and worn out from his long journey, he was hard-pressed, and the struggle was going poorly for him. Just then, a wardsman, who happened to pass that way riding in a sedan chair, saw the fight, jumped down from his chair, and drawing his dagger, came to the rescue. Between the two of them, they put the robbers to flight.

It turned out that this kind tradesman, who had so fortunately come to the assistance of Gompachi, was none other than Chôbei of Bandzuin, the chief of the <term>Otokodaté</term>, or Friendly Society of the wardsmen of Yedo—a man famous in the annals of the city, whose life, exploits, and adventures are recited to this day and form the subject of another tale.

When the highwaymen had disappeared, Gompachi, turning to his deliverer, said:

> “I do not know who you may be, sir, but I must thank you for rescuing me from a great danger.”

And as he proceeded to express his gratitude, Chôbei replied:

> “I am but a poor wardsman, a humble man in my way, sir; and if the robbers ran away, it was more by good luck than due to any merit of mine. But I am filled with admiration at the way you fought; you displayed a courage and a skill that were beyond your years, sir.”

<note>Japanese cities are divided into wards, and every tradesman and artisan is under the authority of the chief of the ward in which he resides. The word <term>chônin</term>, or wardsman, is generally used in contrast to the word <term>samurai</term>, which has already been explained as denoting a man belonging to the military class.</note>

Gompachi accepted the offer of his new but trusty friend with thanks; so Chôbei led him to his house, where he lodged him and hospitably entertained him for several months. Now Gompachi, being idle and having nothing to occupy him, fell into bad habits and began to lead a dissolute life, thinking of nothing but satisfying his whims and passions. He began to frequent the <term>Yoshiwara</term>, the quarter of the town set aside for tea-houses and other haunts of wild young men, where his handsome face and figure attracted attention and soon made him a great favorite with all the beauties of the neighborhood.

About this time, people began to speak loudly in praise of the charms of Komurasaki, or "<term>Little Purple</term>," a young girl who had recently come to the Yoshiwara and who outshone all her rivals in beauty and accomplishments. You saved me once—do not, I implore you, abandon me now!” As she told her piteous story, tears streamed from her eyes.

“This is indeed a sad story,” replied Gompachi, deeply moved by her account. “There must have been a remarkable run of bad luck to bring such misfortune upon your family, which I remember being so prosperous only a short while ago. However, mourn no more, for I will not desert you. It is true that I am too poor to buy your freedom from your servitude, but at any rate I will arrange things so that you shall be tormented no more. Love me, therefore, and put your trust in me.” When she heard him speak so kindly, she was comforted and wept no more; she poured out her whole heart to him and forgot her past sorrows in the great joy of meeting him again.

When it became time for them to separate, he embraced her tenderly and returned to Chôbei’s house; but he could not banish Komurasaki from his mind, and all day long he thought of her alone. And so it happened that he went daily to the Yoshiwara to see her; and if any accident delayed him, she, missing his accustomed visit, would become anxious and write to him to inquire about the cause of his absence. At last, by following this way of life, his supply of money ran short, and as he was a *rônin* without any fixed employment, he had no means of replenishing his funds. He was ashamed to show himself penniless at “The Three Sea-coasts.” It was then that an evil spirit arose within him; he went out and murdered a man, and having robbed him of his money, he carried it to the Yoshiwara.

It is an easy step from bad to worse, and the tiger that has once tasted blood is dangerous. Blinded and infatuated by his excessive love, Gompachi kept on killing and robbing, so that while his outward appearance was handsome to look upon, the heart within him was that of a hideous devil. At last, his friend Chôbei could no longer endure the sight of him and turned him out of his house. As virtue and vice eventually meet with their reward, it came to pass that Gompachi’s crimes became notorious; the Government set spies upon his track, and he was caught red-handed and arrested. Once his evil deeds had been fully proved against him, he was carried off to the execution ground at Suzugamori, the “Bell Grove,” and beheaded as a common criminal.

Now when Gompachi was dead, Chôbei’s old affection for the young man returned; being a kind and pious man, he went and claimed the body and head and buried him at Meguro, in the grounds of the temple called Boronji.

When Komurasaki heard the people at the Yoshiwara gossiping about her lover’s end, her grief was boundless. She fled secretly from “The Three Sea-coasts” and came to Meguro, where she threw herself upon the newly-made grave. For a long time she prayed and bitterly she wept over the tomb of him whom, with all his faults, she had loved so well, and

Then, drawing a dagger from her belt, she plunged it into her breast and died. When the priests of the temple saw what had happened, they wondered greatly and were astonished at the loving faithfulness of this beautiful girl. Taking compassion on her, they laid her side by side with Gompachi in one grave, and over the grave they placed a stone which remains to this day, bearing the inscription “The Tomb of the Shiyoku.” And the people of Yedo still visit the place, and they still praise the beauty of Gompachi and the filial piety and fidelity of Komurasaki.

Let us linger for a moment longer in the old graveyard. The word which I translated a few lines above as “loving faithfulness” means literally “chastity.” When Komurasaki sold herself to provide for the needs of her ruined parents, she was not, according to her beliefs, forfeiting her claim to virtue. On the contrary, she could perform no greater act of filial piety, and, far from being reproached by her people, her self-sacrifice would be worthy of all praise in their eyes. This idea has led to grave misunderstandings abroad; indeed, no phase of Japanese life has been so misrepresented as this. I have heard it stated, and seen it in print, that it is no disgrace for a respectable Japanese man to sell his daughter, that men of position and family often choose their wives from such places as “The Three Sea-coasts,” and that a young girl’s conduct up to the time of her marriage is a matter of no importance whatever. Nothing could be more unjust or more untrue. It is only the poorest people who sell their children to be waitresses, singers, or prostitutes. It does occasionally happen that the daughter of a *Samurai*, or gentleman, is found in a house of ill-repute, but such a case could only occur upon the death or total ruin of the parents, and an official investigation of the matter has proved it to be so exceptional that the presence of a young lady in such a place is an enormous attraction, her superior education and accomplishments bringing prestige to the house. As for gentlemen marry—

<summary>Following Komurasaki’s suicide at Gompachi’s grave, the author defends Japanese social customs, explaining that selling oneself into service for one's parents is viewed as a supreme act of filial piety rather than a loss of virtue. He corrects Western misconceptions by stating that such instances are rare among the upper classes and usually born of extreme desperation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of Japanese morality against foreign misconceptions, specifically addressing the social status of women in houses of ill-repute and the strict separation between virtuous society and the "quarters" of vice.</meta>

# THE LOVES OF GOMPACHI AND KOMURASAKI.

...being women of bad character, are not such things known in Europe? Do ladies of the *demi-monde* never make good marriages? *Mésalliances* (unsuitable marriages) are far rarer in Japan than with us. Certainly among the lowest class of the population, such marriages may occasionally occur, for it often happens that a woman can save a tempting dowry from her wretched earnings; but among the gentry of the country, they are unknown.

And yet a girl is not disgraced if, for her parents' sake, she sells herself to a life of misery so great that when a Japanese man enters a house of ill-repute, he is forced to leave his sword and dagger at the door for two reasons: first, to prevent brawling; and second, because it is known that some of the women inside so loathe their existence that they would end it if they could get hold of a weapon.

It is a curious fact that in all the Daimyo’s castle-towns—with the exception of some that are also seaports—open prostitution is strictly forbidden, although, if reports are true, public morality suffers rather than gains from this prohibition.

The misunderstanding that exists regarding prostitution in Japan may be explained by the fact that foreign writers—basing their judgment on the vice seen in the open ports—have not hesitated to declare Japanese women unchaste. Just as fairly might a Japanese person, writing about England, judge the wives, sisters, and daughters of these very authors by the street-walkers of Portsmouth or Plymouth. In some respects, the gulf fixed between virtue and vice in Japan is even greater than in England. The Eastern courtesan is confined to a specific quarter of the town and is distinguished by a peculiarly gaudy costume and a head-dress consisting of a forest of light tortoiseshell hairpins stuck around her head like a saint’s halo—a halo of shame that a modest woman would sooner die than wear. Vice jostling virtue in public places, virtue imitating the fashions set by vice, and buying trinkets or furniture at the sale of a courtesan's belongings—these are social phenomena that the East does not know.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of Japanese morality, specifically refuting foreign misconceptions about women's chastity by addressing the cultural context of public bathing and the social habits of the lower classes.</meta>

<page-num>42</page-num>

# TALES OF OLD JAPAN.

The common practice among the lower classes of bathing in public bathhouses without separating the sexes is another factor that has spread very false ideas abroad regarding the chastity of Japanese women. Every traveler is shocked by it, and every writer finds it a subject for a page of vivid description. Yet it is only those who are so poor—and they must be poor indeed—that they cannot afford a bath at home, who go to the public bathhouse at the end of their workday to refresh themselves before sitting down to their evening meal. Having been used to the scene since childhood, they see no indecency in it; it is a matter of course, and *honi soit qui mal y pense* (shame to him who thinks evil of it). Certainly, there is far less indecency and immorality resulting from this public bathing than from the crowded mixing together of all sexes and ages which disgraces our own lodging houses in the great cities, and the hideous shacks in which some of our laborers must pass their lives. Nor can it be said that there is more mixing of the sexes among the lowest classes in Japan than in Europe. Speaking on the subject once with a Japanese gentleman, I remarked that we consider it an act of indecency for men and women to wash together. He shrugged his shoulders as he answered, "But then Westerners have such prurient minds." Some time ago, at the open port of Yokohama, the government—out of respect for the prejudices of foreigners—forbade men and women to bathe together, and no doubt this was the first step toward ending the practice altogether. As for women bathing in tubs in the open streets of Yedo, I have read of such things in books written by foreigners; but during a residence of three and a half years, in which time I traveled through every part of the great city at all hours of the day, I never once saw such a sight. I believe myself that it can only be seen at certain hot mineral springs in remote country districts.

The best answer to the general charge of immorality which has been brought against Japanese women during their time as unmarried women lies in the fact that every man who can afford to do so keeps the young women of his family closely

...guarded in the strictest seclusion. The daughter of the poor, indeed, must work and go out in public, but no man is allowed to approach the daughter of a gentleman. She is taught that if any insult should accidentally be offered to her, the knife she carries at her belt is meant for use, and not merely as a symbol of her rank. Not long ago, a tragedy took place in the house of one of the chief nobles in Yedo. One of the Lady’s tire-women <note>Personal lady's maids responsible for a lady's clothing and hair.</note>, herself a young woman of noble birth and gifted with rare beauty, had attracted the attention of a retainer in the palace, who fell desperately in love with her. For a long time, the strict rules of decorum by which she was surrounded prevented him from declaring his passion; but at last, he managed to gain access to her presence, and so far lost his self-control that she, drawing her poniard <note>A slim dagger.</note>, stabbed him in the eye, so that he was carried off fainting and soon died. The girl’s statement that the dead man had attempted to insult her was held to be sufficient justification for her action; instead of being blamed, she was praised and highly honored for her courage and chastity. As the affair had taken place within the private walls of a powerful noble, there was no official investigation into the matter, as the palace authorities were competent to deal with it themselves. The truth of this story was guaranteed by two or three people whose word I have no reason to doubt, and who had themselves been involved in it; I can testify that it is completely consistent with Japanese ideas. Certainly, it seems more just that Lucretia should kill Tarquin than herself.

The better the Japanese people are known and understood, the more certain I am that it will be felt that a great injustice has been done to them in the sweeping attacks made upon their women. Writers agree, I believe, that their married women are, as a rule, beyond reproach. If their young women are chaste—as I argue that, by the very force of their circumstances, they cannot help but be—what becomes of all these charges of vice and immodesty? Do they not rather reflect back upon the accusers, who seem to have studied the Japanese woman only by observing the prostitutes of Yokohama?

# TALES OF OLD JAPAN.

Having said this much, I will now try to give some account of the famous Yoshiwara <note>The name Yoshiwara, which is becoming a generic term for "Flower Districts"—in English, quarters occupied by brothels—is sometimes said to come from the town of Yoshiwara in Suruga, because it was said that the women of that place provided a large proportion of the beauties of the Yedo Yoshiwara. The correct derivation is probably the one given below.</note> of Yedo, to which frequent references will be made in the course of these tales.

At the end of the sixteenth century, the courtesans of Yedo lived in three special places: these were the street called Kôjimachi, where the women who came from Kiôto lived; Kamakura Street; and a spot opposite the great bridge. In these last two places lived women brought from Suruga. Besides these, women later came from Fushimi and from Nara, who stayed scattered here and there throughout the town. This appears to have scandalized a certain reformer named Shôji Jinyémon, who, in the year 1612, submitted a petition to the Government, requesting that the women who lived in different parts of the town should be collected into one "Flower Quarter." His petition was granted in the year 1617, and he chose a place called Fukiyacho, which, because of the large amount of rushes that grew there, was named Yoshi-Wara, or the "rush-moor." Nowadays, by a play on the word *yoshi*, the name is written with two Chinese characters meaning the "good" or "lucky moor." The place was divided into four streets, called Yedo Street, Second Yedo Street, Kiôto Street, and Second Kiôto Street.

In the eighth month of the year 1655, when Yedo was beginning to increase in size and importance, the Yoshiwara, keeping its name, was moved entirely to the spot which it now occupies at the northern end of the town. And the streets in it were named after the places from which the majority of their inhabitants originally came, such as "Sakai Street," "Fushimi Street," etc.

The official Guide to the Yoshiwara for 1869 reports 153 brothels, containing 3,289 courtesans of all classes.

From the *Oiran*, or proud beauty—who, dressed in gorgeous gold and silver brocade, with a painted face, gilded lips, and teeth fashionably blackened, has all the young men of Yedo at her feet—down to the humble *Shinzo*, or white-toothed woman, who wastes her life away in the common brothels. These figures do not, however, represent the entirety of prostitution in Yedo; the <term>Yoshiwara</term> is the primary, but not the only, residence for these public women. At Fukagawa, there is another Flower District, built on the same principle as the Yoshiwara; while at Shinagawa, Shinjiku, Itabashi, Senji, and Kadzukappara, the hotels contain women who, though nominally only waitresses, are in reality prostitutes. There are also women called *Jigoku-Onna*, or hell-women, who, without being registered on the books of any brothel, live in their own houses and conduct their business in secret. On the whole, I believe the amount of prostitution in Yedo is surprisingly small, considering the vast size of the city.

There are 394 tea-houses in the Yoshiwara, which are largely used as places for private meetings, and on those occasions, they are paid not by the visitors who frequent them, but by the keepers of the brothels. It is also fashionable to host dinners and drinking parties at these houses, for which the services of *Taikomochi*, or jesters (among whom there are thirty-nine major celebrities), and of singing and dancing girls, are hired. The Guide to the Yoshiwara gives a list of fifty-five famous singing-girls, besides a host of minor stars. These women should not be confused with the courtesans. Their conduct is very closely watched by their masters, and they always go out to parties in pairs or in groups, so that they may keep an eye on one another. Doubtless, however, despite all precautions, a "shower of gold" occasionally finds its way to Danaë’s lap; and to be the favored lover of a fashionable singer or dancer is quite a point of pride for a worldly young Japanese gentleman. The fee paid to singing-girls for performing for a space of two hours is one shilling and fourpence each; for six hours the fee is quadrupled, and it is customary to give the girls a

Courtesans, singing women, and dancers are bought by contractors, either as children, when they are educated for their calling, or at a more advanced age, when their accomplishments and charms make them desirable investments. The engagement is never lifelong, for once past the flower of their youth the poor creatures would be mere burdens to their masters; a courtesan is usually bought until she reaches the age of twenty-seven, after which she becomes her own mistress. Singers remain at work longer, but even they rarely work after the age of thirty; for Japanese women, like Italians, age quickly, and have none of that intermediate stage between youth and old age, which seems to be confined to countries where there is a twilight.

Children destined to be trained as singers are usually bought when they are five or six years old, a promising child fetching from about thirty-five to fifty shillings; the purchaser undertakes the education of his charge and brings the little thing up as his own child. The parents sign a paper absolving him from all responsibility in case of sickness or accident; but they know that their child will be well treated and cared for, as the interests of the buyer are their practical guarantee. Girls of fifteen or older who are sufficiently skilled to join a company of singers fetch ten times the price paid for children; for in their case there is no risk and no expense for education.

Little children who are bought for the purposes of prostitution at the age of five or six years fetch about the same price as those bought to be singers. During their apprenticeship, they are employed to wait upon the *Oiran*, or fashionable courtesans, in the capacity of little female pages (*Kamuro*). They are mostly the children of impoverished people or orphans, whom their relatives cruelly sell rather than endure the expense and trouble of raising them. The best time to see the Yoshiwara is just after nightfall, when the lamps are lit. This is when the women—who for the last two hours have been busy painting their lips gold, their eyebrows black, and their throats and bosoms a snowy white, carefully leaving three brown Vandyke-collar points where the back of the head joins the neck, according to one of the strictest rules of Japanese cosmetic science—leave the back rooms and take their places, side by side, in a kind of long, narrow cage, the wooden bars of which open onto the public street. Here they sit for hours, gorgeous in dresses of silk with gold and silver embroidery, as speechless and motionless as wax figures, until they have attracted the attention of some of the passers-by who begin to crowd the place. In Yokohama and at the other open ports, the women of the Yoshiwara are loud in their invitations to visitors, often breaking the monotony of their own language with some blasphemous term of endearment learned from British and American sailors; but in the Flower District of Yedo, and wherever Japanese customs remain unaffected, the greatest decorum prevails. Although the form that vice takes is ugly enough, it still has the merit of being unobtrusive. The pure never need to be contaminated by contact with the impure; he who goes to the Yoshiwara goes there knowing full well what he will find, but a virtuous man may live his whole life without having this kind of vice forced upon his sight. Here again, the open ports contrast poorly with other places: Yokohama at night is as corrupt a place as the London Haymarket.

<sig>E</sig>

# KAZUMA'S REVENGE.

It is a law that he who lives by the sword shall die by the sword. In Japan, where a large armed class exists over whom there is practically little or no control, party and clan brawls, and individual quarrels ending in bloodshed and death, are daily occurrences. It has been observed that Edinburgh in the olden days—when clansmen, carousing through the streets at night, would move from heated words to deadly blows—is perhaps the best European parallel to modern Yedo or Kiôto.

It follows that of all his possessions, the Samurai values his sword most; it is his constant companion and his ally in both defense and offense. The price of a sword made by a famous maker can reach a high sum. A Japanese noble will sometimes be seen wearing a sword with a blade that, even unmounted, is worth from six hundred to a thousand riyos (roughly £200 to £300), and the mounting, rich in skillful metalwork, will be of proportionate value. These swords are handed down as heirlooms from father to son and become almost a part of the wearer's own self. Ieyasu, the founder of the last dynasty of Shoguns, wrote in his *Legacy* <note>The Legacy of Ieyasu, translated by F. Lowder. Yokohama, 1868. (Printed for private circulation.)</note>—a code of rules drawn up to guide his successors and their government advisors—"The worn sword is the living soul of the Samurai. In the case of a Samurai forgetting his sword, act as is prescribed; it must not be overlooked."

The occupation of a swordsmith is an honorable profession—

profession, whose members are men of noble birth. In a country where trade is looked down upon as degrading, it is unusual to find this single exception to the general rule. The traditions of the craft are many and fascinating. During the most critical moment of the forging of the sword, when the steel edge is being welded into the body of the iron blade, it is a custom that still prevails among old-fashioned armorers to put on the cap and robes worn by the <term>Kugé</term>, or nobles of the Mikado’s court. Closing the doors of the workshop, they labor in secrecy and freedom from interruption, the dim light adding to the mystery of the operation. Sometimes the occasion is even treated with a certain sanctity; a tasseled cord of straw, such as those hung before the shrines of the <term>Kami</term>, or native gods of Japan, is suspended between two bamboo poles in the forge, which for the time being is converted into a holy altar.

In Osaka, I lived across from one Kusano Yoshiaki, a <term>swordsmith</term>, a most intelligent and friendly gentleman who was famous throughout his neighborhood for his good and charitable deeds. His philosophy was that, having been raised in a calling that deals in life and death, he was bound, as far as it lay within him, to atone for this by seeking to relieve the suffering that is in the world; and he carried out his principle to the extent of impoverishing himself. No neighbor ever appealed to him in vain for help in caring for the sick or burying the dead. No beggar or <term>lazar</term> was ever turned from his door without receiving some mark of his generosity, whether in money or in goods. Nor was his strict honesty any less remarkable than his charity. While other smiths are in the habit of earning large sums of money by forging the marks of famous ancient makers, he was able to boast that he had never produced a weapon that bore any mark other than his own. From his father and his ancestors he inherited his trade, which, in his turn, he will hand over to his son—a hardworking, honest, and sturdy man whose hammer and anvil can be heard clanking from sunrise to sunset.

# KAZUMA'S REVENGE.
<sig>E 2</sig>

The sharp edge of the Japanese sword is famous. It is said that the best blades, in the hands of an expert swordsman, will cut through the corpses of three men stacked one on top of the other with a single blow. The Shogun’s swords were usually tested on the bodies of executed criminals; the public executioner was entrusted with this duty, and for a "nose medicine"—a bribe of two <term>bus</term> (about three shillings)—he would substitute a private individual's weapon for that of his Lord. Dogs and beggars, lying helpless by the roadside, often serve to test a ruffian's sword; but the executioner earns many fees from those who wish to see how well their blades can cut off a head.

The statesman who enacts a law forbidding the carrying of this deadly weapon will indeed have served his country well; but it will be a difficult and dangerous task to undertake. I would not give much for that man's life. The hand of every armed bully in the empire would be against him. One day, as we were talking over this and other related subjects, a friend of mine—a man of progressive and liberal views—wrote down his opinion, in the Japanese style, in a verse of poetry which ran as follows:

> "I wish that all the swords and daggers in the country could be collected in one place and melted down, and that, from the metal so produced, one huge sword might be forged, which, as the only blade left, should be the sword worn by Great Japan."

The following history is, in more ways than one, a "Tale of a Sword."

About two hundred and fifty years ago, Ikéda Kunaishôyu was the Lord of the Province of Inaba. Among his retainers were two gentlemen, named Watanabé Yukiyé and Kawai Matazayémon, who were bound together by strong ties of friendship and frequently visited each other's houses. One day Yukiyé was sitting and talking with Matazayémon in the latter's house when, suddenly, a sword lying in the raised part of the room caught his eye. As he saw it, he started and said:

> "Please tell me, how did you come by that sword?"
