"Well, as you know, when my Lord Ikeda followed my Lord Tokugawa Iyéyasu to fight at Nagakudé, my father went in his train; and it was at the battle of Nagakudé that he picked up this sword."

"My father went as well and was killed in the fight. This sword, which had been an heirloom in our family for many generations, was lost at that time. As it is of great value in my eyes, I do wish that, if you do not place any special importance on it, you would have the great kindness to return it to me."

"That is a very simple matter, and no more than what one friend should do for another. Please, take it."

Upon this, Yukiyé gratefully took the sword, and having carried it home, he put it carefully away.

At the beginning of the following year, Matazayémon fell ill and died. Yukiyé, mourning bitterly for the loss of his good friend and anxious to repay the favor which he had received regarding his father's sword, performed many acts of kindness for the dead man's son—a young man twenty-two years of age named Matagorô.

Now, this Matagorô was a dishonorable scoundrel who begrudged the sword that his father had given to Yukiyé. He complained publicly and often that Yukiyé had never made any present in return; in this way, Yukiyé gained a bad reputation in the Lord's palace as a stingy and ungenerous man.

But Yukiyé had a son named Kazuma, a youth sixteen years of age, who served as one of the Prince's pages of honor. One evening, as he and one of his fellow pages were talking together, the latter said—

"Matagorô is telling everyone that your father accepted a handsome sword from him and never gave him any present in return, and people are beginning to gossip about it."

"Indeed," replied the other, "my father received that sword from Matagorô's father as a mark of friendship and goodwill. Considering that it would be an insult to send a gift of money in return, he thought to repay the favor by acts of kindness toward Matagorô. I suppose it is money he wants."

# KAZUMA'S REVENGE.

When Kazuma’s service was over, he returned home and went to his father’s room to tell him about the rumors being spread in the palace, and he begged him to send a generous gift of money to Matagorô. Yukiyé reflected for a while and said—

“You are too young to understand the proper line of conduct in such matters. Matagorô’s father and I were very close friends; so, seeing that he had willingly given me back my ancestral sword, I rendered important services to Matagorô after his father's death, intending to repay his kindness. It would be easy to settle the matter by sending a gift of money, but I would rather take the sword and return it than be under an obligation to this petty person, who does not know the laws that govern the behavior and dealings of men of noble birth.”

So Yukiyé, in his anger, took the sword to Matagorô’s house and said to him—

“I have come to your house tonight for no other purpose than to return the sword which your father gave me;” and with this, he placed the sword before Matagorô.

“Indeed,” replied the other, “I hope that you will not offend me by returning a gift which my father gave you.”

“Among men of noble birth,” said Yukiyé, laughing scornfully, “it is the custom to repay gifts, first with kindness and later with a suitable gift offered with a generous heart. But it is no use talking to someone like you, who is ignorant of the basic principles of good manners; so I have the honor of returning the sword to you.”

As Yukiyé continued to bitterly rebuke Matagorô, the latter grew very angry and, being a thug, would have killed Yukiyé on the spot. However, Yukiyé—old as he was—was a skilled swordsman, so Matagorô, like a coward, decided to wait until he could attack him by surprise. Suspecting no treachery, Yukiyé started to return home, and Matagorô, under the pretense of escorting him to the door, came behind him with his sword drawn and slashed him in the shoulder. The older man turned around, drew his weapon, and defended himself;

“I will follow you. Go and seek out Lord Abé Shirogorô, a chief among the Hatamotos,¹ who was my foster child. You should flee to him for protection and stay in hiding.”

So the old woman persuaded her son to escape and sent him to Shirogorô’s palace.

It happened that at this time, the Hatamotos had formed a league against the powerful Daimios; and Abé Shirogorô, along with two other noblemen named Kondô Noborinosuké and Midzuno Jiurozayémon, was at the head of the league. As a result, his forces were often joined by wicked men who had no way of making a living. He received them and treated them kindly without asking any questions about their pasts. Therefore, when the son of his own foster mother applied to him for asylum, he even more willingly extended his patronage to him and guaranteed his safety. So he called a meeting of the principal Hatamotos and introduced Matagorô to them, saying—

“This man is a retainer of Ikéda Kunaishôyu. Because he hated a man named Watanabé Yukiyé, he has killed him and fled to me for protection. This man’s

When the affair was reported to the Prince, he was very angry and ordered that the old woman should remain bound and be cast into prison until her son's whereabouts were discovered. Then Kazuma buried his father’s body with great ceremony, and the widow and the orphan mourned their loss.

When Danyémon saw that he had not only been cheated into surrendering the old woman, but was being made a laughingstock into the bargain, he flew into a great rage and thought to break into the house and seize Matagorô and his mother by force; but, looking into the courtyard, he saw that it was filled with Hatamotos, carrying guns and drawn swords. Not wishing then to die fighting a hopeless battle, and at the same time feeling that, after having been so cheated, he would be put to shame before his lord, Sasawo Danyémon went to the burial place of his ancestors and disemboweled himself in front of their graves.

When the Prince heard how his messenger had been treated, he was indignant. Summoning his councilors, he resolved—although he was suffering from illness—to collect his retainers and attack Abé Shirogorô. When the matter became publicly known, the other chief Daimios took up the cause and determined that the Hatamotos must be punished for their insolence. On their side, the Hatamotos put forth all their efforts to resist the Daimios. So Yedo became disturbed, and the riotous state of the city caused great anxiety to the Government, who consulted together on how they might restore peace. Since the Hatamotos were directly under the orders of the Shogun, it was not a difficult matter to suppress them; the hard question to solve was how to restrain the great Daimios. However, one of the Gorôjiu, <note>The first Council of the Shogun’s ministers; literally, “assembly of imperial elders.”</note> named Matsudaira Idzu no Kami, a man of great intelligence, devised a plan by which he might achieve this end.

Tsusen agreed to undertake the deed; and on the following day, when he went to see Kunaishôyu, he carried poisoned drugs with him. He drank half the medicine himself <note>A physician attending a person of high rank always has to drink half the potion he prescribes to prove his good faith.</note>, and thus put the Prince off his guard, so that he swallowed the remainder fearlessly. Tsusen, seeing this, hurried away, and as he was carried home in his litter, the death-agony seized him; he died, vomiting blood.

My Lord Kunaishôyu died in the same way in great torture, and in the confusion attending his death and funeral ceremonies, the impending struggle with the Hatamotos was delayed.

In the meanwhile, the Gorôjiu Idzu no Kami summoned the three leaders of the Hatamotos and addressed them as follows:

> “The secret plottings and treasonable, turbulent conduct of you three men, so unbecoming of your position as Hatamotos, have enraged my lord the Shogun to such a degree that he has been pleased to order that you be imprisoned in a temple, and that your inheritance be given over to your next heirs.”

Accordingly, after having been severely admonished, the three Hatamotos were confined in a temple called Kanyeiji; and the remaining Hatamotos, scared by this example, dispersed in peace. As for the great Daimios, because the Hatamotos were all dispersed after the death of my Lord Kunaishôyu, there was no enemy left for them to fight with; so the tumult was quelled, and peace was restored.

Thus it happened that Matagorô lost his patron; so, taking his mother with him, he went and placed himself under the protection of an old man named Sakurai Jiuzayémon. This old man was a famous teacher of lance exercise and enjoyed both wealth and honor; he took in Matagorô, and having engaged thirty Ronins as a guard—all resolute fellows and well-skilled in the arts of war—they all fled together to a distant place called Sagara.

All this time, Watanabé Kazuma had been brooding over his father’s death and thinking how he should be revenged upon the murderer; so when my Lord Kunaishôyu suddenly died, he went to the young Prince who succeeded him and obtained leave of absence to go and seek out his father’s enemy. Now, Kazuma’s elder sister was married to a man named Araki Matayémon, who at that time was famous as the premier swordsman in Japan. The shopkeeper answered that he was the attendant of a party of thirty-six gentlemen who were staying at a certain inn. Then Matayémon, having found out all that he wanted to know, went home and told Kazuma, who was delighted at the prospect of carrying out his revenge the next day. > “Many thanks to you, sir. I will go and support Kazuma.”

# KAZUMA'S REVENGE.

...weakened by his wounds, and blinded by the blood which was streaming into his eyes from a cut on his forehead, had given himself up for lost when Matayémon came and cried—

“Be of good cheer, Magohachi; it is I, Matayémon, who have come to the rescue. You are badly hurt; get out of harm’s way, and rest yourself.”

Then Magohachi, who until then had been sustained by his anxiety for Kazuma’s safety, gave way and fell, fainting from loss of blood; and Matayémon defeated and killed Gentan; and even then, although he had received two wounds, he was not exhausted, but drew near to Kazuma and said—

“Courage, Kazuma! The Rônins are all killed, and there now remains only Matagorô, your father’s murderer. Fight and win!”

The youth, thus encouraged, redoubled his efforts; but Matagorô, losing heart, quailed and fell. So Kazuma’s vengeance was fulfilled, and the desire of his heart was accomplished.

The two faithful retainers, who had died in their loyalty, were buried with great ceremony, and Kazuma carried the head of Matagorô and piously laid it upon his father’s tomb.

So ends the tale of Kazuma’s revenge.

***

I fear that stories in which killing and bloodshed are the principal features can hardly gain much sympathy in these peaceful days. Still, when such tales are based upon history, they are interesting to students of social phenomena. The story of Kazuma’s revenge is mixed up with events which at the present time are particularly significant: I mean the feud between the great <term>Daimios</term> and the <term>Hatamotos</term>. Those who have followed the modern history of Japan will see that the recent struggle, which has ended

...in the ruin of the <term>Tycoon’s</term> power and the abolition of his office, was the outburst of a hidden fire which had been smoldering for centuries. But the repressive power had been gradually weakened, and contact with Western powers had rendered even more repugnant a feudal system which men felt to be out of date. The revolution which has ended in the triumph of the <term>Daimios</term> over the <term>Tycoon</term> is also the triumph of the vassal over his feudal lord, and is the herald of political life to the people at large. In the time of <term>Iyéyasu</term>, the burden might have been hateful, but it had to be endured; and so it would have been to this day, had not external circumstances broken the spell. The Japanese <term>Daimio</term>, in advocating the isolation of his country, was clinging to the very yoke which he hated. Strange to say, however, there are still men who, while they embrace the new political creed, yet praise the past and look back with regret upon the day when Japan stood alone, without part or share in the great family of nations.

<note>
***Hatamoto.*** This word means "**under the flag.**" The <term>Hatamotos</term> were men who, as their name implied, rallied around the standard of the <term>Shogun</term>, or <term>Tycoon</term>, in wartime. They were eighty thousand in number. When <term>Iyéyasu</term> left the Province of <term>Mikawa</term> and became <term>Shogun</term>, the retainers whom he ennobled—and who received from him grants of land yielding revenue from ten thousand <term>kokus</term> of rice a year down to one hundred <term>kokus</term>—were called <term>Hatamoto</term>. In return for these grants of land, the <term>Hatamotos</term> had to furnish a contingent of soldiers in wartime in proportion to their revenue. For every thousand <term>kokus</term> of rice, five men were required. Those <term>Hatamotos</term> whose revenue fell short of a thousand <term>kokus</term> substituted a payment of money. In peacetime, most of the minor offices of the <term>Tycoon's</term> government were filled by <term>Hatamotos</term>, while the more important places were held by the <term>Fudai</term>, or vassal <term>Daimios</term> of the <term>Shogun</term>. Seven years ago, in imitation of the customs of foreign nations, a standing army was established; and then the <term>Hatamotos</term> had to contribute their share of men or money, whether the country was at peace or at war. KAZUMA'S REVENGE. 67

in 1868 to the rank of a simple <term>Daimio</term>, his revenue of eight million <term>kokus</term> reverted to the Government, with the exception of seven hundred thousand <term>kokus</term>. The title of <term>Hatamoto</term> no longer exists, and those who held the rank until just a few months ago are, for the most part, ruined or dispersed. Having been perhaps the proudest and most overbearing class in Japan, they have been driven to the extreme depths of poverty. Some have entered into trade, using their family heirlooms as their inventory; others are wandering through the country as <term>Rônins</term>; while a small minority have been allowed to follow the fallen fortunes of their master's family, the current head of which is known as the Prince of Tokugawa. In this way, the eighty thousand are dispersed.

The <term>koku</term> of rice, which is used to calculate all revenue, varies in value. At its cheapest, it is worth a bit more than a pound sterling, and sometimes nearly three times that amount. Since official salaries are paid in rice, a large and influential class throughout the country is interested in keeping the price of this staple food high. This explains the opposition that free trade in rice has faced, even during times of famine. This is also the reason for the frequent occurrences known as "Rice Riots."

The assessed values of the lands formerly held by the chief <term>Daimios</term>—which they have now patriotically surrendered to the <term>Mikado</term>—sound incredible. The Prince of Kaga alone had an income of more than one million two hundred thousand <term>kokus</term>. Yet these great landowners were, at least in recent times, financially troubled men. They had many thousands of people to feed and were cheated out of their dues from all sides; meanwhile, their obsession with buying foreign ships and war munitions, often at excessive prices, had plunged them deeply into debt.

# A STORY OF THE <term>OTOKODATÉ</term> OF YEDO;

### BEING THE SUPPLEMENT OF

# THE STORY OF GOMPACHI AND KOMURASAKI.

The word <term>Otokodaté</term> occurs several times in these tales; and as I cannot convey its full meaning by a simple translation, I must preserve it in the text, explaining it by the following note, taken from the Japanese of a native scholar.

The <term>Otokodaté</term> were friendly associations of brave men bound together by an obligation to stand by one another in prosperity or in woe, regardless of their own lives, and without inquiring into one another’s past. A bad man, however, who joined the <term>Otokodaté</term> had to forsake his evil ways; for their principle was to treat the oppressor as an enemy and to help the feeble as a father does his child. If they had money, they gave it to those who had none, and their charitable deeds won them the respect of all men. The head of the society was called its "Father"; if any of the others, who were his apprentices, were homeless, they lived with the Father and served him, paying him at the same time a small fee, in consideration of which, if they fell sick or fell into misfortune, he took charge of them and assisted them.

The Father of the <term>Otokodaté</term> pursued the calling of hiring out <term>coolies</term> to the <term>Daimios</term> and great personages for their journeys to and from Yedo, and in return for this, he received from them rations in rice. He had more influence with the lower classes than even the officials; and if the <term>coolies</term> had struck work or refused to accompany a <term>Daimio</term> on his journey, a word from the Father would produce as many

When Prince Tokugawa Iyémochi, the second to last of the Shoguns, left Yedo for Kiyôto, one Shimmon Tatsugorô, chief of the <term>Otokodaté</term>, undertook the management of his journey, and some three or four years ago was raised to the dignity of <term>Hatamoto</term> for many faithful services. After the battle of Fushimi and the abolition of the Shogunate, he accompanied the last of the Shoguns in his retirement.

In the old days, there were also <term>Otokodaté</term> among the <term>Hatamotos</term>; this was after the civil wars of the time of Iyéyasu, when, though the country was at peace, the minds of men were still in a state of high excitement and could not be reconciled to the dullness of a state of rest; it followed that brawls and faction fights were continually taking place among the young men of the <term>Samurai</term> class, and that those who distinguished themselves by their personal strength and valor were looked up to as captains. Leagues after the manner of those existing among the German students were formed in different quarters of the city, under various names, and used to fight for the honor of victory. When the country became more thoroughly tranquil, the custom of forming these leagues among gentlemen fell into disuse.

The past tense is used in speaking even of the <term>Otokodaté</term> of the lower classes; for although they nominally exist, they no longer have the power and importance which they enjoyed at the time to which these stories belong. They then, like the apprentices of Old London, played a considerable part in the society of the great cities, and that man was lucky, whether he was a noble <term>Samurai</term> or a simple wardsman, who could claim the Father of the <term>Otokodaté</term> for his friend.

The word, taken by itself, means a manly or plucky fellow.

“When I went in, I made many apologies; but I was beaten and kicked in the head, and treated with the greatest indignity. “Think well about what you are doing,” answered Shônosuké. “After all, we have only lost a football; and my father will not care, nor will he scold us.”

But Tsunéhei would not listen to him and was determined to wipe out the insult he had received. As they were talking, a messenger arrived from Zempachi, demanding the surrender of Tsunéhei on the grounds that he had insulted him. To this, Shônosuké replied that his father was away from home and that, in his absence, he could do nothing.

At last Shôzayémon came home; and when he heard what had happened, he was deeply grieved and at a loss for what to do. Then a second messenger arrived from Zempachi, demanding that Tsunéhei should be given up without delay. Seeing that the matter was serious, Shôzayémon called the youth to him and said—

“This Zempachi is heartless and cruel, and if you go to his house, he will surely kill you. Take, therefore, these fifty <term>riyos</term> and flee to Osaka or Kiyôto, where you may safely set up in business.”

“Sir,” answered Tsunéhei, with tears of gratitude for his lord’s kindness, “from my heart I thank you for your great goodness; but I have been insulted and trampled upon, and even if I lose my life in the attempt, I will repay Zempachi for what he has done today.”

“Well, then, since you must have your revenge, go and fight, and may success go with you! Still, as much depends upon the blade you carry, and I fear yours is likely to be only a poor weapon, I will give you a sword.” With this, he offered Tsunéhei his own.

“It seems that your master wants to speak to me. Please be so good as to take me to see him.”

“Ha! So you have come back; and now for your insolence, I mean to kill you with my own hand this day.”

“You are the insolent one!” replied Tsunéhei. “Beast, and no <term>Samurai</term>! Come, let us see which of us is the better man.”

Furiously incensed, Zempachi thrust with his spear at Tsunéhei; but he, trusting to his good sword, attacked Zempachi, who, cunning warrior that he was, could gain no advantage. At last Zempachi, losing his temper, began fighting less carefully, so that Tsunéhei found an opportunity to cut the shaft of his spear. Zempachi then drew his sword, and two of his retainers came up to assist him; but Tsunéhei killed one of them and wounded Zempachi in the forehead. The second retainer fled, frightened by the youth’s valor, and Zempachi was blinded by the blood flowing from the wound on his forehead. Then Tsunéhei said—

“To kill one who is as a blind man would be unworthy of a soldier. Wipe the blood from your eyes, Sir Zempachi, and let us fight it out fairly.”

So Zempachi, wiping away his blood, bound a handkerchief around his head and fought again desperately. But at last, the pain of his wound and the loss of blood overcame him, and Tsunéhei cut him down with a wound in the shoulder and easily dispatched him.

Then Tsunéhei went and reported the whole matter to the Governor of Yedo and was put in prison until an inquiry could be made. But the Chief Priest of Bandzuin, who had heard of the affair, went and told the governor all the bad deeds of Zempachi, and having procured Tsunéhei's pardon, took him home and employed him as a porter in the temple. So Tsunéhei changed his name to Chôbei and earned much respect in the neighborhood, both for his talents and for his many good works. If any man were in distress, he would help him, heedless of his own advantage or danger, until men came to look up to him as a father, and many youths joined him and became his apprentices. So he built a house at Hanakawado, in Asakusa, and lived there with his apprentices, whom he hired out as spearmen and footmen to the <term>Daimios</term> and <term>Hatamotos</term>, taking for himself a tenth of their earnings. But if any of them were sick or in trouble, Chôbei would nurse and support them, and provide physicians and medicine. And the fame of his goodness spread abroad until his apprentices numbered more than two thousand men and were employed in every part of the city. As for Chôbei, the more he prospered, the more he gave in charity, and all men praised his good and generous heart.

This was the time when the <term>Hatamotos</term> had formed themselves into bands of <term>Otokodaté</term>,¹ of which Midzuno Jiurozayémon, Kondô Noborinosuké, and Abé Shirogorô were the chiefs. And the leagues of the nobles despised the leagues of the wardsmen and treated them with scorn, and tried to shame Chôbei and his brave men; but the nobles' weapons recoiled upon themselves, and whenever they tried to bring contempt upon Chôbei, they themselves were brought to ridicule. So there was great hatred on both sides.

One day, when Chôbei went to amuse himself at a tea-house in the Yoshiwara, he saw a felt carpet spread in an upper room that had been decorated as if for a special occasion; he asked the master of the house which distinguished guest was expected. The landlord replied that Lord Jiurozayémon, the leader of the <term>Otokodaté</term> of the <term>Hatamotos</term>, was due there that afternoon. On hearing this, Chôbei replied that since he very much wished to meet Lord Jiurozayémon, he would lie down and await his arrival. The landlord was annoyed by this and did not know what to say; yet he did not dare to oppose Chôbei, the powerful chief of the <term>Otokodaté</term>. So Chôbei took off his clothes and lay himself down upon the carpet. After a while, Lord Jiurozayémon arrived, and going upstairs, he found a man of large build lying naked upon the carpet which had been spread for him.

“What low ruffian is this?” he shouted angrily at the landlord.

“My lord, it is Chôbei, the chief of the <term>Otokodaté</term>,” answered the man, trembling.

Jiurozayémon immediately suspected that Chôbei was doing this to insult him; so he sat down beside the sleeping man, and lighting his pipe, began to smoke. When he had finished his pipe, he emptied the burning ashes into Chôbei’s navel; but Chôbei, patiently enduring the pain, still pretended to be asleep. Ten times Jiurozayémon filled his pipe,¹ and ten times he shook out the burning ashes onto Chôbei’s navel; but he neither stirred nor spoke. Then Jiurozayémon, amazed by his endurance, shook him and woke him up, saying—

“Chôbei! Chôbei! Wake up, man.”

On the other hand, the swords of one Tôshirô Yoshimitsu are especially auspicious for the Tokugawa family for the following reason. After Iyéyasu had been defeated by Takéta Katsuyori at the battle of the Tenrin River, he took refuge in the house of a village doctor. Thinking that the dagger must be of poor quality, he took up an iron mortar used for grinding medicines and tested the blade on it; the point entered and pierced through the mortar. He was about to stab himself a second time when his followers, who had missed him and had been searching for him everywhere, arrived. Seeing their master about to kill himself, they stayed his hand and took the dagger away by force. Then they set him upon his horse and compelled him to flee to his own province of Mikawa while they kept his pursuers at bay. After this, when by the favor of Heaven Iyéyasu became Shogun, it was believed that there must certainly have been a benevolent spirit in the blade that refused to drink his blood; ever since that time, the blades of Yoshimitsu have been considered lucky in his family.

Now Banzayémon was proud of his skill and thought he had no equal in fencing; so he expected to gain an easy victory over Sanza, and promised himself the luxury of giving his adversary a beating that should fully make up for the humiliation which he had felt regarding the dispute about the sword. After this affair Sanza rose high in the favor of his lord; and Banzayémon, who was more than ever jealous of him, faked illness and stayed at home devising schemes for Sanza’s ruin.

Now it happened that the Prince, wishing to have the Muramasa blade mounted, sent for Sanza and entrusted it to his care, ordering him to employ the most skillful craftsmen in the manufacture of the scabbard, hilt, and ornaments; and Sanza, having received the blade, took it home and put it carefully away. It soon became known that Banzayémon, who had fled the province, was the thief; and the councillors made their report accordingly to the Prince. Sanza, who from the first had made up his mind that his punishment would be severe, accepted the decree without a murmur; and, having entrusted his wife and son to the care of his relatives, prepared to leave the country as a <term>Rônin</term> and search for Banzayémon.

Suddenly, a thought struck him. So they buried the body honorably in a nearby temple and wrote to Sanza’s wife and son, describing to them the manner of his death.

When Kosanza heard this generous speech, he could not hide his admiration; and the widow, prostrating herself at Umanosuké’s feet, shed tears of gratitude.

The two youths, having agreed to stand by one another, made everything ready for their journey and obtained permission from their lord to go in search of the traitor Banzayémon. They reached Yedo without incident and, taking up residence at a cheap inn, began to make their inquiries; but although they searched far and wide, they could learn no news of their enemy. When three months had passed in this way, Kosanza began to grow discouraged by their repeated failures; but Umanosuké supported and comforted him, urging him to fresh efforts. But soon a great misfortune befell them: Kosanza fell sick with ophthalmia <note>A severe inflammation or infection of the eyes.</note>, and neither the tender nursing of his friend nor the medicines and doctors upon whom Umanosuké spent all their money had any effect on the suffering boy, who soon became stone blind. Friendless and penniless, with one deprived of his sight and now a burden to the other, the two youths were left to their own resources. Then Umanosuké, reduced to the extreme of distress, was forced to lead Kosanza to Asakusa to beg by the roadside, while he himself, wandering here and there, collected what he could from the charity of those who saw his wretched condition. But all this while, he never lost sight of his revenge. He almost felt thankful for the chance that had made him a beggar, for the opportunity it gave him to search through the strange and hidden haunts of vagabond life where, in his more prosperous condition, he could never have entered. So he walked back and forth through the city, leaning on a sturdy staff in which he had hidden his sword, waiting patiently for fortune to bring him face to face with Banzayémon.

It was at this time that Shirai Gompachi—who was living under the protection of Chôbei, the Father of the <term>Otokodaté</term>—was in love with Komurasaki, the beautiful courtesan who lived at the sign of the Three Sea-shores in the Yoshiwara. He had long ago exhausted the meager supplies he possessed and was now in the habit of filling his purse through murder and robbery, so that he might have the means to pursue his wild and extravagant life.

Gompachi, little dreaming that anyone was following him, swaggered along the street until he encountered a townsman, whom he struck down and robbed. However, the loot proved to be small, so he waited for a second chance. Seeing a light moving in the distance, he hid himself in the shadow of a large rain-water tub until the bearer of the lantern came closer. 

When the man drew near, Gompachi saw that he was dressed as a traveler and wore a long dagger; so he sprang out from his hiding place and tried to kill him. But the traveler nimbly jumped to one side and proved to be a formidable opponent, for he drew his own dagger and fought stoutly for his life. However, he was no match for a swordsman as skilled as Gompachi, who, after a sharp struggle, killed him and carried off his purse, which contained two hundred <term>riyos</term>. 

Overjoyed at having found such a rich prize, Gompachi was heading for the Yoshiwara when Seibei, who had watched both murders in horror, came up and began to reproach him for his wickedness. But Gompachi was so charming and so well-liked by his comrades that he easily persuaded Seibei to keep the matter quiet and accompany him.

But who can say how Umanosuké thanked Chôbei for his help; or how, when he had returned to his own province, he cherished his gratitude in his heart, looking upon Chôbei as more than a second father?

Thus did Chôbei use his power to punish the wicked and to reward the good—giving from his abundance to the poor and helping the unfortunate, so that his name was honored far and near. It remains only to record the tragic manner of his death.

Now, since even if I succeed in killing him in his own house, my life must pay the forfeit for the deed, come tomorrow night with a burying-tub, <note>The lowest classes in Japan are buried in a squatting position, in a sort of barrel. One would have expected a person of Chôbei's condition and means to have ordered a square box. It is a mistake to suppose the cremation of the dead to be universal in Japan: only about thirty percent of the lower classes, chiefly belonging to the Monto sect of Buddhism, are cremated. The rich and noble are buried in several square coffins, one inside the other, in a sitting position; and their bodies are partially preserved from decay by filling the nose, ears, and mouth with vermilion. In the case of the very wealthy, the coffin is completely filled with vermilion. The family of the Princes of Mito, and some other nobles, bury their dead in a recumbent position.</note> and fetch my corpse from this Jiurozayémon's house."

On the following day, around noon, he prepared to go to Jiurozayémon's house, telling one of his apprentices to go before him with a complimentary gift.<sup>1</sup> Jiurozayémon, who was waiting impatiently for Chôbei to come, as soon as he heard of his arrival, ordered his retainers to usher him into his presence; and Chôbei, having told his apprentices to come and fetch him that night without fail, entered the house.

Deftly avoiding their blows, however, he tripped one of them and, kicking the other in the ribs, sent him reeling and breathless against the wall; then, as calmly as if nothing had happened, he presented himself before Jiurozayémon, who, peeping through a crack in the sliding doors, had watched his retainers' failure.

“Welcome, welcome, Master Chôbei,” he said. “I had always heard that you were a man of spirit, and I wanted to see what you were made of; so I told my retainers to put your courage to the test. That was a masterly throw of yours. Well, you must excuse this rude reception; come and sit down by me.”

“Please do not mention it, my lord,” said Chôbei, smiling somewhat scornfully. “I know that my poor skill cannot be compared with that of a noble <term>Samurai</term>; and if these two gentlemen got the worst of it just now, it was merely luck—that is all.”

So, after the usual compliments had been exchanged, Chôbei sat down by Jiurozayémon, and the attendants

Chôbei’s wife, who had bought a burial tub, came with seven other apprentices to fetch the Father of the <term>Otokodaté</term> from Jiurozayémon’s house. When the retainers saw them, they mocked them and said—

His son Chômatsu inherited his property, and his wife remained a faithful widow until her dying day, praying that she might sit with him in paradise upon the cup of the same lotus flower.
Many times, the apprentices of Chôbei met together to avenge him, but Jiurozayémon eluded all their efforts until he was eventually imprisoned by the government in the temple called Kanyeiji at Uyéno (as related in the story of “Kazuma’s Revenge”), which placed him beyond the reach of their hatred.
So lived and so died Chôbei of Bandzuin, the Father of the <term>Otokodaté</term> of Yedo.

### NOTE ON ASAKUSA.

ASAKUSA is the most bustling place in all Yedo. It is famous for the Sensôji Temple on the hill of Kinriu, or the Golden Dragon, which from morning until night is thronged with visitors—rich and poor, old and young—crowding in sleeve to sleeve. Having become a <term>Rônin</term>, or masterless man, he took up his residence on the Golden Dragon Hill with two retainers, who were brothers named Hinokuma Hamanari and Hinokuma Takénari. These three men, having fallen on hard times and being without the means to earn a living, became fishermen. It happened that on the 6th day of the 3rd month of the 36th year of the reign of Emperor Suiko (<term>A.D.</term> 1241), they went down in the morning to the Asakusa River to practice their trade. Having cast their nets, they caught no fish; instead, at every throw, they pulled up a figure of the Buddhist god <term>Kwannon</term>, which they threw back into the river. They rowed their boat to another spot, but the same luck followed them, and nothing came into their nets except the figure of <term>Kwannon</term>. Struck by the miracle, they carried the image home, and after fervent prayer, built a temple on the Golden Dragon Hill in which they enshrined it. The temple founded in this way was enriched by the donations of wealthy and pious people, whose care raised its buildings to the status of the primary temple in Yedo. Tradition says that the figure of <term>Kwannon</term> fished up in the net was one and eight-tenths inches tall.

The main hall of the temple is sixty feet square and is adorned with much intricate craftsmanship in gold and silver leaf, so that no place could be more exquisitely beautiful. There are two gates in front of it. The first is called the Gate of the Spirits of the Wind and of the Thunder and is adorned with figures of those two gods. Passing through the gate of the gods <term>Niô</term>, the main hall of the temple comes into view. At <term>Asakusa</term>, as is the case throughout <term>Yedo</term>, one can find fortune-tellers who prey on the foolishness of the superstitious. With a book on <term>physiognomy</term> laid on a desk before them, they call out to one man that he has an unlucky forehead, and to another that the space between his nose and his lips is ill-omened. Their tongues wag like flowing water until passers-by are attracted to their stalls. If the seer finds a customer, he closes his eyes and, reverently lifting the <term>divining-sticks</term> to his forehead, mutters incantations under his breath. Then, suddenly dividing the sticks into two bundles, he prophesies good or evil according to the number in each. With a magnifying glass, he examines his dupe's face and the palms of his hands. By the style of his clothes and his general manner, the prophet determines whether he is a countryman or from the city. The class of diviners called <term>Ichiko</term> claim to provide news of the dead, or of those who have gone to distant countries. The <term>Ichiko</term> corresponds exactly to the spirit medium of the West. The trade is followed by women, from fifteen or sixteen to about fifty years of age, who walk through the streets carrying a divining box about a foot square on their backs; they have no shop or stall, but wander about and are invited into their customers’ houses. The ceremony of divination is very simple. A porcelain bowl filled with water is placed upon a tray, and the customer, having written the name of the person with whom he wishes to communicate on a long slip of paper, rolls it into a spill, which he dips into the water and sprinkles the <term>Ichiko</term>, or medium, three times. She, resting her elbow upon her divining box and leaning her head upon her hand, mutters prayers and incantations until she has summoned the soul of the dead or absent person, which takes possession of her and answers questions through her mouth. The prophecies that the <term>Ichiko</term> utters during her trance are held in high regard by the superstitious and the common people.

Hard by <term>Asakusa</term> is the theater street. The theaters are called <term>Shiba-i</term>,<note>1</note> “turf places,” from the fact that the first theatrical performances were held on a turf plot. The origin of the drama in Japan, as elsewhere, was religious. In the reign of the <term>Emperor Heijô</term> (805 A.D.), there was a sudden volcanic sinking of the earth close by a pond called <term>Sarusawa</term>, or the Monkey’s Marsh, at <term>Nara</term>, in the province of <term>Yamato</term>, and a poisonous smoke issuing from the cavity struck down with sickness all those who came within its harmful influence; so the people brought quantities of firewood, which they burned in order that the poisonous vapor might be dispelled. The fire, being the male influence, would harmonize with and act as an antidote to the foul-smelling smoke, which was a

female influence.<note>This refers to the Chinese doctrine of the <term>Yang and Yin</term>, the male and female influences that spread through all creation.</note> Besides this, as a further charm to drive away the bad omen, the dance called <term>Sambasô</term>—which is still performed as a prelude to theatrical shows by an actor dressed as a venerable old man, symbolizing long life and happiness—was danced on a plot of grass in front of the <term>Temple Kofukuji</term>. By these means, the smoke was cleared away, and the drama originated. The story is found in the <term>Zoku Nihon Ki</term>, or supplementary history of Japan.

Three centuries later, during the reign of the <term>Emperor Toba</term> (1108 AD), there lived a woman named <term>Iso no Zenji</term>, who is regarded as the mother of Japanese drama. Her performances, however, seem only to have consisted of dancing or posturing while dressed in the costumes of the Court nobles; because of this, her dance was called <term>Otoko-mai</term>, or the man’s dance. Her name is only worth mentioning because of the respect with which actors hold her memory.

It was not until the year 1624 AD that a man named <term>Saruwaka Kanzaburô</term>, by order of the Shogun, opened the first theater in <term>Yedo</term> in <term>Nakabashi</term>, or Middle Bridge Street. It remained there until eight years later, when it was moved to <term>Ningiyô</term>, or Doll Street. The company of this theater was formed by two families named <term>Miako</term> and <term>Ichimura</term>. They did not enjoy their monopoly for long, because in the year 1644, we find a third family, the <term>Yamamura</term>, setting up a rival theater in <term>Kobiki</term>, or Sawyer Street.

In the year 1651, the Asian custom of keeping people of one profession in one place showed itself when the playhouses were moved to their present site. The street was named Saruwaka Street, after <term>Saruwaka Kanzaburô</term>, the founder of the drama in <term>Yedo</term>.

Theatrical performances take place from six in the morning until six in the evening. Just as the day is about to dawn in the east, the sound of the drum is heard, and the <term>Sambasô</term> dance is performed as a prelude. This is followed by the dances of famous actors of old; these are called the extra performances (<term>waki kiyôgen</term>).

One night, as Yorimitsu was feasting with his retainers, he said, “Who dares to go and defy the demon of the Rashô Gate, and leave a token to prove he has been there?” 

“I dare,” answered Tsuna, who, after putting on his armor, mounted his horse and rode out through the dark, bleak night to the Rashô Gate. Having written his name upon the gate, he was about to turn homeward when his horse began to shiver with fear, and a huge hand reaching out from the gate seized the back of the knight’s helmet. Tsuna, not at all discouraged, struggled to get free, but in vain; so, drawing his sword, he cut off the demon’s arm, and the spirit fled into the night with a howl. 

Tsuna carried the arm home in triumph and locked it in a box. One night, the demon took the shape of Tsuna’s aunt, came to him, and said, “I pray you, show me the arm of the fiend.” 

Tsuna answered, “I have shown it to no one, yet I will show it to you.” 

So he brought out the box and opened it, when suddenly a black cloud shrouded the figure of the supposed aunt, and the demon, having reclaimed its arm, disappeared. From 그 time on, the people were more troubled by the demon than ever; it carried off all the most beautiful young women of Kyoto to the hills, where it violated and ate them, until there was hardly a beautiful girl left in the city. 

Then the Emperor was very sorrowful, and he commanded Yorimitsu to destroy the monster. The hero, after preparing himself, went out with four trusted knights and another great captain to search among the hidden places of the mountains. One day, as they were traveling far from human settlements, they met an old man who invited them into his home, treated them kindly, and served them wine. When they took their leave of him, he gave them a gift of more wine to take away with them. 

Now, this old man was a mountain god. As they continued on their way, they met a beautiful lady who was washing blood-stained clothes in the waters of the valley, weeping bitterly all the while. When they asked her why she was crying, she answered, “Sirs, I am a woman from Kyoto whom the demon has kidnapped; he makes me wash his clothes, and when he is tired of me, he will kill and eat me. The heroes commanded the woman to lead them to the ogre’s cave, where a hundred devils stood guard and served him. The woman, having gone in first, told the demon of their arrival; and he, thinking to kill and eat them, summoned them to him. So they entered the cave, which reeked of the scent of human flesh and blood, and they saw Shudendôji, a massive monster with the face of a small child. The six men offered him the wine they had received from the mountain god, and he, laughing to himself, drank and made merry until, little by little, the fumes of the wine went to his head and he fell asleep. The heroes, pretending to sleep themselves, watched for a moment when the devils were all off their guard to put on their armor and steal one by one into the demon’s chamber. Then Yorimitsu, seeing that everything was still, drew his sword and cut off Shudendôji’s head. The head sprang up and bit at him; fortunately, however, Yorimitsu had put on two helmets, one over the other, so he was not hurt. When all the devils had been killed, the heroes and the woman returned to Kyoto, carrying Shudendôji’s head, which was presented to the Emperor; and the fame of their deed spread throughout the land.

This Shudendôji is the ogre represented in the Nakamura dance. The Ichimura dance represents the seven gods of wealth; and the Morita dance represents a large ape and symbolizes the drinking of wine.

As soon as the sun begins to rise in the sky, signboards glistening with paintings and gold are displayed, and the playgoers flock in crowds to the theater. The farmers and country folk hurry through their breakfast, and the women and children—who rose in the middle of the night to paint and adorn themselves—come from all directions to crowd into the gallery, which is hung with curtains as bright as a rainbow in the fading clouds. The place soon becomes so crowded that the heads of the spectators look like the scales on a dragon’s back. When the play begins, if the subject is tragic, the spectators are so moved that they weep until they must wring their sleeves dry. If the piece is comic, they laugh until their jaws are out of joint. The tricks and plots of the drama are beyond description, and the actors are as graceful as a swallow in flight. The triumph of persecuted virtue and the punishment of wickedness always conclude the story.

<meta>This page continues the description of Japanese theater, moving from the audience's excitement to the cultural role of plays, the lives and salaries of actors, and the public's devotion to famous performers.</meta>

# A STORY OF THE OTOKODATE OF YEDO.

When a favorite actor appears, his entrance is greeted with cheers. Fun and diversion are the order of the day, and rich and poor alike forget the worries they left behind at home; and yet it is not all idle entertainment, for there is a moral lesson taught and a practical sermon preached in every play.

The subjects of the pieces are mainly historical, with fake names being substituted for those of the real heroes. Indeed, it is in these popular tragedies that we must look for an account of many events of the last two hundred and fifty years; for only one very sparse history¹ of those times has been published. Only a limited number of copies of that work were printed from copper plates, and its circulation was strictly forbidden by the <term>Shogun’s</term> Government. The stories are presented with great precision and detail—so much so that it sometimes takes a series of performances to act out a single piece in its entirety. The Japanese are far ahead of the Chinese in their scenery and props, and their productions are sometimes excellently staged; a revolving stage allows them to shift from one scene to another with great speed. Top-tier actors receive as much as a thousand <term>riyos</term> (about £300) as their yearly salary. This is a high rate of pay, however, and many a man has to perform before the public for little more than his daily rice; to a talented young actor, it is almost enough reward just to be allowed to join a company that features a famous star. The salary of the actor, however, may depend upon the success of the theater; for dramatic performances are often undertaken as investments by wealthy people, who pay their company in proportion to their own profits. Besides his regular pay, a popular Japanese actor has a small gold mine in his patrons, who open their purses freely for the privilege of visiting the <term>green-room</term>. The women’s roles are all taken by men, just as they used to be in England in the past. Regarding the popularity of plays, it is said that in the year 1833, when two actors called Bandô Shûka and Segawa Rokô—both famous players of women’s roles—died at the same time, the people of <term>Yedo</term> mourned to the heavens and the earth; and if a million <term>riyos</term> could have brought them back to life, the money would have been readily available. and the richness of their coffins and of the clothes laid upon them was admired by all.
“When I heard this,” says Terakado Seiken, the author of the *Yedo Hanjôki*, “I lifted my eyes to heaven and heaved a great sigh. When my friend Saitô Shimei, a learned and good man, died, there was barely enough money to bury him; his needy pupils and friends contributed to give him a humble coffin. Alas! Alas! Here was a teacher who from his youth onward had honored his parents, and whose heart knew no deceit: if his friends were in need, he attended to their wants; he spared no effort to teach his fellow men; his goodwill and charity were beyond praise; under the blue sky and bright day he never did a shameful deed. His merits were like those of the ancient sages; but because he lacked the cunning of a fox or badger, he received no patronage from the wealthy, and, remaining poor to the day of his death, never had an opportunity to make his worth known. Alas! Alas!”

The drama is exclusively the amusement of the middle and lower classes. Etiquette, that sternest of tyrants, forbids Japanese people of high rank from being seen at any public exhibition, with the exception of wrestling matches. Actors are, however, occasionally hired to perform in private for the enlightenment of the lord and his ladies; and there is a kind of classical opera, called <term>Nô</term>, which is performed on stages specially built for the purpose in the palaces of the principal nobles. These Nô represent the entertainments by which the Sun Goddess was lured out of the cave in which she had hidden—a fable said to be based upon an eclipse. In the reign of Emperor Yômei (A.D. 586–593), Hada Kawakatsu, a man born in Japan but of Chinese descent, was commanded by the Emperor to arrange an entertainment to appease the gods and ensure the prosperity of the country. Kawakatsu wrote thirty-three plays, introducing fragments of Japanese poetry accompanied by musical instruments. Two performers, named Takéta and Hattori, having especially distinguished themselves in these entertainments, were ordered to prepare other similar plays, and their productions remain to the present day. Since the holy purpose of the Nô is to pray for the prosperity of the country, they are held in the highest esteem by the court nobles, the <term>Daimios</term>, and the military class: in the old days, they were the only ones who performed in these plays, but now ordinary actors take part in them.

The Nô are played in sets. The first of the set is specially dedi-

...dedicated to the propitiation of the gods; the second is performed in full armor and is designed to terrify evil spirits and to ensure the punishment of malefactors; the third has a gentler purpose, and its special object is the representation of all that is beautiful, fragrant, and delightful. The performers wear hideous wigs and masks, not unlike those of ancient Greece, and gorgeous brocade dresses. The masks, which belong to what was once the Shogun’s private company, are many centuries old and have been carefully preserved as heirlooms from generation to generation; being made of very thin lacquered wood and kept each in a silken bag, they have remained undamaged by the passage of time.

During the Duke of Edinburgh’s stay in Yedo, this company was hired to give a performance in the *Yashiki* of the Prince of *Kishiu*, which has the reputation of being the most beautiful palace in all Yedo. As far as I know, such a performance had never before been witnessed by foreigners, and it may be interesting to provide an account of it. Opposite the main reception room, where his Royal Highness sat, and separated from it by a narrow courtyard, was a covered stage, accessed from the dressing room by a long gallery at a forty-five-degree angle. Half a dozen musicians, dressed in ceremonial robes, marched slowly down the gallery and, having seated themselves on the stage, bowed gravely. The performances then began. There was no scenery or stage equipment; the descriptions provided by the chorus or the actors took their place. The dialogue and choruses are delivered in a nasal recitative, accompanied by the mouth-organ, flute, drum, and other classical instruments, and are completely incomprehensible. The ancient poetry is full of puns and wordplay, and it was with considerable difficulty that, with the assistance of a scholar, I prepared the summaries of the various pieces beforehand.

The first play was entitled *Hachiman of the Bow*. *Hachiman* is the name under which the Emperor Ojin (270–312 <term>A.D.</term>) was deified as the God of War. He is specifically worshipped because of his miraculous birth; his mother, the Empress *Jingo*, having, by the power of a magic stone which she wore at her belt, carried him in her womb for three years, during which she went to war and conquered the Koreans. The plot is set in the reign of Emperor Uda the Second (1275–1289 <term>A.D.</term>). In the second month of the year, pilgrims

A worshiper steps forth, sent by the Emperor, and delivers a congratulatory oration upon the peace and prosperity of the land. On being asked who he is, the old man answers that he is an aged servant of the shrine, and that he wishes to present his mulberry-wood bow to the Emperor; being too humble to draw near to His Majesty, he has waited for this festival, hoping that an opportunity might present itself. He explains that with this bow, and with certain arrows made of the Artemisia, the heavenly gods pacified the world. On being asked to show his bow, he refuses; it is a mystic protector of the country, which in old days was overshadowed by the mulberry tree. The peace which prevails in the land is likened to a calm at sea. The Emperor is the ship, and his subjects the water. The old man dwells upon the ancient worship of Hachiman, and relates how his mother, the Empress Jingo, sacrificed to the gods before invading Corea, and how the present prosperity of the country is to be attributed to the acceptance of those sacrifices. After having revealed himself as the god Hachiman in disguise, the old man disappears. The worshiper, awe-struck, declares that he must return to Kiyôto and tell the Emperor what he has seen. The chorus announces that sweet music and fragrant perfumes issue from the mountain, and the piece ends with felicitations upon the visible favor of the gods, and especially of Hachiman.

The second piece was *Tsunémasa*. *Tsunémasa* was a hero of the twelfth century, who died in the civil wars; he was famous for his skill in playing on the *biwa*, a sort of four-stringed lute.

A priest enters, and announces that his name is Giyôkei, and that before he retired from the world he held high rank at court. He relates how Tsunémasa, in his childhood the favorite of the Emperor, died in the wars by the western seas. During his lifetime the Emperor gave him a lute, called Sei-zan, "the Azure Mountain"; this lute at his death was placed in a shrine erected to his honor, and at his funeral music and plays were performed during seven days within the palace, by the special grace of the Emperor. Although the sky is clear, the wind rustles through the trees like the sound of falling rain; and although it is now summer-time, the moonlight on the sand looks like hoar-frost. All nature is sad and downcast. The ghost appears and sings that it is the spirit of Tsunémasa, and has come to thank those who have piously celebrated his funeral rites. No one answers him, and the spirit vanishes, its voice becoming fainter and fainter—an unreal and illusory vision haunting the scenes where its life was spent. The priest muses on the omen. Is it a dream or a reality? Marvelous! The ghost, returning, speaks of former days when it lived as a child in the palace and received the Azure Mountain lute from the Emperor—that lute with the four strings which his hand knew so well, and the attraction of which now draws him from the grave. The chorus recites the virtues of Tsunémasa—his benevolence, justice, humanity, talents, and truth; his love of poetry and music; the trees, the flowers, the birds, the breezes, the moon—all had a charm for him. The ghost begins to play upon the Azure Mountain lute, and the sounds produced from the magical instrument are so delicate that everyone thinks a shower is falling from heaven. The priest declares that it is not rain, but the sound of the enchanted lute. The sound of the first and second strings is like the sound of gentle rain or the wind stirring the pine trees; and the sound of the third and fourth strings is like the song of birds and pheasants calling to their young. A rhapsody in praise of music follows. Would that such strains could last forever! The ghost bewails its fate—that it cannot remain to play on but must return to the place from where it came. The priest addresses the ghost and asks whether the vision is indeed the spirit of Tsunémasa. Upon this, the ghost calls out in an agony of sorrow and terror at having been seen by mortal eyes and commands that the lamps be put out: upon its return to the abode of the dead, it will suffer for having shown itself; it describes the fiery torments which will be its fate. Poor fool! It has been lured to its destruction, like the summer insect that flies into the flame. Summoning the winds to its aid, it puts out the lights and disappears.

at the foot of Fujiyama, the Peerless Mountain. The waves are still, and there is a great calm; the fishermen are all out plying their trade. The speaker’s name is Hakuriyô, a fisherman living in the pine grove of Miwo. The rains are now over and the sky is serene; the sun rises bright and red over the pine trees and rippling sea, while last night’s moon is still seen faintly in the heavens. A breeze springs up and the weather begins to change; clouds and waves will follow the sunshine and calm, and the fishermen must return home. No; it is only the gentle breath of spring, after all; it scarcely stirs the stout fir trees, and the waves are hardly heard breaking upon the shore. The men may go out in safety.

The fisherman then relates how, while he was marveling at the view, flowers began to rain from the sky and sweet music filled the air, which was perfumed by a mystical fragrance. Looking up, he saw hanging on a pine tree a fairy’s suit of feathers, which he took home and showed to a friend, intending to keep it as a relic in his house. A heavenly fairy appears and claims the suit of feathers, but the fisherman holds onto his treasure trove. She argues that his act is impious—a mortal has no right to take what belongs to the fairies. He declares that he will hand down the feather suit to future generations as one of the country's treasures. 

The fairy mourns her fate; without her wings, how can she return to heaven? She recalls the familiar joys of heaven, now closed to her; she sees the wild geese and the gulls flying to the skies and longs for their power of flight. The tide has its ebb and flow, and the sea breezes blow where they wish; yet for her alone there is no power of movement, and she must remain on earth. At last, touched by her plea, the fisherman consents to return the feather suit on the condition that the fairy shall dance and play heavenly music for him. She agrees, but must first obtain the feather suit, without which she cannot dance. The fisherman refuses to give it up, fearing she might fly away to heaven without fulfilling her promise. The fairy reproaches him for his lack of faith: how could a heavenly being be capable of lying? He is ashamed and gives her the feather suit, which she puts on and begins to dance, singing of the delights of heaven, where she is one of the fifteen attendants who serve the moon. The fisherman is so overcome with joy that he imagines himself in heaven and wishes to keep the fairy to live with him forever.

The last of the Nô was *The Little Smith*, which is set in the reign of the Emperor Ichijô (987–1011 A.D.). A noble of the court enters and introduces himself as Tachibana Michinari. He has been commanded by the Emperor—who had an auspicious dream the previous night—to order a sword from the smith Munéchika of Sanjô. He calls for Munéchika, who appears and, after receiving the order, explains the difficulty of his situation: at that time, he has no suitable partner to assist him, and he cannot forge a blade alone. The excuse is not accepted; the smith pleads earnestly to be spared the shame of failure. Forced to comply, there is nothing left for him to do but appeal to the gods for help. He prays to the patron god of his family, Inari Sama.<note>The note at the end of the "Story of the Grateful Foxes" contains an account of Inari Sama and explains how the foxes serve him.</note> A man suddenly appears and calls the smith; this man is the god Inari Sama in disguise. The smith asks who his visitor is and how he knows his name. The stranger answers, “You have been ordered to make a blade for the Emperor.” “This is very strange,” says the smith. “I received the order only a moment ago; how do you know of it?” “Heaven has a voice that is heard upon the earth. Walls have ears, and stones tell tales.<note>This is a literal translation of a Japanese proverb.</note> There are no secrets in the world. The sword the Emperor has sent for shall be inferior to none of these; the smith may set his mind at ease. The smith, awestruck, expresses his wonder and asks again who is addressing him. The subjects of the <term>Nô</term> are all taken from old legends of the country; a shrine at Miwo, by the seashore, marks the spot where the feather robe was found, and the miraculously forged sword is supposed to be in the Emperor's armory to this day. The beauty of the poetry—and it is very beautiful—is marred by the lack of scenery and by the grotesque costumes and make-up. In the *Suit of Feathers*, for instance, the fairy wears a hideous mask and a wig of scarlet matted locks: the feather robe itself is left entirely to the imagination; and the heavenly dance is a series of whirls, stamps, and jumps, accompanied by unearthly yells and shrieks; while the vanishing into thin air is represented by pirouettes something like the movement of a dancing dervish. The intoning of the recitative is unnatural and unintelligible, so much so that not even a highly educated Japanese person could understand what is going on unless they were previously acquainted with the piece. This, however, is assuming something that is not the case, for the <term>Nô</term> are as familiarly known as the masterpieces of our own dramatists.

The classical severity of the <term>Nô</term> is relieved by the introduction between the pieces of light farces called <term>Kiyôgen</term>. Since the entire entertainment has a religious purpose, the <term>Kiyôgen</term> stand in the same relation to the <term>Nô</term> as small shrines do to the main temple; they, too, are played to appease the gods and to soften men’s hearts. The farces are acted without wigs or masks; the dialogue is in the common spoken language, and since there is no musical accompaniment, it is quite easy to follow. ### NOTE ON THE GAME OF FOOTBALL.

THE game of football <note>Kemari: a traditional Japanese ball game resembling hacky-sack more than modern football.</note> is in great favor at the Japanese Court. The days on which it takes place are carefully noted in the "Daijôkwan Nishi," or Government Gazette. On February 25, 1869, for instance, we find two entries: "The Emperor wrote characters of good omen," and "The game of football was played at the palace." The game was first introduced from China during the reign of the Empress Kôkiyoku, in the middle of the seventh century. The Emperor Mommu, who reigned at the end of the same century, was the first emperor to take part in the sport. His Majesty Toba the Second became very expert at it, as did the noble Asukai Chiujo, and from that time a sort of football club was formed at the palace. During the days of extreme poverty for the Mikado and his Court, the Asukai family, despite their high rank, used to supplement their meager income by giving lessons in the art of playing football.

## THE WONDERFUL ADVENTURES OF FUNAKOSHI JIUYÉMON

The brave deeds and marvelous experiences of Funakoshi Jiuyémon are perhaps more traditional than historical, much like those of Robin Hood and his Merry Men. However, even if all or part of the deeds that popular belief attributes to him are legends, his story provides a true picture of manners and customs. Above all, the nature of the vengeance he took upon the wife who had dishonored him, and upon her lover, shows the great importance the Japanese place on the sanctity of the marriage tie.

The 50th and 51st chapters of the "Legacy of Iyéyasu," previously quoted, state: "If a married woman of the agricultural, artisan, or commercial class secretly has sexual relations with another man, the husband does not need to file a complaint against the persons thus disrupting the fundamental relationship of humanity; instead, he may put them both to death. Nevertheless, if he kills one of them and spares the other, his guilt is considered equal to that of the wrongdoers.

"In the event, however, that advice is sought and the parties have not been killed, comply with the wishes of the complainant regarding whether or not to put them to death.

"Humanity, in whose bodies the male and female elements produce a natural desire for each other, does not view such practices with total disgust; therefore, the legal judgment of such cases requires special deliberation and consultation.

"Men and women of the military class are expected to know better than to cause a disturbance by violating exist-

...ing regulations; and anyone breaking the regulations through lewd, frivolous, or illicit intercourse shall be punished immediately, without deliberation or consultation. This is not the same as in the case of farmers, artisans, and traders.”

As a criminal offense, adultery was, according to the ancient laws of Japan, punished by crucifixion. In more modern times, it has been punished by decapitation and the disgraceful exposure of the head after death; but if the murder of the wronged husband accompanies the crime of adultery, then the guilty parties are still crucified to this day. At the present time, the husband is no longer allowed to take the law into his own hands: he must report the matter to the Government and trust the State to avenge his honor.

Sacred as the marriage tie is while it lasts, the law that dissolves it is strangely easy—or rather, there is no law: a man may turn his wife out of doors whenever it suits his whim. An example of this practice was shown in the story of “The Forty-seven Ronin.” A husband only has to report the matter to his lord, and the ceremony of divorce is completed. Thus, in the days of the Shogun’s power, a Hatamoto who had divorced his wife reported the matter to the Shogun. A Daimyo’s retainer reports the matter to his Prince.

The ease of divorce, however, seems to be rarely taken advantage of; this is probably due to the practice of keeping concubines. It has often been asked: are the Japanese polygamists? The answer is yes and no. They marry only one wife, but a man may, according to his rank and means, have one or more concubines in addition. The Emperor has twelve concubines, called Kisaki; and Ieyasu, referring forcefully to excess in this regard as *teterrima belli causa*, decreed that the princes might have eight, high officers five, and ordinary Samurai two handmaids. “In ancient times,” he writes, “the downfall of castles and the overthrow of kingdoms all resulted from this alone. Why is the indulgence of passions not guarded against?”

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Japanese legal and social customs, transitioning from the laws regarding adultery and divorce to the status of concubines and the vital role of adoption in maintaining the family line.</meta>

<page-num>120</page-num>
<header>TALES OF OLD JAPAN.</header>

The difference between the status of a wife and that of a concubine is distinct. The legitimate wife stands in relation to the handmaid as a lord does to his vassal. Since concubinage is a legitimate institution, the son of a handmaid is not illegitimate, nor is he in any way a child of shame; nevertheless, as a general rule, the son of the bondwoman does not inherit alongside the son of the free woman, for the wife's son inherits before the son of a concubine, even if the latter is older. It frequently happens that a nobleman, having children by his concubines but none by his wife, chooses his own younger brother, or even adopts the son of a relative, to succeed him in the family honors. The family line is considered to be more purely preserved this way. The law of succession is, however, extremely flexible. Exceptional personal merit will sometimes secure the ancestral inheritance for the <term>left-handed son</term>; and it often happens that the son of a concubine, who is prevented from succeeding his own father, is adopted as the heir of a relative or friend of even higher rank. When the wife of a nobleman has a daughter but no son, the custom is to adopt a young man of suitable family and age, who marries the girl and inherits as a son.

The principle of adoption is universal among all classes, from the Emperor down to his lowest subject; nor is the family line considered to have been broken because an adopted son has succeeded to the estates. Indeed, should a nobleman die without a male heir, whether biological or adopted, his lands are forfeited to the State. Care is taken to ensure that the person adopted is himself descended from a social rank suited to that of the family into which he is to be received.

Since sixteen and older is considered the marriageable age for a man, it is not common for persons below that age to adopt an heir; yet an infant on the verge of death may adopt a person older than himself so that the family line does not become extinct.

An account of the marriage ceremony can be found in the Appendix regarding that subject.

# THE ADVENTURES OF FUNAKOSHI JIUYÉMON. 121

In ancient times, on the island of Shikoku <note>Shikoku is one of the southern islands separated from the main island of Japan by the beautiful "Inland Sea." It is called Shikoku, or the "Four Provinces," because it is divided into the four provinces of Awa, Sanuki, Iyo, and Tosa.</note>, there lived one Funakoshi Jiuyémon, a brave samurai and accomplished man who was in great favor with the prince, his master. One day, during a drinking party, a quarrel sprang up between him and a fellow officer, which resulted in an immediate duel in which Jiuyémon killed his opponent. When Jiuyémon realized what he had done, he was struck with remorse and thought to disembowel himself; but, receiving a private summons from his lord, he went to the castle, and the prince said to him—

"So, it seems that you have been getting drunk and quarrelling, and that you have killed one of your friends; and now I suppose you have determined to perform *hara-kiri*. It is a great pity, and in the face of the laws, I can do nothing for you openly. Still, if you will escape and flee from this part of the country for a while, in two years' time the affair will have blown over, and I will allow you to return."

And with these words, the prince presented him with a fine sword, made by Sukésada <note>Sukésada refers to a famous family of swordsmiths belonging to the Bizen clan. The Bizen men are notoriously good armorers, and their blades command high prices. Jiuyémon's sword is said to have been made by one of the Sukésada who lived about 290 years ago.</note>, and a hundred ounces of silver. Having bid him farewell, the prince entered his private apartments. Jiuyémon, prostrating himself, wept tears of gratitude; then, taking the sword and the money, he went home and prepared to flee from the province. He secretly took leave of his relations, each of whom gave him a parting gift. These gifts, together with his own money and what he had received from the prince, amounted to a sum of two hundred and fifty ounces of silver. Things continued in this way for some time, until at last, one fine day, O Hiyaku, looking out of the house, saw the wrestler Takaségawa passing in the street, so she called out to him—

“Goodness, Master Takaségawa, is that really you! It has been such a long time since we have met! Please come in and have a chat.”

“Thank you, I am very much obliged to you; but since I do not like the sort of scene we had the other day, I think I would rather not accept your invitation.”

“Please do not talk in such a cowardly way. Next year, when Jiuyémon goes back to his own country, he is sure to give me this house, and then you and I can marry and live as happily as possible.”

“I do not like being in too great a hurry to accept generous offers.”¹

“Nonsense! There is no need for showing such hesitation about accepting what is given to you.”

And as she spoke, she caught the wrestler by the hand and led him into the house. After they had talked together for some time, she said—

“Listen to me, Master Takaségawa. I have been thinking over all of this for some time, and I see no other way but to kill Jiuyémon and put an end to him.”

“Why do you want to do that?”

“As long as he is alive, we cannot be married. What I propose is that you should buy some poison, and I will put it secretly into his food. When he is dead, we can be happy to our hearts’ content.”

At first Takaségawa was startled and bewildered by the boldness of the scheme; but forgetting the gratitude which he owed to Jiuyémon for sparing his life on the previous occasion, he replied—

“Well, I think it can be managed. I have a friend who is a physician, so I will get him to prepare some poison for

After reading the letter, she put it away carefully in a cupboard drawer and waited until Jiuyémon expressed a desire to eat some macaroni.

One day, near the New Year, when O Hiyaku had gone out to a party with a few of her friends, it happened that Jiuyémon, being alone in the house, needed something. Failing to find it anywhere, he finally decided to look for it in O Hiyaku’s cupboard; and as he was searching through the odds and ends it contained, he discovered the fatal letter. When he read the plan to put poison in his macaroni, he was stunned and said to himself, “When I caught those two beasts in their wickedness, I spared them because their blood would have defiled my sword; and now they are not even grateful for my mercy. Their crime is beyond words, and I will kill them both together.”

So he put the letter back in its place and waited for his wife to come home. As soon as she appeared, he said—

“You have come home early, O Hiyaku. I feel quite bored and lonely this evening; let’s have some wine.”

Because he spoke without any sign of anger, it never occurred to O Hiyaku’s mind that he had seen the letter; so she went about her household duties with a calm mind.

It would have defiled my sword to have killed such an ungrateful hound with it; but luckily here is your own dirk, and I will slay you with that.”

However, Jiuyémon, who was afraid of nothing, cared little for the appearance of the place; and having made himself as comfortable as he could in such a dreary spot, he sat down on the floor, lit his pipe, and kept a sharp lookout for the goblins. The fame of this exploit soon spread throughout Osaka, so that everyone praised Jiuyémon’s courage; and shortly after this, he was elected chief of the Otokodaté,¹ or friendly society of the wardsmen, and no longer worked at his trade, but lived off the contributions of his many apprentices.

Now Kajiki Tônoshin was in love with a singing-girl named Kashiku, upon whom he was in the habit of spending a great deal of money. She, however, cared nothing for him, for she had a sweetheart named Hichirobei, whom she managed to meet secretly, although, in order to support her parents, she was forced to become Tônoshin’s mistress. One evening, when the latter was on guard at the office of his chief, the Governor of Osaka, Kashiku sent word privately to Hichirobei, inviting him to come to her house, as the coast was clear.

While the two were making merry over a small feast, Tônoshin—who had persuaded a friend to take his duty for him on the excuse of urgent business—knocked at the door. Kashiku, in a great fright, hid her lover in a long clothes-box and went to let Tônoshin in.
