It immediately occurred to him that this was the very sword which had been a parting gift to him from his lord: the hilt, the mountings, and the tip of the scabbard were all the same, though the blade had been shortened and made into a long dirk. Then he looked more closely at Chôbei’s features and saw that he was none other than Akagôshi Kuroyémon, the pirate chief. Two years had passed, but he could not forget that face.

Jiuyémon would have liked to arrest him at once; but thinking that it would be a pity to give such a vile robber a chance to escape, he restrained himself. Taking his leave, he went straight away and reported the matter to the Governor of Osaka. When the officers of justice heard of the target that awaited them, they made their preparations immediately. Three men of the secret police went to Chôbei’s wine shop and, having called for wine, pretended to start a drunken brawl. As Chôbei went up to them and tried to pacify them, one of the policemen seized hold of him, and another tried to pin him down. It at once flashed across Chôbei’s mind that his old misdeeds had come to light at last, so with a desperate effort he shook off the two policemen and knocked them down. Rushing into the inner room, he seized the famous Sukésada sword and sprang upstairs. The three policemen, never thinking that he could escape, climbed the stairs right after him; but with a terrible cut, Chôbei split the lead man’s head in two, and the other two fell back, appalled by their comrade’s fate. Then Chôbei climbed onto the roof and, looking out, saw that the house was surrounded on all sides by armed men. Seeing this, he decided that his final moment had come; at any rate, he determined to sell his life dearly and to die fighting. At the first break of day, he reported the incident to the proper authorities and handed Kashiku over to custody. So, after a proper investigation, the two pirate brothers and the girl Kashiku were executed, and their heads were put on public display together.²

The fat wrestlers of Japan, whose heavy bellies and unwieldy, puffy limbs—however much they may be admired by their own people—form a striking contrast to our Western ideas of training, have attracted some attention from travelers; and those who are interested in athletic sports may care to learn something about them.
The first historical record of wrestling occurs in the sixth year of the Emperor Suinin (24 B.C.), when one Taima no Kéhaya, a noble of great stature and strength, boasting that he had no match under heaven, begged the Emperor to have his strength put to the test. The Emperor accordingly had the challenge proclaimed; and one Nomi no Shikuné answered it, and having wrestled with Kéhaya, kicked him in the ribs and broke his bones, so that he died. After this, Shikuné was promoted to high office and became further famous in Japanese history for having substituted earthen images for the living men who, before his time, used to be buried with the coffin of the Mikado.
In the year 858 A.D., the throne of Japan was wrestled for. The Emperor Buntoku had two sons, called Koréshito and Korétaka, both of whom aspired to the throne. Their claims were decided in a wrestling match, in which one Yoshirô was the champion of Koréshito, and Natora was the champion of Korétaka. Natora having been defeated, Koréshito ascended his father’s throne under the name of Seiwa.
In the eighth century, when Nara was the capital of Japan, the Emperor Shômu instituted wrestling as part of the ceremonies of the autumn festival of the Five Grains, or Harvest Home; and as the year proved to be a fruitful one, the custom was continued as auspicious. The strong men of the various pro-

#### TALES OF OLD JAPAN.

provinces were collected, and one Kiyobayashi was proclaimed the champion of Japan. Many a brave and strong man tried a throw with him, but none could master him. Rules of the ring were now drawn up; and in order to prevent disputes, the Emperor appointed Kiyobayashi to be the judge of wrestling matches. He was presented, as a badge of his office, with a fan upon which were inscribed the words “the Prince of Lions.” The wrestlers were divided into those from the eastern and western provinces, with Omi being taken as the center province. The eastern wrestlers wore the badge of the hollyhock in their hair; the western wrestlers took the gourd flower for their sign. Consequently, the passage leading up to the wrestling stage was called the “Flower Path.” Forty-eight various falls were established as fair—twelve throws, twelve lifts, twelve twists, and twelve throws over the back. All other throws not included in these were considered fouls, and it was the duty of the umpire to see that no illegal tricks were used. It was decided that the covered stage should be composed of sixteen rice bales, arranged in the shape of one huge bale and supported by four pillars at the four points of the compass. Each pillar was painted a different color, which, together with certain paper pendants, made up five colors to symbolize the Five Grains.

The civil wars that disturbed the country for a time put a stop to the practice of wrestling; but when peace was restored, it was proposed to re-establish the athletic games. The umpire Kiyobayashi, the “Prince of Lions,” was sought out; but he had died or disappeared and could not be found, so no umpire was available. The various provinces were searched for a man who might fill his place, and one Yoshida Iyétsugu, a Rônin from the province of Echizen who was reported to be well-versed in the noble science, was summoned to the capital and proved to be a pupil of Kiyobayashi. The right of acting as umpire in wrestling matches was granted to his family, so that the "Driving Wind" might preside over athletic sports for future generations. In ancient days, the prizes for the three champion wrestlers were a bow, a bowstring, and an arrow: these are still brought into the ring, and, at the end of the match, the successful competitors perform a variety of rituals with them.

To the champion wrestlers—to only two or three men in a generation—the family of the "Driving Wind" awards the privilege of wearing a rope girdle. In the time of the <term>Shogunate</term>, these champions used to wrestle before the <term>Shogun</term>.

At the beginning of the 17th century (A.D. 1606), wrestling matches as a regular part of a religious ceremony were discontinued. They are still held, however, at the shrines of Kamo, at Kyoto, and of Kasuga, in Yamato. They are also held at Kamakura every year, and at the shrines of the patron saints of the various provinces, in imitation of the ancient customs.

In the year 1623, one Akashi Shiganosuké obtained permission from the Government to hold public wrestling matches in the streets of Yedo. In the year 1644, the first wrestling match for the purpose of raising a collection for building a temple was held. This was done by the priests of Kofukuji, in Yamashiro. In the year 1660, the same method was used in Yedo, and the custom of organizing wrestling matches for the benefit of temple funds remains in practice to this day.

The umpire watches until the two men draw their breath at the same time, and with his fan gives the signal. They jump up and close with one another, like tigers springing on their prey, or dragons playing with a ball. Each is intent on throwing the other by twisting or by lifting him. It is no mere trial of brute strength; it is a tussle of skill against skill. Each of the forty-eight throws is tried in turn. From left to right, and from right to left, the umpire hovers about, watching for the victory to declare itself. Some of the spectators back the east, others back the west. The patrons of the ring are so excited that they feel the strength tingling within them; they clench their fists, and watch their men, without so much as blinking their eyes. At last one man, east or west, gains the advantage, and the umpire lifts his fan as a token of victory. The cheers of the bystanders shake the neighborhood, and they throw their clothes or valuables into the ring, to be redeemed afterward in money; indeed, in his excitement, a man will even tear off his neighbor’s jacket and throw it in.

Before beginning their tussle, the wrestlers build up their strength by stamping their feet and slapping their huge thighs. This custom is derived from the following tale of the heroic or mythological age:

After the seven ages of the heavenly gods came the reign of Tensho Daijin, the Sun Goddess, and first Empress of Japan. Her younger brother, Sosanöô no Mikoto, was a mighty and a brave hero, but turbulent, and he delighted in hunting the deer and the boar. After killing these beasts, he would throw their dead bodies into the sacred hall of his sister, and otherwise defile her dwelling. When he had done this several times, his sister was angry, and hid in the cave called the Rock Gate of Heaven; and when her face was not seen, there was no difference between the night and the day. Then the hero Tajikaraô, or “Great Strength,” clapping his hands and stamping his feet, with a great effort grasped and threw down the stone door, and the heroes brought back the Sun Goddess.<note>The author of the history called “Kokushi Riyaku” explains this fable as an account of the first eclipse.</note> As Tajikaraô is the patron god of Strength, wrestlers, upon entering the ring, still commemorate his deed by clapping their hands and stamping their feet as a preparation for putting forth their strength.

The great Daimyos are in the habit of attaching wrestlers to their service and assigning to them a yearly portion of rice. It is usual for these athletes to take part in funeral or wedding processions and to escort the princes on journeys. The rich merchants and townspeople give money to their favorite wrestlers and invite them to their houses to drink wine and feast. Though they are common, unrefined fellows, they are allowed some of the same familiarity that is granted to prize-fighters, jockeys, and the like by their patrons in our own country.

The Japanese wrestlers appear to have no regular system of training; they harden their naturally powerful limbs by much beating and by butting at wooden posts with their shoulders. Their diet is heartier than that of the ordinary Japanese, who rarely eat meat.

# THE ETA MAIDEN AND THE HATAMOTO.

It will be a long time before those who were present at the newly opened port of Kôbé on February 4, 1868, forget that day. The civil war was raging, and the foreign Legations—warned by the flames of burning villages, as well as by the flight of the Shogun and his ministers—had left Osaka to take shelter at Kôbé. In Kôbé, they were not, as they had been in the former place, separated from their ships by more than twenty miles of road occupied by armed troops in a highly excited state, nor did they face the alternative of crossing a dangerous sandbar in stormy weather, which had already claimed many valuable lives. It was a fine winter’s day, and the place was full of bustle, with people busy moving in and caring for their goods and possessions. All of a sudden, a procession of armed men belonging to the Bizen clan was seen leaving the town and advancing along the high road leading to Osaka. Without any apparent reason—though it was said afterward that two Frenchmen had crossed their line of march—there was a halt, a commotion, and a command was given. Then, little clouds of white smoke puffed up, and the sharp “ping” of rifle bullets came whizzing over the open space intended for a foreign settlement, as fast as the repeating breech-loaders could be discharged. Fortunately, their marksmanship was very poor; for had the men of Bizen been good shots, almost all the principal foreign officials in the country, besides many merchants and private gentlemen, must have been killed. As it was, only two or three men were wounded. If they were bad marksmen, however, they were mighty

In an incredibly short time, the guards of the various Legations and the sailors and marines from the warships were in hot pursuit of the enemy, who were scampering away over the hills as fast as their legs could carry them. They left their baggage ingloriously scattered over the road, as many a cheap lacquered hat and flimsy paper cartridge box—kept by our *Blue Jackets* as trophies—will testify. The stampede was so complete that the enemy’s losses amounted only to one elderly coolie who, being too feeble to run, was taken prisoner after having seventeen revolver shots fired at him without effect. The only injury our men inflicted was upon a solitary old woman, who was accidentally shot through the leg.

If it had not been for the serious nature of the offense—which was an attack upon the flags of all the Treaty Powers—and for the terrible retribution that was necessarily demanded, the whole affair would be remembered chiefly for the ridiculous events it caused. The mounted escort of the British Legation performed a brilliant cavalry charge down an empty road; a very fine line of skirmishers along the fields fired away a great deal of ammunition with no result; earthworks were built, and Kôbé was held under military occupation for three days. During this time, there were alarms, "cutting-out" expeditions with armed boats, steamers seized, and all kinds of martial excitement. In fact, it was like fox hunting: it had "all the excitement of war, with only ten percent of the danger."

The first thought of the kind-hearted doctor of the British Legation was for the poor old woman who had been wounded and was pitifully mourning her situation. were admitted within its sacred precincts. No account of Japanese society would be complete without mentioning the <term>Etas</term>; and the following story shows well, I think, the position they hold.

Their occupation is to slaughter animals, work leather, attend to criminals, and perform other degrading work. Several accounts are given of their origin; the most probable of which is that when Buddhism—the tenets of which forbid the taking of life—was introduced, those who lived by inflicting death became accursed in the land. Their trade was made hereditary, just as the office of executioner was in some European countries. Another story is that they are the descendants of the Tartar invaders left behind by <term>Kublai Khan</term>. Some further facts connected with the <term>Etas</term> are given in a note at the end of the story.

When the Eta heard this, he was embarrassed, and for a while he remained silent; but at last taking courage, he said to Genzaburô, “Sir, having been honored by your commands, I am quite put to shame. I was originally a gardener, and I used to go to your honor’s house and lend a hand in trimming the garden. Since those days I have gradually fallen into wasteful habits, and little by little have sunk to be the wretched thing that you now see me.”

When Genzaburô heard this he was very much surprised, and, remembering his old friendship for his playmate, he was filled with pity and said, “Truly, you have fallen very low. Now, all you have to do is to persevere and use your best efforts to find a means of escape from the class into which you have fallen, and become a <term>wardsman</term> <note>A commoner or townsperson (chōnin).</note> again. Take this sum: small as it is, let it be a foundation for your future.” And with these words he took ten <term>riyos</term> <note>Ryō; gold coins used as currency.</note> out of his pouch and handed them to Chokichi, who at first refused to accept the present, but, when it was pressed upon him, received it with thanks. Genzaburô was leaving him to go home, when two wandering singing-girls came up and spoke to Chokichi; so Genzaburô looked to see what the two women were like. One was a woman about twenty years of age, and the other was a peerlessly beautiful girl of sixteen; she was neither too heavy nor too thin, neither too tall nor too short; her face was oval, like a melon-seed, and her complexion was fair and white; her eyes were narrow and bright, her teeth small and even; her nose was elegant, and her mouth delicately formed, with lovely red lips; her eyebrows were long and fine; she had a wealth of long black hair; she spoke modestly, with a soft sweet voice; and when she smiled, two lovely dimples appeared—

For the first time, he has realized the folly of his actions and, full of remorse, he has commissioned me to devise a strategy to break off the affair. I have come to fulfill this promise; and now, please, advise your daughter to think no more of his lordship.”

However, Chokichi would not consent on any account; so Genzaburô returned home, and, from that time forward, daily pleaded with Chokichi to bring O Koyo to him. Receiving nothing but advice from him in return, Genzaburô was very sad and lonely.

One day Genzaburô, intent on ridding himself of the grief he felt at his separation from O Koyo, went to the Yoshiwara <note>The famous red-light district of Edo (modern Tokyo).</note>. Going into a house of entertainment, he ordered a feast to be prepared; but, in the midst of the gaiety, his heart yearned all the while for his lost love, and his merriment was only mourning in disguise. At last the night wore on; and as he was walking down the corridor, he saw a man about forty years of age with long hair coming toward him, who, when he saw Genzaburô, cried out, “Dear me! Why, this must be my young lord Genzaburô who has come out to enjoy himself.”

Genzaburô thought this rather strange; but, looking at the man attentively, he recognized him as a retainer whom he had employed the year before, and said—

“This is a curious meeting; tell me, what have you been doing since you left my service? At any rate, I may congratulate you on being well and strong. Where are you living now?”

“Well, sir, since I parted from you I have been earning a living as a fortune-teller at Kanda, and have changed my name to Kaji Sazen. I am living in a poor and humble house; but if your lordship, at your convenience, would honor me with a visit——”

As for Kihachi, the Eta chief, and his daughter O Koyo, they were handed over for punishment to the chief of the Etas, and by him they too were banished; while Sazen, against whom the murder of Chokichi had been fully proved, was executed according to law.

### NOTE.

At <term>Asakusa</term>, in <term>Yedo</term>, there lives a man called <term>Danzayémon</term>, the chief of the <term>Etas</term>. This man traces his pedigree back to <term>Minamoto no Yoritomo</term>, who founded the <term>Shogunate</term> in the year 1192 A.D. All of the Etas in Japan are under his jurisdiction: his

<summary>Sazen murders Chokichi but is caught because of a lost letter, leading to his execution and the banishment of Genzaburô and O Koyo. The text concludes with historical context regarding Danzayémon, the leader of the Eta class.</summary>
<keywords>Sazen, Chokichi, Genzaburô, O Koyo, Eta, Hatamoto, Danzayémon, Minamoto no Yoritomo, Shogunate, Yedo, justice, banishment</keywords>

--- Page 221 ---
<meta>This page continues the historical note regarding the Eta class and their social standing, following the conclusion of the story of the Eta maiden and the Hatamoto.</meta>

<page-num>168</page-num>
<header>TALES OF OLD JAPAN.</header>

Subordinates are called <term>Koyagashira</term>, or "chiefs of the huts"; and he and they constitute the government of the <term>Etas</term>. In the "Legacy of Iyéyasu," already quoted, the 36th Law provides as follows:

> "All wandering mendicants, such as male sorcerers, female diviners, hermits, blind people, beggars, and tanners (<term>Etas</term>), have had their respective rulers from of old. Do not be disinclined, however, to punish any such people who cause disputes, or who overstep the boundaries of their own classes and are disobedient to existing laws."

The occupation of the <term>Etas</term> is to kill and skin horses, oxen, and other beasts, to stretch drums, and make shoes; and if they are very poor, they wander from house to house, working as cobblers, mending old shoes and leather, and so earn a meager livelihood. Besides this, their daughters and young married women gain a small amount as wandering minstrels, called <term>Torioi</term>, playing on the *shamisen*, a sort of banjo, and singing ballads. They never marry outside of their own fraternity, but remain apart, a despised and shunned race.

At executions by crucifixion, it is the duty of the <term>Etas</term> to pierce the victims with spears; and, besides this, they have to perform all sorts of degrading duties regarding criminals, such as carrying sick prisoners from their cells to the hall of justice and burying the bodies of those who have been executed. Thus, their race is considered polluted and accursed, and they are hated accordingly.

Now this is how the <term>Etas</term> came to be under the jurisdiction of <term>Danzayémon</term>:

When <term>Minamoto no Yoritomo</term> was still a child, his father, <term>Minamoto no Yoshitomo</term>, fought with <term>Taira no Kiyomori</term> and was killed by treachery. Thus his family was ruined, and <term>Yoshitomo’s</term> concubine, whose name was <term>Tokiwa</term>, took her children and fled from the house to save her life and theirs. But <term>Kiyomori</term>, desiring to destroy the family of <term>Yoshitomo</term> root and branch, ordered his retainers to divide themselves into bands and seek out the children. At last they were found; but <term>Tokiwa</term> was so exceedingly beautiful that <term>Kiyomori</term> was inflamed with love for her and desired her to become his own concubine. Then <term>Tokiwa</term> told <term>Kiyomori</term> that if he would spare her little ones, she would share his bed; but that if he killed her children, she would kill herself rather than yield to his desire. When he heard this,

Kiyomori, bewildered by the beauty of Tokiwa, spared the lives of her children but banished them from the capital.

So Yoritomo was sent to Hirugakojima, in the province of Idzu; and when he grew up and became a man, he married the daughter of a peasant. After a while, Yoritomo left the province and went to the wars, leaving his wife pregnant; and in due time she gave birth to a male child, to the delight of her parents, who rejoiced that their daughter should have a child by a nobleman. But she soon fell sick and died, and the old people took charge of the baby. And when they also died, the care of the child fell to his mother’s kinsmen, and he grew up to be a peasant.

Now Kiyomori, the enemy of Yoritomo, had died; and Yoritomo had avenged the death of his father by killing Munémori, the son of Kiyomori; and there was peace throughout the land. And Yoritomo became the chief of all the noble houses in Japan and first established the government of the country. When Yoritomo had thus raised himself to power, if the son that his peasant wife had borne to him had proclaimed himself the son of the mighty prince, he would have been made lord over a province; but he gave no thought to this and remained a farmer, forfeiting a glorious inheritance. His descendants after him lived as peasants in the same village, increasing in prosperity and in good reputation among their neighbors.

But the princely line of Yoritomo came to an end in three generations, and the house of Hôjô was all-powerful in the land.

Now it happened that the head of the house of Hôjô heard that a descendant of Yoritomo was living as a peasant in the land, so he summoned him and said—

“It is a hard thing to see the son of an illustrious house live and die a peasant. I will promote you to the rank of Samurai.”

Then the peasant answered, “My lord, if I become a Samurai and the retainer of some noble, I shall not be so happy as when I was my own master. If I may not remain a farmer, let me be a chief over men, however humble they may be.”

But my lord Hôjô was angry at this and, thinking to punish the peasant for his insolence, said—

“Since you wish to become a chief over men, no matter how humble, there is no way of satisfying your strange wish but by—”

## FAIRY TALES.

I think that their charm is a sufficient justification for the following short children’s stories. With the exception of "The Elves and the Envious Neighbor," which comes from a curious book on etymology and proverbs called the <term>Kotowazagusa</term>, these stories are found printed in small separate pamphlets with illustrations; the printing blocks for these have become so worn that the print is barely legible. These are the first tales given to Japanese children, and it is with these and others like them that Japanese mothers hush their little ones to sleep. Knowing the interest that many adults take in such nursery stories, I was eager to collect more of them. I was disappointed, however, because those I provide here are the only ones I could find in print; and if I asked Japanese people to tell me others, they only thought I was mocking them and changed the subject. The stories of the "Tongue-Cut Sparrow" and "The Old Couple and Their Dog" have been paraphrased in other works about Japan, but I am not aware of them being literally translated before.

<summary>The author introduces a collection of Japanese fairy tales, noting that they are traditional stories used by mothers to soothe children and are sourced from old, illustrated pamphlets. He explains that while some of these tales have been summarized elsewhere, he is providing literal translations of the few printed versions he could find.</summary>

## THE TONGUE-CUT SPARROW.

Once upon a time, there lived an old man and an old woman. The old man, who had a kind heart, kept a young sparrow, which he tenderly cared for. But the wife was an ill-tempered old thing; and one day, when the sparrow had pecked at some paste with which she was going to starch her linen, she flew into a great rage, cut the sparrow’s tongue, and let it loose. When the old man came home from the hills and found that the bird had flown, he asked what had become of it; so the old woman answered that she had cut its tongue and let it go because it had stolen her starching paste. Now the old man, hearing this cruel story, was deeply saddened and thought to himself, “Alas! Where can my bird have gone? Poor thing! Poor little tongue-cut sparrow! Where is your home now?” and he wandered far and wide, searching for his pet and crying, “Mr. Sparrow! Mr. Sparrow! Where are you living?”

One day, at the foot of a certain mountain, the old man fell in with the lost bird; and when they had congratulated one another on their safety, the sparrow led the old man to his home. Having introduced him to his wife and chicks, the sparrow set all sorts of delicacies before him and entertained him hospitably.

“Please partake of our humble food,” said the sparrow; “poor as it is, you are very welcome.”

“What a polite sparrow!” answered the old man, who remained for a long time as the sparrow’s guest and was feasted royally every day. At last the old man said that he must take his leave and return home; and the bird, offering

him two wicker baskets and begged him to carry them with him as a parting present. One of the baskets was heavy and the other was light; so the old man, saying that since he was feeble and advanced in years he would only accept the light one, shouldered it and trudged off home, leaving the sparrow family sad at parting from him.

When the old man got home, the old woman grew very angry and began to scold him, saying, “Well, and where have you been all these days? A fine thing, indeed, to be wandering about at your age!”

“Oh!” he replied, “I have been visiting the sparrows; and when I left, they gave me this wicker basket as a parting gift.” Then they opened the basket to see what was inside, and, lo and behold! It was full of gold, silver, and precious things. When the old woman, who was as greedy as she was bad-tempered, saw all the riches displayed before her, she changed her scolding tone and could not contain herself for joy.

“I’ll go and visit the sparrows, too,” she said, “and get a nice present.” So she asked the old man the way to the sparrows’ house and set out on her journey. Following his directions, she at last met the tongue-cut sparrow and exclaimed—

“Greetings! Greetings, Mr. Sparrow! I have been looking forward to the pleasure of seeing you.” She tried to flatter and coax the sparrow with sweet words.

The bird could not help but invite the woman to its home; however, it made no effort to feast her and said nothing about a parting gift. She, however, was not to be ignored; so she asked for something to take away with her in memory of her visit. The sparrow accordingly produced two baskets, as before, and the greedy old woman, choosing the heavier of the two, carried it off with her. But when she opened the basket to see what was inside, all sorts of hobgoblins and elves sprang out of it and began to torment her.

But the old man adopted a son, and his family grew rich and prosperous. What a happy old man!

# THE ACCOMPLISHED AND LUCKY TEA-KETTLE.

A long time ago, at a temple called Morinji, in the province of Jôshiu, there was an old tea-kettle. One day, when the priest of the temple was about to hang it over the hearth to boil the water for his tea, to his amazement, the kettle all of a sudden sprouted the head and tail of a badger. What a remarkable kettle, to be covered all over in fur! The priest, shocked, called in the novices of the temple to see the sight; and while they were staring foolishly, one suggesting one thing and another something else, the kettle, jumping up into the air, began flying about the room. 

More astonished than ever, the priest and his pupils tried to chase it; but no thief or cat was ever half as quick as this wonderful badger-kettle. At last, however, they managed to knock it down and secure it; and, holding it down with their combined efforts, they forced it into a box, intending to carry it away and throw it in some distant place, so that they would no longer be plagued by the goblin. For that day their troubles were over; but, as luck would have it, the tinker who usually worked for the temple stopped by, and the priest suddenly thought that it was a pity to throw the kettle away for nothing, and that he might as well get a small sum for it, no matter how small. So he brought out the kettle, which had returned to its former shape and had lost its head and tail, and showed it to the tinker. When the tinker saw the kettle, he offered twenty copper coins for it, and the priest was only too glad to close the deal and be rid of his troublesome piece of furniture. The tinker trudged off home with his pack and his new purchase. That

<summary>A tea kettle at Morinji temple transforms into a badger and flies around the room, causing a panic among the monks. After capturing the creature, the priest sells the kettle—now returned to its normal shape—to a traveling tinker.</summary>

The tinker started up in a fright to see what it could all mean, when all of a sudden the kettle resumed its former shape. This happened over and over again, until at last the tinker showed the tea kettle to a friend of his, who said, “This is certainly an accomplished and lucky tea kettle. You should take it around as a show, with songs and musical accompaniments, and make it dance and walk on the tightrope.”

The tinker, thinking this was good advice, made arrangements with a showman and set up an exhibition. The fame of the kettle’s performances soon spread abroad, until even the princes of the land sent orders for the tinker to come to them; and he grew rich beyond all his expectations. Even the princesses, too, and the great ladies of the court, took great delight in the dancing kettle, so that no sooner had it shown its tricks in one place than it was time for them to keep some other engagement. At last the tinker grew so rich that he took the kettle back to the temple, where it was placed as a precious treasure and worshipped as a saint.

# THE CRACKLING MOUNTAIN.

Once upon a time, there lived an old man and an old woman who kept a pet white hare, which they valued very much. One day, a badger that lived nearby came and ate up the food that had been put out for the hare; so the old man, flying into a great rage, seized the badger. After tying the beast to a tree, he went off to the mountain to cut wood, while the old woman stayed at home and ground the wheat for the evening porridge. Then the badger, with tears in his eyes, said to the old woman—

“Please, ma'am, please untie this rope!”

The old woman, thinking that it was a cruel thing to see a poor beast in pain, untied the rope; but no sooner was the ungrateful brute loose than he cried out—

“I’ll have my revenge for this!” and he was off in an instant.

When the hare heard this, he went off to the mountain to warn the old man; and while the hare was away on this errand, the badger came back and killed the woman. Then the beast, having taken the old woman’s form, made her body into broth and waited for the old man to come home from the mountain. When he returned, tired and hungry, the fake old woman said—

“Come, come; I’ve made such a delicious broth from the badger you tied up. Sit down and have a good supper.”

With these words, she served the broth, and the old man ate a hearty meal, licking his lips and praising the savory dish. But as soon as he had finished eating, the badger, returning to its natural shape, cried out—

<vocab>badger, hare, Crackling Mountain, broth, porridge, transformation</vocab>

<summary>A malicious badger tricks an old woman into releasing him, then kills her and feeds her remains to her husband while disguised in her form. The story sets up the conflict between the deceitful badger and the couple's pet hare.</summary>
<keywords>The Crackling Mountain, Japanese folklore, badger, hare, revenge, deception, Kachi-Kachi Yama</keywords>

--- Page 235 ---
<meta>This page continues the story of "The Crackling Mountain," following the badger's cruel revelation that he had killed the old man's wife and fed her to him in a broth.</meta>

->TALES OF OLD JAPAN.<-

"Nasty old man! You’ve eaten your own wife. Look at her bones, lying in the kitchen sink!" And, laughing contemptuously, the badger ran away and disappeared.

Then the old man, horrified at what he had done, let out a great cry of grief; and while he was bewailing his fate, the hare came home. Seeing how matters stood, the hare determined to avenge the death of his mistress. So he went back to the mountain and, coming across the badger, who was carrying a bundle of sticks on his back, he struck a light and set fire to the sticks without letting the badger see him. When the badger heard the crackling noise of the bundle of sticks burning on his back, he called out—

> "Hello! What is that noise?"

> "Oh!" answered the hare, "this is called the Crackling Mountain. There’s always this noise here."

And as the fire grew stronger and went pop! pop! pop! the badger said again—

> "Oh dear! What can this noise be?"

> "This is called the 'Pop! Pop! Mountain,'" answered the hare.

All at once the fire began to singe the badger’s back, so he fled, howling with pain, and jumped into a nearby river. But, although the water put out the fire, his back was burnt as black as a cinder. The hare, seeing an opportunity for torturing the badger to his heart’s content, made a poultice of cayenne pepper, which he carried to the badger’s house. Pretending to sympathize with him and to have an excellent remedy for burns, he applied his hot plaster to his enemy’s sore back. Oh! How it smarted and pained! And how the badger yelled and cried!

When, at last, the badger got well again, he went to the hare's house, intending to reproach him for having caused him so much pain. When he got there, he found that the hare had built himself a boat.

> "What have you built that boat for, Mr. Hare?" said the badger.

# FAIRY TALES.

“I am going to the capital of the moon,”¹ answered the hare; “won’t you come with me?”

“I have had enough of your company on the Crackling Mountain, where you played such tricks on me. I would rather make a boat for myself,” replied the badger, who immediately began building himself a boat of clay.

The hare, seeing this, laughed secretly; and so the two launched their boats upon the river. The waves came splashing against the two boats; but the hare’s boat was built of wood, while the badger’s was made of clay. As they rowed down the river, the clay boat began to crumble away; then the hare, seizing his paddle and brandishing it in the air, struck savagely at the badger’s boat until he had smashed it to pieces and killed his enemy.

When the old man heard that his wife’s death had been avenged, he was glad in his heart. He petted and loved the hare more than ever, whose brave deeds had allowed him to welcome the returning spring with joy.

## THE STORY OF THE OLD MAN WHO MADE WITHERED TREES TO BLOSSOM.

In the old, old days, there lived an honest man and his wife who had a favorite dog. They used to feed him fish and tidbits from their own kitchen. One day, as the old couple went out to work in their garden, the dog went with them and began playing around. All of a sudden, the dog stopped short and began to bark, “Bow, wow, wow!” while wagging his tail excitedly. The old people thought there must be something good to eat under the ground, so they brought a spade and began digging. Then—lo and behold!—the place was full of gold and silver coins, along with all sorts of precious things that had been buried there. They gathered the treasure together and, after giving charity to the poor, bought themselves rice fields and corn fields and became wealthy.

Now, in the next house lived a greedy and stingy old man and woman. When they heard what had happened, they came and borrowed the dog. After taking him home, they prepared a great feast for him and said—

“If you please, Mr. Dog, we would be very grateful if you would show us a place with plenty of money in it.”

The dog, however, who until then had received nothing but blows and kicks from these neighbors, would not eat any of the treats they set before him. So the old people began to get angry; they put a rope around the dog’s neck and led him out into the garden. But it was all in vain; no matter where they led him, the dog would not make a sound—he had no “bow-wow” for them. At last, however, the dog stopped at a certain spot and began to sniff. Thinking...

# FAIRY TALES.

Thinking that this must surely be the lucky place, they dug and found nothing but a quantity of dirt and nasty offal, over which they had to hold their noses. Furious at being disappointed, the wicked old couple seized the dog and killed him.

When the good old man saw that the dog, whom he had lent, did not come home, he went next door to ask what had become of him; and the wicked old man answered that he had killed the dog and buried him at the root of a pine tree. So the good old fellow, with a heavy heart, went to the spot and, having set out a tray with delicate food, burned incense and adorned the grave with flowers as he shed tears over his lost pet.

But there was more good luck in store yet for the old people—the reward of their honesty and virtue. How do you think that happened, my children? It is very wrong to be cruel to dogs and cats.

That night, when the good old man was fast asleep in bed, the dog appeared to him and, after thanking him for all his kindness, said—

> “Have the pine tree under which I am buried cut down and made into a mortar, and use it, thinking of it as if it were myself.”

The old man did as the dog had told him to do and made a mortar out of the wood of the pine tree; but when he ground his rice in it, each grain of rice was turned into some rich treasure. When the wicked old couple saw this, they came to borrow the mortar; but no sooner did they try to use it than all their rice was turned into filth; so, in a fit of rage, they broke up the mortar and burned it. But the good old man, little suspecting that his precious mortar had been broken and burned, wondered why his neighbors did not bring it back to him.

One night the dog appeared to him again in a dream and told him what had happened, adding that if he would take the ashes of the burned mortar and sprinkle them on withered trees, the trees would revive and suddenly put out flowers. After saying this, the dream vanished, and the old

The man, who heard for the first time about the loss of his mortar, ran off weeping to the neighbors' house and begged them at least to give him back the ashes of his treasure. Having obtained these, he returned home and tested their power on a withered cherry tree which, upon being touched by the ashes, immediately began to sprout and blossom. When he saw this wonderful effect, he put the ashes into a basket and went around the country, announcing himself as an old man who had the power of bringing dead trees back to life.

A certain prince, hearing of this and thinking it a very strange thing, sent for the old man, who demonstrated his power by causing all the withered plum and cherry trees to sprout and put forth flowers. So the prince gave him a rich reward of silk, cloth, and other presents, and sent him home rejoicing.

As soon as the neighbors heard of this, they collected all the ashes that remained. Having put them in a basket, the wicked old man went out into the castle town and announced that he was the old man who had the power of reviving dead trees and causing them to flower. He did not have to wait long before he was called into the prince's palace and ordered to exhibit his power. But when he climbed up into a withered tree and began to scatter the ashes, not a bud nor a flower appeared. Instead, the ashes all flew into the prince's eyes and mouth, blinding and choking him. When the prince's retainers saw this, they seized the old man and beat him almost to death, so that he crawled home in a pitiful state. When he and his wife found out what a trap they had fallen into, they stormed and scolded and flew into a rage, but that did no good at all.

The good old man and woman, as soon as they heard of their neighbors' distress, sent for them. After scolding them for their greed and cruelty, they gave them a share of their own riches which, by repeated strokes of luck, had now increased to a substantial sum. So the wicked old people changed their ways and led good and virtuous lives ever after.

# THE BATTLE OF THE APE AND THE CRAB.

If a man thinks only of his own profit and tries to benefit himself at the expense of others, he will incur the hatred of Heaven. Men should keep the story of the Battle of the Ape and the Crab in their hearts and teach it as a valuable lesson to their children.

Once upon a time, there was a crab who lived in a marsh in a certain part of the country. It happened one day that, after the crab had picked up a rice cake, an ape, who had found a nasty hard persimmon seed, came up and begged the crab to make an exchange with him. The crab, who was a simple-minded creature, agreed to this proposal; and they each went their way, the ape chuckling to himself at the good bargain he had made.

When the crab got home, he planted the persimmon seed in his garden, and as time passed, it sprouted and gradually grew into a large tree. The crab watched the growth of his tree with great delight; but when the fruit ripened and he was about to pluck it, the ape came by and offered to gather it for him. The crab consented, and the ape climbed up into the tree and began eating all the ripe fruit himself, while he only threw down the sour persimmons to the crab, inviting him at the same time to eat his fill. The crab, however, was not pleased with this arrangement and thought that it was his turn to play a trick on the ape; so he called out to him to come down head-first. The ape did as he was told; and as he crawled down head-first, the ripe fruit all came tumbling out of his pockets. The crab, having picked up the persimmons, ran off and hid himself in a hole. The ape,

<summary>A selfish ape tricks a simple-minded crab into trading a rice cake for a persimmon seed, but the crab later outwits the ape after the seed grows into a fruitful tree. The story is presented as a moral lesson against greed and taking advantage of others.</summary>

<keywords>ape, crab, persimmon seed, rice cake, trickery, moral lesson, Japanese folklore, greed</keywords>

--- Page 247 ---
<meta>This page continues the story of "The Battle of the Ape and the Crab." After the crab outwitted the ape by making him drop the ripe persimmons, the ape became enraged.</meta>

->TALES OF OLD JAPAN.<-

The ape, seeing this, lay in ambush, and as soon as the crab crept out of his hiding place, gave him a sound beating and went home. Just at this time, a friendly egg and a bee, who were the apprentices of a certain rice mortar, happened to pass that way; seeing the crab's pitiful condition, they bandaged his wounds and, having escorted him home, began to plan their revenge upon the cruel ape.

Having agreed upon a scheme, they all went to the ape's house while he was away. Each one having undertaken to play a specific part, they waited in secret for their enemy to return home. The ape, little dreaming of the mischief that was brewing, returned home and, wanting to drink a cup of tea, began lighting the fire on the hearth. Suddenly, the egg, which was hidden in the ashes, burst from the heat and splattered the frightened ape's face. He fled, howling with pain and crying, "Oh! What an unlucky beast I am!" Driven mad by the heat of the burst egg, he tried to go to the back of the house, but the bee darted out of a cupboard. A piece of seaweed, who had joined the group, came up at the same time, and the ape was surrounded by enemies. In despair, he seized the clothes rack and fought valiantly for a while, but he was no match for so many and was forced to run away with the others in hot pursuit. Just as he was making his escape through a back door, however, the piece of seaweed tripped him up, and the rice mortar, falling on him from behind, finished him off.

So the crab, having punished his enemy, went home in triumph and lived ever after in brotherly love with the seaweed and the mortar. Was there ever such a wonderful bit of fun!

# THE ADVENTURES OF LITTLE PEACHLING.

Many hundreds of years ago, there lived an honest old woodcutter and his wife. One fine morning, the old man went off to the hills with his billhook to gather a bundle of sticks, while his wife went down to the river to wash the dirty clothes. When she came to the river, she saw a peach floating down the stream; so she picked it up and carried it home with her, thinking to give it to her husband to eat when he came in. The old man soon came down from the hills, and the good wife set the peach before him; then, just as she was inviting him to eat it, the fruit split in two, and a little whimpering baby was born into the world. So the old couple took the baby and brought him up as their own; and, because he had been born in a peach, they called him *Momotarô*,¹ or Little Peachling.

Gradually, Little Peachling grew up to be strong and brave, and at last one day he said to his old foster-parents—

> “I am going to the ogres’ island to carry off the riches that they have stored up there. Please, then, make me some millet dumplings for my journey.”

So the old folks ground the millet and made the dumplings for him; and Little Peachling, after taking an affectionate leave of them, cheerfully set out on his travels.

As he was journeying on, he met an ape, who gibbered at him and said, “Kia! kia! kia! where are you off to, Little Peachling?”

---

<note>¹ *Momo* means a peach, and *Tarô* is the suffix for the names of eldest sons, such as *Hikotarô*, *Tokutarô*, etc. In modern times, however, the suffix has been applied without distinction to any male child.</note>

<summary>An old couple discovers a baby boy inside a giant peach and names him Momotarô. After growing into a strong young man, Momotarô sets out on a quest to the ogres' island to find treasure, starting his journey with homemade millet dumplings.</summary>
<keywords>Little Peachling, Momotarô, millet dumplings, ogres' island, woodcutter, Japanese folklore, adventure</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the story of Little Peachling's journey to the ogres' island, picking up from his meeting with the ape.</meta>

"I'm going to the ogres' island to carry off their treasure," answered Little Peachling.

"What are you carrying at your belt?"

"I'm carrying the very best millet dumplings in all Japan."

"If you'll give me one, I will go with you," said the ape.

So Little Peachling gave one of his dumplings to the ape, who received it and followed him. When he had gone a little further, he heard a pheasant calling—

"Ken! ken! ken!<note>The country people in Japan claim that the pheasant's call is a sign of an approaching earthquake.</note> where are you off to, Master Peachling?"

Little Peachling answered as before; and the pheasant, having begged for and received a millet dumpling, entered his service and followed him. A little while after this, they met a dog, who cried—

"Bow! wow! wow! where are you going, Master Peachling?"

"I'm going off to the ogres' island to carry off their treasure."

"If you will give me one of those nice millet dumplings of yours, I will go with you," said the dog.

"With all my heart," said Little Peachling. So he went on his way, with the ape, the pheasant, and the dog following after him.

When they got to the ogres' island, the pheasant flew over the castle gate, and the ape clambered over the castle wall, while Little Peachling, leading the dog, forced open the gate and entered the castle. Then they fought with the ogres, put them to flight, and took their king prisoner. So all the ogres did homage to Little Peachling and brought out the treasures which they had stored up. There were caps and coats that made their wearers invisible, jewels that controlled the ebb and flow of the tide, coral, musk, emeralds, amber, and tortoiseshell, besides gold and silver. All these were laid before Little Peachling by the conquered ogres.

So Little Peachling went home laden with riches and supported his foster-parents in peace and plenty for the rest of their lives.

<summary>Little Peachling assembles a team of animal companions—an ape, a pheasant, and a dog—by sharing his millet dumplings. Together, they invade the ogres' island, defeat the ogres, and return home with vast treasures to provide for Peachling's foster-parents.</summary>

# THE FOXES’ WEDDING.

Once upon a time, there was a young white fox named Fukuyemon. When he had reached the appropriate age, he shaved off his forelock <note>See the Appendix on "Ceremonies."</note> and began to think of taking a beautiful bride for himself. His father, the old fox, resolved to pass his inheritance to his son <note>See the note on the word *Inkiyo* in the story of the "Prince and the Badger."</note> and retired into private life; so the young fox, out of gratitude for this, worked hard and earnestly to increase his estate. Now it happened that in a famous old family of foxes, there was a beautiful young lady-fox with such lovely fur that the fame of her jewel-like charms spread far and wide. The young white fox, having heard of this, was determined to make her his wife, and a meeting was arranged between them. There was not a fault to be found on either side, so the arrangements were settled. Wedding presents were sent from the bridegroom to the bride’s house, accompanied by congratulatory speeches from the messenger, which were duly acknowledged by the person appointed to receive the gifts; the bearers, of course, received the customary fee in copper coins.

When the ceremonies were concluded, a lucky day was chosen for the bride to go to her husband’s house, and she was carried off in a formal procession during a rain shower, even while the sun was shining. <note>A rain shower during sunshine, which we call "the devil beating his wife," is called in Japan "the fox's bride going to her husband's house."</note> After the wine-drinking ceremonies were finished, the

<summary>A young white fox named Fukuyemon seeks a bride and arranges a marriage with a beautiful lady-fox from a prestigious family. The wedding procession takes place during a sun-shower, a phenomenon associated with fox weddings in Japanese folklore.</summary>
<keywords>Fukuyemon, white fox, Japanese folklore, fox's wedding, kitsune no yomeiri, Inkiyo, marriage customs, sun-shower</keywords>

bride changed her dress, and the wedding was concluded, without any obstacles or delays, amid singing and dancing and merrymaking.

The bride and bridegroom lived lovingly together, and a litter of little foxes was born to them, to the great joy of the old grandfather, who treated the little cubs as tenderly as if they had been butterflies or flowers. “They are the very image of their old grandfather,” he said, as proud as possible. “As for medicine, bless them, they are so healthy that they will never need even a copper coin’s worth!”

As soon as they were old enough, they were carried off to the temple of Inari Sama, the patron deity of foxes, and the old grandparents prayed that they might be delivered from dogs and all the other ills that foxes are subject to.

In this way the white fox gradually grew old and prosperous, and his children, year by year, became more and more numerous around him; so that, happy in his family and his business, every recurring spring brought him fresh cause for joy.

# THE HISTORY OF SAKATA KINTOKI.

A long time ago, there was an officer of the Emperor’s bodyguard named Sakata Kurando, a young man who, although he excelled in valor and in the arts of war, was of a gentle and loving disposition. This young officer was deeply enamored with a fair young lady named Yaégiri, who lived at Gojôzaka, in Kyoto. Now it happened that, after incurring the jealousy of certain other people, Kurando fell into disgrace with the Court and became a <term>Ronin</term>; consequently, he was no longer able to maintain any communication with his love, Yaégiri. Indeed, he became so poor that it was difficult for him even to survive. So he left the place and fled, and no one knew where he went. As for Yaégiri, lovesick and forlorn, and pining for her lost darling, she escaped from the house where she lived and wandered here and there through the country, seeking everywhere for Kurando.

Now Kurando, after he left the palace, became a tobacco merchant; as he was traveling about hawking his goods, it happened that he encountered Yaégiri. Having shared his last wishes with her, he took leave of her and ended his life.

Poor Yaégiri, after burying her lover, went to the Ashigara Mountain, a distant and lonely spot. There she gave birth to a little boy who, as soon as he was born, possessed such wonderful strength that he walked about and ran playing all over the mountain. A woodcutter, who happened to see the marvel, was greatly frightened at first and thought the sight altogether uncanny; but after a while, he grew used to the child, became quite fond of him, and called him

<summary>After the disgraced officer Sakata Kurando ends his life, his lover Yaégiri flees to Ashigara Mountain and gives birth to a boy of supernatural strength. This child, the future Sakata Kintoki, is discovered by a local woodcutter.</summary>

<keywords>Sakata Kintoki, Sakata Kurando, Yaégiri, Ronin, Ashigara Mountain, Japanese folklore, Kyoto</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the story of the child "Little Wonder," who was born on Ashigara Mountain to the lady Yaégiri after the death of his father, Sakata Kurando.</meta>

->TALES OF OLD JAPAN.<-

"Little Wonder," and gave his mother the name of the "Old Woman of the Mountain."

One day, as "Little Wonder" was playing about, he saw that on the top of a high cedar tree there was a tengu's nest <note>A *tengu*, or the Heavenly Dog, is a hobgoblin who lives in desolate places and is used to frighten naughty little children.</note>; so he began shaking the tree with all his might, until at last the tengu's nest came tumbling down.

As luck would have it, the famous hero Minamoto no Yorimitsu, with his retainers Watanabé Isuna, Usui Sadamitsu, and several others, had come to the mountain to hunt. Seeing the feat which "Little Wonder" had performed, he concluded that he could be no ordinary child. Minamoto no Yorimitsu ordered Watanabé Isuna to find out the child's name and parentage. The Old Woman of the Mountain, on being asked about him, answered that she was the wife of Kurando and that "Little Wonder" was the child of their marriage. She then proceeded to relate all the adventures which had happened to her.

When Yorimitsu heard her story, he said, "Certainly this child does not contradict his lineage. Give the boy to me, and I will make him my retainer." The Old Woman of the Mountain gladly consented and gave "Little Wonder" to Yorimitsu; but she herself remained in her mountain home. So "Little Wonder" went off with the hero Yorimitsu, who named him Sakata Kintoki; and in later times he became a famous and illustrious warrior, and his deeds are told to this day. He is the favorite hero of little children, who carry his portrait with them and wish that they could emulate his bravery and strength.

# THE ELVES AND THE ENVIOUS NEIGHBOR.

Once upon a time, there was a certain man who, being overtaken by darkness among the mountains, was driven to seek shelter in the trunk of a hollow tree. In the middle of the night, a large company of elves gathered at the place; and the man, peeping out from his hiding place, was frightened out of his wits. After a while, however, the elves began to feast and drink wine, and to amuse themselves by singing and dancing, until at last the man, caught up in the fun, forgot all about his fright and crept out of his hollow tree to join in the revelry. When the day was about to dawn, the elves said to the man, “You are a very jolly companion, and you must come out and have a dance with us again. You must make us a promise and keep it.” So the elves, intending to bind the man to return, took a large wen <note>A wen is a benign cyst or prominent lump on the skin.</note> that grew on his forehead and kept it as security; then they all left the place and went home. The man walked off to his own house in high spirits at having passed a jovial night and getting rid of his wen into the bargain. He told the story to all his friends, who congratulated him warmly on being cured of his wen. But there was a neighbor of his who was also troubled with a long-standing wen; and when he heard of his friend’s luck, he was filled with envy and went off to search for the hollow tree, in which, once he had found it, he spent the night.

Towards midnight the elves came, as he had expected, and began feasting and drinking, with songs and dances as before. As soon as he saw this, he came out of his hollow tree and began dancing and singing just as his neighbor had done. The

## THE GHOST OF SAKURA.

The misfortunes and death of the farmer Sôgorô are historical facts familiar to every Japanese person. Although the supernatural appearances said to have followed them might provoke a smile, they provide a powerful illustration of the relationship between the tenant and the lord of the soil, and of the boundless power for good or evil wielded by the latter. It is quite remarkable that in a country where the peasant is highly regarded—ranked second only to the soldier, and above the artisan and merchant in the four social classes—the lord of the manor should be left practically without control in his dealings with his people. This is especially striking because agriculture is protected by law from the encroachment of wild vegetation, even to the point of trimming overshadowing branches and cutting down hedgerow timber.

The land tax, or rather the yearly rent paid by the tenant, is usually set at forty percent of the produce; however, there is no clearly defined principle for this, and the landowner and the cultivator frequently divide the proceeds of the harvest in equal shares. Rice land is divided into three classes. According to these classes, it is calculated that one *tan* (1,800 square feet) of the best land should yield the owner a revenue of five bags of rice per year. Each of these bags holds four *tô* (a *tô* is slightly less than half an imperial bushel) and is worth at present (1868) three *riyos*, or about sixteen shillings. Land of the middle class should yield a revenue of three or four bags. The rent is paid

<meta>This page continues the explanation of the Japanese land tenure system, detailing how rents are paid for different types of crops and describing the economic hardships and social unrest caused by the extortionate practices of landlords during the feudal era.</meta>

either in rice or in money, according to the actual price of the grain, which varies considerably. It is due in the eleventh month of the year, when the crops have all been gathered and their market value has been fixed.

The rent of land bearing crops other than rice—such as cotton, beans, root vegetables, and so forth—is payable in money during the twelfth month. The choice of which crops to grow appears to be left to the tenant.

When pressed by poverty, the Japanese landlord does not limit himself to raising his legitimate rents; he can always force his needy tenants to pay a year’s rent in advance, or to provide a loan for whatever amount of money is required to meet his immediate needs. If the lord is just, the peasant is repaid in installments with interest over ten or twenty years. However, it too often happens that unjust and merciless lords do not repay these loans; instead, they demand further advances. It is then that the farmers—dressed in their grass raincoats and carrying sickles and bamboo poles—gather before the gate of their lord’s palace in the capital to present their grievances. They beg for the intervention of the retainers and even of the women who might happen to come out. Sometimes they pay for their boldness with their lives; but, at any rate, they have the satisfaction of shaming their persecutor in the eyes of his neighbors and the public.

Official reports of recent travels into the interior of Japan have fully proven the hard life the peasantry had to endure during the government of the <term>Tycoons</term> <note>The Shoguns</note>, and especially under the <term>Hatamotos</term> <note>Vassals directly serving the Shogun</note>, the nobility created by the dynasty. In one province where the village mayors seem to have supported their lord’s extortions, they had to flee from an enraged population. Taking advantage of the revolution, the people destroyed and looted the mayors' houses while loudly calling for a new and just land assessment. Meanwhile, throughout the country, farmers have cheered the resumption of sovereign power by the <term>Mikado</term> <note>The Emperor</note> and the abolition of the petty nobility.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Hatamotos from the previous page, who were vassals of the Shogun that prospered while their dependents suffered, and then transitions into a detailed explanation of the Japanese village administrative hierarchy and agricultural economics.</meta>

THE GHOST OF SAKURA.
O 2

who exalted themselves upon the misery of their dependents. Warming themselves in the sunshine of the court at Yedo, the Hatamotos grew fat and celebrated lavishly, and they cared little for those who groaned or starved. Money had to be found, and it was found.

It is necessary here to add a word regarding the position of the village mayors, who play such an important part in the story.

The peasants of Japan are ruled by three classes of officials: the *Nanushi*, or mayor; the *Kumigashira*, or chiefs of companies; and the *Hiyakushôdai*, or farmers' representatives. The village, which is governed by the *Nanushi*, or mayor, is divided into companies; these, consisting of five families each, are directed by a *Kumigashira*. These companies, again, are subdivided into groups of five men each, who choose one of their number to represent them in case they have any petition to present or any affairs to settle with their superiors. This official is the *Hiyakushôdai*. The mayor, the chief of the company, and the representative keep registers of the families and people under their control, and they are responsible for their good and orderly behavior. They pay taxes like the other farmers but receive a salary, the amount of which depends on the size and wealth of the village. Five percent of the yearly land tax forms the salary of the mayor, and the other officials each receive five percent of the tax paid by the small groups over which they respectively rule.

The average amount of land for one family to cultivate is about one *chô*, or 9,000 square yards; but there are farmers who have inherited as much as five or even six *chô* from their ancestors. There is also a class of farmers called, because of their poverty, "water-drinking farmers," who have no land of their own but hire land from those who have more than they can keep in their own hands. The rent paid in this way varies; but good rice land will bring in as high a rent as from £1 18s. to £2 6s. per *tan* (1,800 square feet).

Farm laborers are paid from six or seven *riyos* a year to as much as thirty *riyos* (the *riyo* being worth about 5s. 4d.);

Besides this, they are clothed and fed—not delicately, indeed, but adequately. The rice which they cultivate is an almost unknown luxury to them; millet is their staple food, and on festivals and holidays, they receive servings of barley or buckwheat. Where the mulberry tree is grown and the silkworm is "raised," the laborer receives the highest wage.

The rice crop on good land should yield twelve and a half times the seed sown, and on ordinary land only six to seven times. Ordinary farmland is only half as valuable as rice land, which cannot be purchased for less than forty *riyos* per *tan* of 1,800 square feet. Common hill or forest land is cheaper, again, than farmland; but orchards and groves of the *Pawlonia* are worth from fifty to sixty *riyos* per *tan*.

Regarding the punishment of crucifixion, by which Sôgorô was put to death, it is inflicted for the following offenses: parricide (including the murder or striking of parents, uncles, aunts, elder brothers, masters, or teachers), coining counterfeit money, and passing the barriers of the Tycoon's territory without a permit.<note>This last crime is, of course, now obsolete.</note> The criminal is attached to an upright post with two crossbars, to which his arms and feet are fastened by ropes. He is then pierced with spears by men belonging to the *Eta* or Pariah class. I once passed the execution ground near Yedo when a body was attached to the cross. The dead man had murdered his employer and, having been condemned to death by crucifixion, had died in prison before the sentence could be carried out. He was accordingly packed, in a squatting position, in a huge red earthenware jar which, after being tightly filled with salt, was hermetically sealed. On the anniversary of the commission of the crime, the jar was carried down to the execution ground and broken; the body was taken out and tied to the cross, the joints of the knees and arms having been cut to allow the extension of the stiffened and shrunken limbs. It was then pierced with spears and allowed to remain exposed for three days. An open grave, the upturned soil of which seemed almost entirely composed

## THE GHOST OF SAKURA.<note>The story, which also forms the subject of a play, is published with altered names so that the Hotta family might not be offended. The real names are preserved here. The events related took place during the rule of the Shogun Iyémitsu in the first half of the seventeenth century.</note>

How true is the principle laid down by Confucius: that the benevolence of princes is reflected in their country, while their wickedness causes sedition and confusion!

In the province of Shimôsa and the district of Sôma, Hotta Kaga no Kami was lord of the castle of Sakura and chief of a family that had for generations produced famous warriors. When Kaga no Kami—who had served in the <term>Gorôjiu</term>, the cabinet of the <term>Shogun</term>—died at the castle of Sakura, his eldest son Kôtsuké no Suké Masanobu inherited his estates and honors and was appointed to a seat in the <term>Gorôjiu</term>. However, he was a different man from the lords who had preceded him. He treated the farmers and peasants unjustly, imposing additional and heavy taxes, so that the tenants on his estates were driven to the extreme limit of poverty. Although year after year and month after month they prayed for mercy and protested against this injustice, no heed was paid to them, and the people throughout the villages were reduced to extreme distress. Accordingly, the chiefs of the one hundred and thirty-six villages, which produced a total revenue of 40,000 <term>kokus</term> of rice, assembled together in council and determined

Then little Kihachi, the third son, who, on account of his young age, should have been spared, was butchered while he was, in his simplicity, eating the sweets which had been thrown to him by the spectators.

When the execution of the children was over, the priests of Tôkôji took their bodies, and, having placed them in their coffins, carried them away amidst the lamentations of the bystanders and buried them with great solemnity.

Then Shigayémon, one of the servants of Danzayémon, the chief of the <term>Etas</term>, who had been hired for the purpose, was just about to thrust his spear, when O Man, Sôgorô's wife, raising her voice, said—

"Remember, my husband, that from the first you had made up your mind to this fate. What if our bodies are disgracefully exposed on these crosses?—we have the promises of the gods before us; therefore, do not mourn. Let us fix our minds upon death: we are drawing near to paradise, and shall soon be with the saints. Be calm, my husband. Let us cheerfully lay down our individual lives for the good of many. A man lives for only one generation; his name lives for many. A good name is more to be prized than life."

So she spoke; and Sôgorô on the cross, laughing cheerfully, answered—

"Well said, wife! What does it matter if we are punished for the sake of many? Our petition was successful, and there is nothing left to wish for. Now I am happy, for I have attained my heart's desire. The changes and chances of life are many. But if I had five hundred lives, and could five hundred times take this form of mine, I would die five hundred times to avenge this injustice. For myself I do not care; but that my wife and children should be punished also is too much."

“Come,” he shouted, “make haste and pierce me with the spear.”

“Your wishes shall be obeyed,” said the <term>Eta</term>, Shigayémon, and he thrust a spear into his right side until it came out at his left shoulder, and the blood streamed out like a fountain. Then he pierced the wife from the left side; and she, opening her eyes, said in a dying voice—

“Farewell, all you who are present. May harm stay far from you. Farewell! Farewell!” And as her voice grew faint, the second spear was thrust in from her right side, and she breathed her last. Sôgorô, with the color of his face not even changing, showed no sign of fear, but opening his eyes wide, said—

“Listen, my masters! All you who have come to see this sight. Remember that I shall pay my thanks to my lord Kôtsuké no Suké for this day’s work. You shall see it for yourselves, so that it shall be talked of for generations to come. As a sign, when I am dead, my head shall turn and face toward the castle. When you see this, do not doubt that my words shall come true.”

When he had spoken thus, the officer directing the execution gave a sign to the <term>Eta</term>, Shigayémon, and ordered him to finish the execution so that Sôgorô should speak no more. So Shigayémon pierced him twelve or thirteen times until he died. And when he was dead, his head turned and faced the castle. In this way, justice was carried out at the palace in Yedo and at the courthouse at home. But in the history of the world, from the dark ages down to the present time, there are few instances of one man laying down his life for the many as Sôgorô did; noble and peasant alike praise him.

Kôtsuké no Suké, terrified, sent his retainers to the temples and shrines to pray that the demons might be cast out; but the noises were heard nightly, just as before. When the eleventh month of the year arrived, the apparitions of human forms in the lady’s apartments became more and more frequent and terrible, with all the spirits shouting at her and howling that they had come to fetch her. The women would all scream and faint; and then the ghosts would disappear amid yells of laughter. This happened night after night, and even in the daytime the visions would manifest themselves; the lady’s sickness grew worse daily, until in the last month of the year she died of grief and terror. Then the ghost of Sôgorô and his crucified wife would appear day and night in the chamber of Kôtsuké no Suké, floating around the room and glaring at him with red and flaming eyes. The hair of the attendants would stand on end with terror; and if they tried to strike at the spirits, their limbs would be cramped, and their feet and hands would not obey their commands. Kôtsuké no Suké would draw the sword that lay by his bedside; but whenever he did so, the ghosts faded away, only to appear again in a more hideous shape than before, until at last, having exhausted his strength and spirits, even he became struck with terror. The whole household was thrown into confusion, and day after day mystic rites and incantations were performed by the priests over <term>braziers</term> of charcoal, while prayers were recited without ceasing; but the visions only became more frequent, and there was no sign of them stopping. After the fifth year of Shôhô, the name of the era was changed to Keian; and during the first year of Keian, the spirits continued to haunt the palace. Now they appeared in the chamber of Kôtsuké no Suké’s eldest son, surrounding themselves with even more terrors than before; and when Kôtsuké no Suké was about to go to the Shogun’s castle, they were seen howling their cries of vengeance in the porch of the house. In the second year of the Keian period, on the eleventh day of the tenth month, on the occasion of the festival of first lighting the fire on the hearth, the various <term>Daimyos</term> and <term>Hatamotos</term> of distinction went to the castle of the Shogun at Yedo to offer their congratulations on this occasion. During the ceremonies, Lord Hotta Kôtsuké no Suké and Sakai Iwami no Kami, lord of the castle of Matsumoto in the province of Shinshiu, had a quarrel, the origin of which was not made public; and Sakai Iwami no Kami, although he came from a brave and noble family, received so severe a wound that he died on the following day at the age of forty-three. In consequence of this, his family was ruined and disgraced.¹ Lord Kôtsuké no Suké, by great good fortune, managed to escape from the castle and took refuge in his own house; from there, mounting a famous horse called Hira-Abumi,² he fled to his castle of Sakura in Shimôsa, covering the distance, which is about sixty miles, in six hours. When he arrived in front of the castle, he called out in a loud voice to the guard within to open the gate, answering, in reply to their challenge, that he was Kôtsuké no Suké, the lord of the castle. At last, Kôtsuké no Suké began to feel that the death of his wife and his own current misfortunes were a just retribution for the death of Sôgorô and his wife and children; he felt like one awakened from a dream. Then, night and morning, in his repentance, he offered up prayers to the sainted spirit of the dead farmer and acknowledged and bewailed his crime. He vowed that if his family were spared from ruin and re-established, intercession should be made at the court of the Mikado, in Kyoto, on behalf of the spirit of Sôgorô. He promised that Sôgorô would be worshipped with even greater honors than before, so that his name should be handed down to all generations.

In the 1st month of the 4th year of Keian, Kôtsuké no Suké received a summons from the Shogun and, having been forgiven, was made lord of Matsuyama Castle in the province of Déwa, with a revenue of twenty thousand koku. In the same year, on the 20th day of the 4th month, the Shogun, Prince Iyémitsu, passed away at the age of forty-eight. Whether by the forgiving spirit of the prince or by the divine intervention of the sainted Sôgorô, Kôtsuké no Suké was promoted to Utsu no Miya Castle in the province of Shimotsuké, with a revenue of eighty thousand koku; and his name was changed to Hotta Hida no Kami. He also received back his original castle of Sakura, with a revenue of twenty thousand koku, so there can be no doubt that the saint was befriending him. In return for these favors, the shrine of Sôgorô was made as beautiful as a gem. It is needless to say how many of the peasants of the estate flocked to the shrine; any good luck that befell the people was attributed to it, and the devout worshipped there night and day.

Here follows a copy of the petition which Sôgorô presented to the Shogun:

> “We, the elders of the one hundred and thirty-six villages of the district of Chiba in the province of Shimôsa, and of the district of Buji in the province of Kadzusa, most reverently offer up this, our humble petition.

---

The belief in ghosts appears to be as universal as the belief in the immortality of the soul, upon which it depends. In both China and Japan, the departed spirit is granted the power of revisiting the earth and, in a visible form, tormenting its enemies and haunting those places where its mortal remains mourned and suffered. Haunted houses are slow to find tenants, for ghosts almost always return with revengeful intent; indeed, the owners of such houses will almost pay men to live in them, such is the dread they inspire and the anxiety to erase the stigma.
One cold winter’s night in Yedo, as I was sitting with a few Japanese friends, huddled around the weak heat of a charcoal brazier, the conversation turned to the story of Sôgorô and to ghostly apparitions in general. Many a strange tale was told that evening, and I noted down the three or four that follow, for the truth of which the storytellers vouched with the utmost confidence.
About ten years ago, there lived a fishmonger named Zenroku on Mikawa Street, in Kanda, Yedo. He was a poor man, living with his wife and one little boy. His wife fell ill and died, so he hired an old woman to look after his boy while he himself went out to sell his fish. It happened one day that he and the other peddlers of his guild were gambling; and when this reached the ears of the authorities, they were all thrown into prison. Although their offense was in itself a minor one, they were still kept for some time in custody while the matter was being investi-
