This is, indeed, a joyful return." Then Zenroku thanked those who had taken care of the child, saying that he had returned secretly that night by the favor of his jailers; but that on the following day his offense would be pardoned, and he would be able to take possession of his house again publicly. For that night, he must return to the prison. With this, he begged those present to continue their kind care for his baby; and, with a sad and reluctant expression, he left the house. On the following day, the officers of that ward were sent for by the prison authorities. They thought that they were summoned so that Zenroku might be handed back to them a free man, as he himself had said to them; but to their surprise, they were told that he had died the night before in prison, and they were ordered to carry away his dead body for burial. Then they knew that they had seen Zenroku's ghost; and that when he said that he would be returned to them on the morrow, he had been referring to his corpse. So they buried him properly, and brought up his son, who is alive to this day.

The next story was told by a professor in the college at Yedo, and, although it is not as recent as the last, he stated it to be well-authenticated and a matter of general notoriety.

About two hundred years ago, there was a chief of police named Aoyama Shuzen, who lived on the street called Bancho in Yedo. His duty was to detect thieves and arsonists. He was a cruel and violent man, without a heart.

This man Shuzen had in his house a servant-maid named O Kiku (the Chrysanthemum), who had lived with the family since her childhood and was well-acquainted with her master's temper. One day O Kiku accidentally broke one of a set of ten porcelain plates, which he valued highly. She knew that she would suffer for her carelessness, but she thought that if she concealed the matter, her punishment would be even more severe; so she went at once to her master's wife and, in fear and trembling, confessed what she had done. When Shuzen came home and heard that one of his favorite plates was broken, he flew into a violent rage. He took the girl to a cupboard, where he left her bound with cords, and every day he cut off one of her fingers. O Kiku, tightly bound and in agony, could not move; but at last she managed to bite or cut the ropes apart, and, escaping into the garden, she threw herself into a well and drowned. From that time on, every night a voice was heard coming from the well, counting: one, two, three, and so on up to nine—the number of the plates that remained unbroken—and then, when the tenth plate should have been counted, there would come a burst of lamentation. The servants of the house, terrified by this, all left their master's service until Shuzen, not having a single retainer left, was unable to perform his public duties; and when the government officers heard of this, he was dismissed from his office. At this time there was a famous priest called Mikadzuki Shônin, of the Denzuin temple, who, having been told of the affair, came to the house one night. When the ghost began to count the plates, he reproved the spirit, and by his prayers and admonitions caused it to stop troubling the living.

One night, his wife, who looked after the house in his absence, was frightened by a terrifying noise coming from a pond in the garden. When her husband came home, she told him what had happened; on the following night, he returned earlier than usual and waited for the ghostly noise. Thinking that there must be some cause for this, he made careful inquiries and learned that the previous tenant, about ten years earlier, had borrowed money from a blind shampooer,¹ and, being unable to pay the debt, had murdered his creditor when he began to press for the money, and had thrown his head into the pond.    The belief in curses hanging over families for generations is as common as the belief in ghosts and supernatural apparitions. There is a strange story of this nature concerning the house of Asai, which belongs to the <term>Hatamoto</term> class. Six generations ago, the ancestor of the current representative had a certain concubine who was in love with a man who frequented the house and wished in her heart to marry him; but, being a virtuous woman, she never thought of doing any wrong. However, the wife of Lord Asai was jealous of the girl and persuaded her husband that her rival for his affections had been unfaithful. When he heard this, he was very angry and beat her with a candlestick so severely that he put out her left eye. The girl, who had indignantly protested her innocence, found herself treated so cruelly that she pronounced a curse against the house. At this, her master seized the candlestick again, dashed out her brains, and killed her. Shortly afterward, Lord Asai lost his left eye, fell sick, and died. From that time until today, it is said that the heads of the house have all lost their left eyes after the age of forty; shortly after, they have fallen sick and died at the same age as the cruel lord who killed his concubine.

### NOTE.

Of the many beautiful scenes in Yedo, none is more worth visiting than the temple of Zôjôji, one of the two great burial places of the <term>Shoguns</term>. Indeed, if you wish to see the most beautiful spots of any Eastern city, ask for the cemeteries; the homes of the dead are always the loveliest places. Standing in a park of glorious, beautifully kept firs and pines—which contains a small town of neat, clean-looking houses, along with thirty-four temples for the use of the priests and shrine attendants—the main temple, with its huge red pillars supporting a heavy Chinese-style roof of gray tiles, is approached through a colossal open hall which

The big bell outside the main hall is remarkable more for the great beauty of the deep bass waves of sound which it rolls through the city than for its size, which is nothing compared with that of the big bells of Moscow and Peking; still, it is not to be despised even in that respect, for it is ten feet high and five feet eight inches in diameter, while its metal is a foot thick: it was hung in the year 1673. But the chief objects of interest in these beautiful grounds are the chapels attached to the tombs of the <term>Shoguns</term>.

It is said that as Prince <term>Iyéyasu</term> was riding into <term>Yedo</term> to take possession of his new castle, the Abbot of <term>Zôjôji</term>—an ancient temple which then stood at <term>Hibiya</term>, near the castle—went out and waited before the gate to do homage to the Prince. <term>Iyéyasu</term>, seeing that the Abbot was no ordinary man, stopped and asked his name, and entered the temple to rest himself. The smooth-spoken monk soon found such favor with <term>Iyéyasu</term> that he chose <term>Zôjôji</term> to be his family temple; and seeing that its grounds were narrow and inconveniently near the castle, he caused it to be moved to its present site. In the year 1610, the temple was raised, through the intercession of <term>Iyéyasu</term>, to the dignity of the Imperial Temples, which, until the last revolution, were presided over by princes of the blood; and the Abbot was granted the right, when going to the castle, of sitting in his litter as far as the entrance hall, instead of dismounting at the usual place and proceeding on foot through several gates and courtyards. Nor were the privileges of the temple limited to empty honors, for it was endowed with lands valued at five thousand <term>kokus</term> of rice annually.

A second gateway, supported by gilt pillars carved all round with figures of dragons, leads into another court, in which are a bell tower, a great cistern cut out of a single block of stone like a sarcophagus, and a smaller number of lanterns of bronze; these are given by the <term>Go San Ké</term>, the three princely families in which the succession to the office of <term>Shogun</term> was vested. Inside this is a third court, partly covered like a cloister, the approach to which is a doorway of even greater beauty and richness than the last; the ceiling is gilt and painted with arabesques and with heavenly angels playing on musical instruments, and the panels of the walls are sculptured in high relief with admirable representations of birds and flowers, life-size and life-like, all being colored to imitate nature. Inside this enclosure stands a shrine, before the closed door of which a priest on one side, and a retainer of the house of <term>Tokugawa</term> on the other, sit mounting guard, mute and immovable as though they themselves were part of the carved ornaments. There is little difference between the three shrines, all of which are decorated in the same manner. It is very difficult to do justice to their beauty in words. Writing many thousand miles away from them, I have the memory before me of a place green in winter, pleasant and cool in the hottest summer; of peaceful cloisters, of the fragrance of incense, of the subdued chant of richly robed priests, and the music of bells; of exquisite designs, harmonious coloring, and rich gilding. The hum of the vast city outside is unheard here: <term>Iyéyasu</term> himself, in the mountains of <term>Nikkô</term>, has no quieter resting place than his descendants in the heart of the city over which they ruled.

Besides the graves of the <term>Shoguns</term>, <term>Zôjôji</term> contains other lesser shrines, in which are buried the wives of the second, sixth, and eleventh <term>Shoguns</term>, and the father of <term>Iyénobu</term>, the sixth <term>Shogun</term>, who succeeded to the office by adoption. There is also a holy place called the <term>Satsuma Temple</term>, which has a special interest; in it is a tablet in honor of <term>Tadayoshi</term>, the fifth son of <term>Iyéyasu</term>, whose title was <term>Matsudaira Satsuma no Kami</term>, and who died young. At his death, five of his retainers, with one <term>Ogasawara Kemmotsu</term> at their head, disemboweled themselves so that they might follow their young master into the next world. They were buried in this place; and I believe that this is the last instance on record of the ancient Japanese custom of <term>Junshi</term>, that is to say, "dying with the master."

There are, during the year, several great festivals which are specially celebrated at <term>Zôjôji</term>; the chief of these are the <term>Kaisanki</term>, or founder's day, which is on the eighteenth day of the seventh month; the twenty-fifth day of the first month, the anniversary of the death of the monk <term>Hônen</term>, the founder of the <term>Jôdo sect</term> of <term>Buddhism</term> (the sect to which the temple belongs); the anniversary of the death of Buddha, on the fifteenth of the second month; the birthday of Buddha, on the eighth day of the fourth month; and from the sixth to the fifteenth of the tenth month.

It faces the <term>Ki-mon</term>, or Devil’s Gate, of the castle, and was erected upon the model of the temple of <term>Hi-yei-zan</term>, one of the most famous of the holy places of <term>Kiôto</term>. Having founded the temple, the next care of <term>Iyémitsu</term> was to pray that <term>Morizumi</term>, the second son of the retired emperor, should come and reside there; and from that time until 1868, the temple was always presided over by a <term>Miya</term>, or member of the <term>Mikado</term>’s family, who was specially charged with the care of the tomb of <term>Iyéyasu</term> at <term>Nikkô</term>, and whose position was that of an ecclesiastical chief or primate over the east of Japan.

The temples in <term>Yedo</term> are not to be compared in point of beauty with those in and about <term>Peking</term>; what is marble there is wood here. Still, they are very handsome, and in the days of its magnificence, the Temple of <term>Uyéno</term> was one of the finest. Alas! the main temple, the hall in honor of the sect to which it belongs, the hall of services, the bell-tower, the entrance-hall, and the residence of the prince of the imperial blood, were all burned down in the battle of <term>Uyéno</term>, in the summer of 1868, when the <term>Shogun</term>’s men made their last stand in <term>Yedo</term> against the troops of the <term>Mikado</term>. The fate of the day was decided by two field guns, which the latter managed to mount on the roof of a neighboring tea-house; and the <term>Shogun</term>’s men, driven out of the place, carried off the <term>Miya</term> in the vain hope of raising his standard in the north as that of a rival <term>Mikado</term>. A few of the lesser temples and tombs, and the beautiful park-like grounds, are but the remnants of the former glory of <term>Uyéno</term>. 

Among these is a temple in the form of a roofless stage, in honor of the thousand-handed <term>Kwannon</term>. In the middle ages, during the civil wars between the houses of <term>Gen</term> and <term>Hei</term>, one <term>Morihisa</term>, a captain of the house of <term>Hei</term>, after the destruction of his clan, went and prayed for a thousand days at the temple of the thousand-handed <term>Kwannon</term> at <term>Kiyomidzu</term>, in <term>Kiôto</term>. His retreat having been discovered, he was seized and brought bound to <term>Kamakura</term>, the chief town of the house of <term>Gen</term>. Here he was condemned to die at a place called <term>Yui</term>, by the sea-shore; but every time that the executioner lifted his sword to strike, the blade was broken by the god <term>Kwannon</term>, and at the same time the wife of <term>Yoritomo</term>, the chief of the house of <term>Gen</term>, was warned in a dream to spare <term>Morihisa</term>’s life. So <term>Morihisa</term> was reprieved, and rose to power in the state; and all this was by the miraculous intervention of the god <term>Kwannon</term>, who takes such good care of

Besides them, five wives of the <term>Shoguns</term> and the father of the eleventh <term>Shogun</term> are buried here.

# HOW TAJIMA SHUMÉ WAS TORMENTED BY A DEVIL OF HIS OWN CREATION.

ONCE upon a time, a certain <term>Rônin</term> named <term>Tajima Shumé</term>, a capable and well-educated man traveling to see the world, went up to <term>Kiyôto</term> by the <term>Tôkaidô</term>.<note>The road of the Eastern Sea, the famous highway leading from Kiyôto to Yedo. The name is also used to indicate the provinces through which it runs.</note> One day, near <term>Nagoya</term> in the province of <term>Owari</term>, he met a wandering priest and struck up a conversation with him. Finding that they were headed for the same place, they agreed to travel together, passing the time on their long journey with pleasant talk on various subjects. Gradually, as they became more friendly, they began to speak freely about their private affairs; and the priest, trusting completely in the honor of his companion, told him the purpose of his journey.

"For some time now," he said, "I have cherished a wish that has occupied all my thoughts. I am determined to cast a metal statue in honor of <term>Buddha</term>. With this goal in mind, I have wandered through various provinces collecting alms, and—who knows through what exhausting labor?—I have succeeded in gathering two hundred ounces of silver. I believe this will be enough to erect a handsome bronze figure."

What does the proverb say? "He who carries a jewel in his breast carries poison." No sooner had the <term>Rônin</term> heard these words from the priest than an evil thought arose within him, and

He thought to himself, “A man’s life, from the womb to the grave, is made up of good and bad luck. Here I am, nearly forty years old, a wanderer without a profession or even a hope of moving up in the world. To be sure, it seems a shame; yet if I could steal the money this priest is boasting about, I could live comfortably for the rest of my days;” and so he began considering how he might best achieve his goal. But the priest, far from guessing the direction of his companion’s thoughts, journeyed cheerfully on until they reached the town of <term>Kuana</term>. Here there is an arm of the sea which is crossed by ferryboats that depart as soon as about twenty or thirty passengers have gathered; and the two travelers embarked on one of these boats. About halfway across, the priest felt a sudden need to go to the side of the boat; and the <term>Rônin</term>, following him, tripped him while no one was looking and threw him into the sea. When the boatmen and passengers heard the splash and saw the priest struggling in the water, they were alarmed and made every effort to save him; but the wind was favorable, and the boat was running swiftly under swelling sails. They were soon a few hundred yards away from the drowning man, who sank before the boat could be turned back to rescue him.

When he saw this, the <term>Rônin</term> faked the greatest grief and dismay, and said to his fellow passengers, “This priest, whom we have just lost, was my cousin. He was going to <term>Kiyôto</term> to visit the shrine of his patron; and as I happened to have business there as well, we decided to travel together. Now, alas! because of this misfortune, my cousin is dead, and I am left alone.”

He spoke so sincerely and wept so freely that the passengers believed his story, and they pitied him and tried to comfort him. Then the <term>Rônin</term> said to the boatmen—

“By right, we should report this matter to the authorities; but since I am pressed for time, and the situation might bring trouble upon you as well, perhaps we had better keep it quiet for now. I will go immediately to <term>Kiyôto</term> and inform my cousin’s patron, as well as writing home about it."

Fortune favored his speculations, and he began to amass great wealth. He lived at his ease, denying himself nothing; and in the course of time, he married a wife who bore him a child.

Thus the days and months wore on, until one fine summer night, about three years after the priest’s death, <term>Tokubei</term> stepped out onto the veranda of his house to enjoy the cool air and the beauty of the moonlight. Feeling dull and lonely, he began musing over all kinds of things, when suddenly the deed of murder and theft committed so long ago vividly recurred to his memory. He thought to himself, "Here am I, grown rich and fat on the money I recklessly stole. Since then, all has gone well with me; yet, if I had not been poor, I would never have turned into an assassin or a thief. Woe to me! What a pity it was!" And as he was turning the matter over in his mind, a feeling of remorse came over him, in spite of all he could do. While his conscience thus struck him, he suddenly, to his utter amazement, saw the faint outline of a man standing near a fir tree in the garden. Looking more attentively, he perceived that the man’s whole body was thin and worn, and his eyes were sunken and dim; and in the poor ghost before him, he recognized the very priest whom he had thrown into the sea at <term>Kuana</term>. Finally, worn down by such constant harassment, Tokubei fell ill and kept muttering, "Oh, misery! Misery! The wandering priest is coming to torture me!" Hearing his moans and the disturbance he made, the people in the house thought he was mad and called in a physician, who prescribed medicine for him. But neither pill nor potion could cure Tokubei, whose strange frenzy soon became the talk of the whole neighborhood.

Now it happened that the story reached the ears of a certain wandering priest who was staying on the next street. When he heard the details, this priest gravely shook his head, as though he knew all about it, and sent a friend to Tokubei's house to say that a wandering priest living nearby had heard of his illness and, no matter how serious it was, would undertake to heal it by means of his prayers. Tokubei's wife, driven half-mad by her husband's sickness, did not lose a moment in sending for the priest and taking him into the sick man's room.

But no sooner did Tokubei see the priest than he yelled out, "Help! Help! Here is the wandering priest come to torment me again. Forgive me! Forgive me!" and hiding his head under the blanket, he lay quivering all over. Then the priest turned everyone else out of the room, put his mouth to the frightened man's ear, and whispered—

> "Three years ago, at the Kuana ferry, you threw me into the water; and you remember it well."

But Tokubei was speechless and could only shake with fear.

"Fortunately," continued the priest, "I had learned to swim and dive as a boy; so I reached the shore and, after wandering through many provinces, succeeded in erecting a bronze statue of Buddha, thus fulfilling my heart's desire. On my journey home, I took a room in the next street and heard of your strange illness. Thinking I could determine its cause, I came to see you, and I am glad to find I was not mistaken. You have done a hateful deed; but am I not a priest? Have I not renounced the things of this world? Would it not be unfitting for me to hold a grudge? Repent, therefore, and abandon your evil ways. To see you do so would be my greatest happiness. Take heart now, and look me in the face; you will see that I am truly a living man, and not a vengeful spirit come to torment you."

Seeing he had no ghost to deal with, and overwhelmed by the priest's kindness, Tokubei burst into tears and answered, "Indeed, indeed, I don't know what to say. In a fit of madness, I was tempted to kill and rob you. Fortune favored me ever after; but the richer I grew, the more keenly I felt how wicked I had been, and the more I foresaw that my victim's vengeance would some day overtake me. Haunted by this thought, I lost my nerve, until one night I saw your ghost, and from that time on I fell ill. But how you managed to escape and are still alive is more than I can understand."

"A guilty man," said the priest with a smile, "trembles at the rustling of the wind or the chattering of a stork's beak; a murderer's conscience preys upon his mind until he sees what is not there. Poverty drives a man to crimes that he repents of once he is wealthy. How true is the doctrine of <term>Môshi</term>,¹ that the heart of man, pure by nature, is corrupted by circumstances."

Thus he preached; and Tokubei, who had long since repented of his crime, begged for forgiveness and gave him a large sum of money, saying, "Half of this is the amount I stole from you three years ago; the other half I beg you to accept as interest, or as a gift."

# CONCERNING CERTAIN SUPERSTITIONS.

CATS, foxes, and badgers are regarded with superstitious awe by the Japanese, who attribute to them the power of assuming human shape in order to bewitch mankind. Like the fairies of our Western tales, however, they work for good as well as for evil ends. To do them a good turn is to secure powerful allies; but woe to him who injures them!—he and his family will surely suffer for it. Cats and foxes seem to have been looked upon as uncanny beasts all the world over; but it is new to me that badgers should have a place in fairy-land. The island of Shikoku, the southernmost of the great Japanese islands, appears to be the part of the country in which the badger is regarded with the greatest veneration. Among the many tricks which he plays upon the human race is one of which I have a clever representation carved in ivory. Lying in wait in lonely places after dusk, the badger watches for lost travelers: should one appear, the beast, drawing a long breath, swells out his belly and drums delicately upon it with his clenched fist, producing such entrancing tones that the traveler cannot resist turning aside to follow the sound, which, like a <term>Will-o'-the-wisp</term> <note>a phosphorescent light seen over marshy ground, often personified as a misleading spirit</note>, recedes as he advances, until it lures him on to his destruction. Love is, however, the most powerful instrument which the cat, the fox, and the badger alike employ for the ruin of man. No German poet ever imagined a more captivating water-nymph than the fair virgins by whom the knight of Japanese romance is assailed: the true hero recognizes and slays the beast; the weaker mortal yields and perishes.

<summary>The author describes Japanese superstitions regarding cats, foxes, and badgers, particularly their ability to shape-shift and trick humans through music or romantic temptation. Special focus is given to the badger’s belly-drumming in the folklore of Shikoku island.</summary>
<keywords>Japanese folklore, superstitions, shape-shifting, cats, foxes, badgers, Shikoku, Will-o'-the-wisp, kitsune, tanuki</keywords>

## THE VAMPIRE CAT OF NABÉSHIMA.

THERE is a tradition in the Nabéshima <note>The family of the Prince of Hizen, one of the eighteen chief Daimyo of Japan.</note> family that, many years ago, the Prince of Hizen was bewitched and cursed by a cat that had been kept by one of his retainers. This prince had in his house a lady of rare beauty called O Toyo: among all his ladies she was the favorite, and there was none who could rival her charms and accomplishments. One day the Prince went out into the garden with O Toyo and remained enjoying the fragrance of the flowers until sunset, when they returned to the palace, never noticing that they were being followed by a large cat. Having parted from her lord, O Toyo retired to her own room and went to bed. At midnight she awoke with a start and became aware of a huge cat that crouched watching her; and when she cried out, the beast sprang on her and, fixing its cruel teeth in her delicate throat, throttled her to death. What a pitiful end for such a beautiful lady, the darling of her prince’s heart, to die suddenly, bitten to death by a cat! Then the cat, having scratched out a grave under the veranda, buried the body of O Toyo, and assuming her form, began to bewitch the Prince.

But my lord the Prince knew nothing of all this, and little thought that the beautiful creature who caressed and fondled him was a demonic and foul beast that had killed his mistress and assumed her shape in order to drain out his life’s blood. Day by day, as time went on, the Prince’s strength dwindled away; the color of his face was changed and became pale and livid; and he was like a man suffering from a deadly

Because of this, his councillors appointed a hundred of his retainers to sit up and watch over him every night; but, strange to say, toward ten o’clock on the very first night that the watch was set, the guards were overcome by a sudden and unaccountable drowsiness which they could not resist, until one by one every man had fallen asleep. The following night the same thing occurred, and the Prince was subjected to the demon’s tyranny, while his guards slept helplessly around him. Night after night this was repeated, until at last three of the Prince’s councillors determined to sit up on guard themselves and see whether they could overcome this mysterious drowsiness; but they fared no better than the others, and by ten o’clock they were fast asleep. Now, as all our efforts are of no use, let us seek out Ruiten, the chief priest of the temple called Miyô In, and beg him to offer prayers for the recovery of my lord.”

And the other councillors, approving what Isahaya Buzen had said, went to the priest Ruiten and hired him to recite litanies so that the Prince might be restored to health.

Therefore, I have no choice but to pray to the gods of the country and to Buddha that my lord may regain his health.”

“Your purpose is indeed a good one; but what a strange sickness this is that afflicts my lord! Every night he suffers from horrible dreams, and the retainers who sit up with him are all overcome by a mysterious sleep, so that not one can stay awake. It is very remarkable.”

So he went his way in high spirits, and at nightfall, having made all his preparations, he took his place among the hundred gentlemen who were on duty in the prince’s bedroom.

Now the Prince slept in the center of the room, and the hundred guards around him sat keeping themselves awake with entertaining conversation and pleasant stories. But, as ten o’clock approached, they began to doze off as they sat; and in spite of all their efforts to keep one another awake, they all gradually fell asleep. All this while, Itô Sôda felt an irresistible urge to sleep creeping over him, and, though he tried all sorts of ways to rouse himself, he saw that there was no way to avoid it except by resorting to an extreme measure for which he had already made his preparations. “What wondrous loyalty!” said the lady.

“Is it not the duty of a retainer to lay down his life for his master? Is such a scratch as this worth thinking about?”

The goblin, however, who had been tormenting the Prince every night in the form of O Toyo and had come again that night for that very purpose, was defeated by the watchfulness of Itô Sôda. At last, day broke, and the other officers, when they awoke and opened their eyes, saw that Itô Sôda had stayed awake by stabbing himself in the thigh. They were deeply ashamed and went home discouraged.

That morning, Itô Sôda went to the house of Isahaya Buzen and told him everything that had occurred the previous night. The councilors were all loud in their praise of Itô Sôda’s behavior and ordered him to keep watch again that night. At the same hour, the false O Toyo came and looked all around the room; all the guards were asleep except for Itô Sôda, who was wide awake. Being frustrated again, she returned to her own apartments.

Now, since Sôda had been on guard, the Prince had passed quiet nights and his health began to improve. There was great joy in the palace, and Sôda was promoted and rewarded with an estate. Meanwhile, O Toyo, seeing that her nightly visits bore no fruit, stayed away; from that time on, the night guards were no longer subject to fits of drowsiness. This coincidence struck Sôda as very strange, so he went to Isahaya Buzen and told him that, for certain, this O Toyo was nothing other than a goblin. Isahaya Buzen reflected for a while and said:

"Well, then, how shall we kill the foul thing?"

But the Prince recovered from his sickness; and Itô Sôda was richly rewarded.

# THE STORY OF THE FAITHFUL CAT.

About sixty years ago, in the summer, a man went to visit a certain house in Osaka and, in the course of conversation, said—

“I have eaten some very extraordinary cakes today,” and on being asked what he meant, he told the following story:—

“I received the cakes from the relatives of a family who were celebrating the hundredth anniversary of the death of a cat that had belonged to their ancestors. When I asked for the history of the matter, I was told that, in former days, a young girl of the family, when she was about sixteen years old, used always to be followed around by a tomcat who was raised in the house, so much so that the two were never separated for an instant. When her father noticed this, he was very angry, thinking that the tomcat—forgetting the kindness with which he had been treated for years in the house—had fallen in love with his daughter and intended to cast a spell upon her; so he determined that he must kill the beast. As he was planning this in secret, the cat overheard him, and that night went to his pillow and, assuming a human voice, said to him—

“‘You suspect me of being in love with your daughter; and although you might well be justified in thinking so, your suspicions are groundless. The fact is this:—There is a very large old rat who has been living for many years in your granary. Now it is this old rat who is in love with my young mistress, and this is why I dare not leave her side for a moment, for fear the old rat should carry her off. There-

The people of the house opened the door and crowded out to see what had happened; and there they saw the two cats and the rat all locked together and panting for breath. So they cut the throat of the rat, which was as big as either of the cats. Then they attended to the two cats; but, although they gave them ginseng<gloss>1</gloss> and other restoratives, they both grew weaker and weaker until at last they died. So the rat was thrown into the river, but the two cats were buried with all honors in a neighboring temple.”

## HOW A MAN WAS BEWITCHED AND HAD HIS HEAD SHAVED BY THE FOXES.

In the village of Iwahara, in the province of Shinshiu, there lived a family that had acquired significant wealth in the wine trade. On a lucky occasion, it happened that a number of guests were gathered together at their house, feasting on wine and fish; and as the wine cup went around, the conversation turned to foxes. Among the guests was a certain carpenter named Tokutarô, a man about thirty years old, of a stubborn and headstrong nature, who said—

"Well, sirs, you have been talking for some time about men being bewitched by foxes; surely you must be under their influence yourselves to say such things. How on earth can foxes have such power over men? At any rate, men must be great fools to be so deluded. Let us have no more of this nonsense."

Upon this, a man who was sitting by him answered—

"Tokutarô knows little of what goes on in the world, or he would not speak so. How many thousands of men are there who have been bewitched by foxes? Why, there have been at least twenty or thirty men tricked by the beasts on the Maki Moor alone. It is hard to disprove facts that have happened before our eyes."

"You are no better than a pack of born idiots!" said Tokutarô. "I will vow to go out to the Maki Moor this very night and prove it. There is not a fox in all Japan that can make a fool of Tokutarô."

Thus he spoke in his pride; but the others were all angry with him for boasting, and said—

"If you return without anything having happened, we will

When Tokutarô had finished his bowing to the priest and the ceremony was over, there was a loud burst of laughter; and at the same moment dawn broke, and Tokutarô found himself alone in the middle of a large moor. At first, in his surprise, he thought that it was all a dream and was much annoyed at having been tricked by the foxes. He then passed his hand over his head and found that he was shaved quite bald. There was nothing for it but to get up, wrap a handkerchief around his head, and go back to the place where his friends were gathered.

“Hello, Tokutarô! So you’ve come back. Well, what about the foxes?”

“Really, gentlemen,” he replied, bowing, “I am quite ashamed to appear before you.”

Then he told them the whole story, and, when he had finished, pulled off the handkerchief and showed his bald head.

“What a great joke!” shouted his listeners, and amid roars of laughter, they claimed the bet of fish and wine. It was duly paid; but Tokutarô never allowed his hair to grow again; he renounced the world and became a priest under the name of Sainen.

There are many stories told of men being shaved by foxes; but this story was personally observed by Mr. Shôminsai, a teacher from the city of Yedo, during a holiday trip he took to the countryside where the event occurred; and I have recorded it in the very same words in which he told it to me.

# THE GRATEFUL FOXES.

One fine spring day, two friends went out to a moor to gather fern, accompanied by a boy carrying a bottle of wine and a box of provisions. As they were wandering about, they saw at the foot of a hill a fox that had brought out its cub to play; and while they watched, struck by the unusual sight, three children came up from a neighboring village with baskets in their hands, out on the same errand as the men. As soon as the children saw the foxes, they picked up a bamboo stick and crept up on the creatures from behind; and when the adult foxes fled, they surrounded them and beat them with the stick until they ran away as fast as their legs could carry them. However, two of the boys pinned down the cub and, seizing it by the scruff of the neck, went off in high spirits.

The two friends watched the whole time, and one of them, raising his voice, shouted out, "Hey there! You boys! What are you doing with that fox?"

The oldest of the boys replied, "We're going to take him home and sell him to a young man in our village. He'll buy him, and then he'll boil him in a pot and eat him."

"Well," the man replied, after considering the matter carefully, "I suppose it is all the same to you whom you sell him to. You had better let me have him."

"Oh, but the young man from our village promised us a large sum of money if we could find a fox, and he convinced us to come out to the hills and catch one; so we can't sell him to you at any price."

"Well, I suppose it cannot be helped, then; but how much would the young man give you for the cub?"

“Oh, he’ll give us at least three hundred cash.”

“Then I’ll give you half a **bu**;¹ and so you’ll gain five hundred cash by the transaction.”

“Oh, we’ll sell him for that, sir. How should we hand him over to you?”

“Just tie him up here,” said the other; and so he secured the cub around the neck with the string of the cloth in which the lunch box was wrapped, and gave half a **bu** to the three boys, who ran away delighted.

The man’s friend, upon this, said to him, “Well, you certainly have strange tastes. Why on earth are you going to keep the fox?”

“How very unkind of you to speak of my tastes like that. If we had not interfered just now, the fox cub would have lost its life. If we had not seen the affair, there would have been nothing to be done. How could I stand by and see a life taken? It was but a small amount I spent—only half a **bu**—to save the cub, but had it cost a fortune, I should not have grudged it. I thought you were close enough to me to know my heart; but today you have accused me of being eccentric, and I see how mistaken I have been about you. However, our friendship shall end from this day forward.”

And when he had said this with a great deal of firmness, the other, stepping backward and bowing with his hands on his knees, replied—

“Indeed, indeed, I am full of admiration for the goodness of your heart. When I hear you speak this way, I feel more than ever how great is the affection I have for you. I thought that you might wish to use the cub as a sort of decoy to lead the parents to you, so that you might beg them to bring prosperity and virtue to your house. When I called you eccentric just now, I was only testing your heart because I had some suspicions about you; and now I am truly ashamed of myself.”

<note>¹ **Bu.** This coin is generally called by foreigners “ichibu,” which means “one bu.” To talk of “a hundred ichibus” is as though a Japanese person were to say “a hundred one-shillings.” Four bu make a ryo, or ounce; and any sum above three bu is spoken of as so many ryo and bu—for example, 101 ryo and three bu equal 407 bu. The bu is worth about one shilling and four pence.</note>

As he spoke, still bowing, the other replied, “Really! Was that indeed your thought? Then I beg you to forgive me for my violent language.”

“Look there! The old foxes have come back, fearing for their cub’s safety. Come, we will set it free!” With these words, they untied the string from around the cub’s neck and turned its head toward the spot where the old foxes sat. As the wounded foot was no longer painful, with one bound the cub dashed to its parents’ side and licked them all over for joy, while they seemed to bow their thanks, looking toward the two friends. So, with peace in their hearts, the men went off to another place and, choosing a pretty spot, brought out the wine bottle and ate their midday meal. After a pleasant day, they returned to their homes and became firmer friends than ever.

Now, the man who had rescued the fox cub was a tradesman in good circumstances. He had three or four agents and two maidservants, besides male servants; altogether, he lived in a generous manner. He was married, and this marriage had given him one son, who had reached his tenth year but had been attacked by a strange disease that defied all the physician’s skill and medicine. Now, the boy who had recovered through the effectiveness of this medicine selected the prettiest spot on the property to erect a shrine to Inari Sama <note>Inari Sama is the title under which a certain mythical figure named Uga was deified; tradition credits him with the honor of having first discovered and cultivated the rice plant. He is depicted carrying a few ears of rice and is symbolized by a snake guarding a bale of rice grain. The foxes wait upon him and do his bidding. Because rice is the most important and necessary product of Japan, the honors that Inari Sama receives are extraordinary. Almost every house in the country has a pretty little shrine in his honor somewhere on the grounds; and on a certain day of the second month of the year, his feast is celebrated with much beating of drums and other noises, in which children take special delight. “On this day,” says the *Ô-Satsuyô*, a Japanese encyclopedia, “at Yedo, where there are countless shrines to Inari Sama, there are all sorts of ceremonies. Long banners with inscriptions are set up, lamps and lanterns are hung, and the houses are decorated with various dolls and figures; the sound of flutes and drums is heard, and people dance and make holiday as they please. In short, it is the most bustling festival of the year in Yedo.”</note>, the Fox God, and offered sacrifices to the two old foxes, for whom he purchased the highest rank at the court of the Mikado.

The passage in the story that speaks of rank being purchased for the foxes at the court of the Mikado is, of course, nonsense. “The saints who are worshipped in Japan,” writes a native authority, “are men who, in remote ages when the country was developing, were sages, and by their great and virtuous deeds having earned the gratitude of future generations, received divine honors after their death. How can the Son of Heaven, who is the father and mother of his people, become a dealer in ranks and honors? If rank were a matter of barter, it would cease to be a reward for the virtuous.”

All matters connected with the shrines of the Shintô, or indigenous religion, are entrusted to the supervision of the families of Yoshida and Fushimi, <term>Kugés</term> or nobles of the Mikado’s court at Kiyôto. The affairs of the Buddhist or imported religion are under the care of the family of Kanjuji. As it is necessary that those who as priests perform the honor-

honorable office of serving the gods should be held by persons of some standing, a certain minor rank is obtained for them through the mediation of the representatives of the noble families mentioned above. Upon the issuing of the required patent, these representatives receive a fee as their perquisite. Although this fee is insignificant in itself, it is nevertheless important to the poor <term>Kugés</term>, whose impoverished condition forms a great contrast to the wealth of their inferiors in rank, the <term>Daimios</term>. I believe that this is the only instance in which rank can be bought or sold in Japan. In China, on the contrary, despite what has been written by Meadows and other admirers of the examination system, a man can be whatever he pleases by paying for it; and the coveted button, which is nominally the reward for learning and ability, is more often the prize for wealthy ignorance.

The saints who are mentioned above are the saints of the whole country, as distinct from those who are worshiped locally for specific deeds. Frequent reference is made to this countless class in these Tales.

Regarding the remedy of the fox’s liver prescribed in the story, I may add that there would be nothing strange in this to a person acquainted with the Chinese pharmacopoeia, which the Japanese followed exclusively for a long time, though they are now successfully studying the art of healing as practiced in the West. When I was in Beijing, I saw a Chinese physician prescribe a decoction of three scorpions for a child suffering from fever; and on another occasion, a groom of mine suffering from dysentery was treated with acupuncture of the tongue. The art of medicine in China appears to be at the present time much like the state in which it existed in Europe in the sixteenth century, when the excretions and secretions of all kinds of animals, lizards, venomous snakes, insects, and even live bugs were administered to patients. “Some physicians,” says <term>Matthiolus</term>, “use the ashes of scorpions, burned alive, for urinary retention caused by either kidney or bladder stones. But I have personally experienced the usefulness of an oil I make myself, of which scorpions form a very large portion of the ingredients. If

# THE BADGER'S MONEY.

It is a common saying among men that to forget favors received is the behavior of a bird or a beast; an ungrateful man will be spoken ill of by the whole world. And yet even birds and beasts will show gratitude, so that a man who does not repay a favor is worse even than dumb brutes. Is this not a disgrace?

Once upon a time, in a hut at a place called Namékata in Hitachi, there lived an old priest famous neither for learning nor wisdom, but intent only on passing his days in prayer and meditation. He did not even have a child to wait on him but prepared his food with his own hands. Night and morning he recited the prayer "Namu Amida Butsu,"¹ intent upon that alone. Although the fame of his virtue did not reach far, his neighbors respected and revered him, and often brought him food and clothing; and when his roof or his walls fell into disrepair, they would mend them for him. Thus, he gave no thought to the things of this world.

One very cold night, when he little expected anyone to be outside, he heard a voice calling, "Your reverence! Your reverence!" So he rose and went out to see who it was, and there he saw an old badger standing. Any ordinary man would have been greatly alarmed by the apparition; but the priest, being as he was described above, showed no sign of fear, but asked the creature its business. At this, the badger respectfully bent its knees and said—

---

<note>¹ A Buddhist prayer in which something approaching the sounds of the original Sanskrit has been preserved. The meaning of the prayer is explained as "Save us, eternal Buddha!" Many even of the priests who repeat it know it only as a formula, without understanding it.</note>

"Until now, sir, my lair has been in the mountains, and I have paid no attention to snow or frost; but now I am growing old, and this severe cold is more than I can bear. I beg you to let me enter and warm myself at the fire of your cottage, so that I may survive this bitter night."

When the priest heard what a helpless state the beast was reduced to, he was filled with pity and said—

"That is a very small matter; hurry and come in and warm yourself."

The badger, delighted by such a kind reception, went into the hut and, squatting down by the fire, began to warm itself. The priest, with renewed fervor, recited his prayers and struck his bell before the image of Buddha, looking straight ahead.

After two hours the badger took its leave with many expressions of thanks and went out. From that time on, it came to the hut every night. Because the badger would collect and bring dried branches and dead leaves from the hills for firewood, the priest eventually became very friendly with it and grew used to its company. If the badger did not arrive as the night wore on, the priest would miss it and wonder why it had not come. When the winter was over and spring arrived at the end of the second month, the badger stopped its visits and was seen no more; but when winter returned, the beast resumed its old habit of coming to the hut. 

When this practice had continued for ten years, the badger said to the priest one day, "Through your reverence’s kindness all these years, I have been able to spend the winter nights in comfort. Your favors are such that I must remember them throughout my life and even after my death. What can I do to repay them? If there is anything you wish for, please tell me."

The priest, smiling at this speech, answered, "Being as I am, I have no desire and no wishes. As glad as I am to hear your kind intentions, there is nothing I can ask you to do for me. You need feel no anxiety on my account. As long as I live, when winter comes, you shall be

The badger, on hearing this, could not hide its admiration for the depth of the old man's benevolence; but having so much to be grateful for, it felt pained at not being able to repay it. As this subject was often renewed between them, the priest at last, touched by the goodness of the badger's heart, said, "Since I have shaved my head, renounced the world, and given up the pleasures of this life, I have no desire to satisfy, yet I admit I should like to possess three <term>riyos</term> in gold. Food and clothing I receive by the favor of the villagers, so I pay no attention to those things. Were I to die tomorrow and achieve my wish of being reborn into the next world, the same kind people have promised to meet and bury my body. Thus, although I have no other reason to wish for money, if I had three <term>riyos</term> I would offer them up at some holy shrine, so that masses and prayers might be said for me, through which I might enter into salvation. Yet I would not get this money by violent or unlawful means; I only think of what might be if I had it. So you see, since you have expressed such kind feelings toward me, I have told you what is on my mind." When the priest had finished speaking, the badger tilted its head to one side with a puzzled and anxious look, so much so that the old man was sorry he had expressed a wish which seemed to give the beast trouble, and he tried to take back what he had said. "Posthumous honors, after all, are the wish of ordinary men. I, who am a priest, ought not to entertain such thoughts or want money; so please pay no attention to what I have said." And the badger, pretending to agree with what the priest had urged upon it, returned to the hills as usual.

From that time on, the badger came no more to the hut. The priest thought this very strange, but imagined either that the badger stayed away because it did not want to come without the money, or that it had been killed in an attempt to steal it; and he blamed himself for adding to his sins for no purpose, repenting when it was too late. Convinced, however, that the badger must have been killed, he spent his time offering prayer after prayer for it.

<header>THE BADGER'S MONEY.</header>

After three years had gone by, one night the old man heard a voice near his door calling out, “Your reverence! Your reverence!”

As the voice was like that of the badger, he jumped up as soon as he heard it and ran out to open the door; and there, sure enough, was the badger. The priest, in great delight, cried out, “And so you are safe and sound, after all! Why have you been so long without coming here? I have been expecting you anxiously for this long while.”

So the badger came into the hut and said, “If the money which you required had been for unlawful purposes, I could easily have procured as much as you might have ever wanted; but when I heard that it was to be offered to a temple for masses for your soul, I thought that if I were to steal the hidden treasure of some other man, you could not apply money which had been obtained at the expense of his sorrow to a sacred purpose. So I went to the island of Sado,<note>An island on the west coast of Japan, famous for its gold mines.</note> and gathering the sand and earth which had been cast away as worthless by the miners, I smelted it again in the fire; and at this work I spent many months and days.” As the badger finished speaking, the priest looked at the money which it had produced, and sure enough he saw that it was bright, new, and clean; so he took the money and received it respectfully, raising it to his head.

“And so you have had all this toil and labor on account of a foolish speech of mine? I have obtained my heart’s desire and am truly thankful.”

As he was thanking the badger with great politeness and ceremony, the beast said, “In doing this I have but fulfilled my own wish; still I hope that you will tell this thing to no man.”

“Indeed,” replied the priest, “I cannot help but tell this story. For if I keep this money in my poor hut, it will be stolen by thieves: I must either give it to someone to keep for me, or else at once offer it up at the temple. And when I do this, when people see a poor old priest with a sum of

## THE PRINCE AND THE BADGER.

In days of yore, there lived an ancestor of the Prince of Tosa named Yamanouchi Kadzutoyo. At the age of fourteen, this prince was amazingly fond of fishing and would often go down to the river for sport. It happened one day, when he had gone there with only one retainer and had made a great catch, that a violent rainstorm suddenly began. Now, the prince had no raincoat with him and was in such a sorry state that he took shelter under a willow tree and waited for the weather to clear. But the storm showed no sign of letting up, and there was nothing else to be done, so he turned to his retainer and said:

"This rain is not likely to stop for some time, so we had better hurry home."

As they trudged homeward, night fell and it grew very dark. Their road lay over a long bank, by the side of which they found a girl, about sixteen years old, weeping bitterly. Filled with wonder, they looked steadfastly at her and perceived that she was exceedingly beautiful. While Kadzutoyo stood wondering what such a strange sight could mean, his retainer, smitten by the girl's charms, stepped up to her and said:

"Little sister, tell us whose daughter you are, and how it happens that you are out by yourself at night in such a rainstorm. Surely it is very strange."

"Sir," she replied, looking up through her tears, "I am the daughter of a poor man in the castle town. My mother died when I was seven years old, and my father has now married a spiteful woman who hates and mistreats me; and in the"

As she spoke, the retainer fell deeply in love with her matchless beauty, while his lord Kadzutoyo, who from the beginning had not uttered a word but stood brooding over the matter, immediately drew his sword and cut off her head. But the retainer stood horrified and cried out—

"Oh! my young lord, what wicked deed is this that you have done? The murder of a man's daughter will bring trouble upon us, for you can be sure the matter will not end here."

"You don't know what you are talking about," answered Kadzutoyo: "only do not tell anyone about it, that is all I ask;" and so they went home in silence.

As Kadzutoyo was very tired, he went to bed and slept undisturbed by any sense of guilt; for he was brave and fearless. But the retainer became very uneasy and went to his young lord's parents and said—

"I had the honor of attending my young lord out fishing today, and we were driven home by the rain. And as we came back along the bank, we saw a girl with a spasm in her stomach, and my young lord immediately killed her; and although he has ordered me to tell no one, I cannot hide it from my lord and my lady."

"But what made you think she must be a goblin just because her clothes were dry?"

"The beast evidently thought that if she could bewitch us with her beauty, she might get the fish my retainer was carrying; but she forgot that, since it was raining, it would not do for her clothes to be dry; so I detected her and killed her."

When the old prince heard his son speak this way, he was filled with admiration for the youth's wisdom; so, judging that Kadzutoyo had given reliable proof of wisdom and prudence, he resolved to abdicate;<sup>1</sup> and Kadzutoyo was proclaimed Prince of Tosa in his place.

<note>1 *Inkiyô*, abdication. The custom of abdication is common among all classes, from the Emperor down to his humblest subject. The Emperor abdicates after consultation with his ministers: the Shogun has to obtain the permission of the Emperor; the Daimios, that of the Shogun. The abdication of the Emperor was called *Sentô*; that of the Shogun, *Ogoshô*; in all other ranks it is called *Inkiyô*. It must be remembered that the princes of Japan, in becoming *Inkiyô*, resign the appearance and the name, but not the reality of power. Both in their own provinces and in the country at large, they play a most important part. The ex-Princes of Tosa, Uwajima, and Owari are far more notable men in Japan than the actual holders of the titles.</note>

## JAPANESE SERMONS.

“SERMONS preached here on the 8th, 18th, and 28th days of every month.” This was the meaning of a sign which used to tempt me daily as I passed the Chô-ô-ji temple. Having confirmed that neither the preacher nor his congregation would have any objection to my hearing one of these sermons, I made arrangements to attend the service, accompanied by two friends, my artist, and a scribe to take notes.

We were shown into an apartment adjoining a small chapel—a room opening onto a tastefully arranged garden, rich with stone lanterns and dwarfed trees. In the portion of the room reserved for the priest stood a high table, covered with a cloth of white and scarlet silk, richly embroidered with flowers and arabesques; upon this stood a bell, a tray containing the rolls of the sacred books, and a small incense burner of ancient Chinese porcelain. In front of the table was a hanging drum, and behind it was one of those high, back-breaking armchairs which adorn every Buddhist temple. In one corner of the space intended to accommodate the faithful was a low writing desk, at which sat—or rather squatted—a lay clerk, wearing a huge pair of horn-rimmed spectacles, through which he glared, like a goblin, at the people as they came to have their names and the amount of their offerings to the temple registered. These offerings must have been small, for the congregation seemed poor enough. It was mainly composed of old women, nuns with bald shiny heads and grotesque faces, a few small tradesmen, and half a dozen chubby children, perfect little

<summary>The narrator describes their visit to the Chô-ô-ji temple to attend a scheduled sermon, detailing the ornate ritual objects and the humble appearance of the congregation.</summary>
<keywords>Chô-ô-ji temple, Japanese sermons, Buddhism, incense burner, religious offerings, temple architecture, Edo period social life</keywords>

--- Page 361 ---
<meta>This page continues the eyewitness account of a Buddhist service at the Chô-ô-ji temple, describing the congregation's behavior and the arrival of the preacher.</meta>

->TALES OF OLD JAPAN.<-

models of decorum and devotion. One lady there was, indeed, who seemed a little better off in the world than the rest; she was nicely dressed and attended by a female servant. She came in with a certain little consequential rustle and displayed some coquetry, and a very pretty bare foot, as she took her place; pulling out a dandy little pipe and tobacco pouch, she began to smoke. Fire-boxes and spittoons, I should mention, were freely handed about, so that the half hour which passed before the sermon began was agreeably spent. In the meanwhile, mass was being celebrated in the main hall of the temple, and the monotonous nasal drone of the plainchant was faintly heard in the distance. As soon as this was over, the lay clerk sat himself down by the hanging drum and, to its accompaniment, began intoning the prayer, “Na Mu Miyô Hô Ren Ge Kiyô,” the congregation fervently joining in unison with him. These words, repeated over and over again, are the distinctive prayer of the Buddhist sect of Nichiren, to which the temple Chô-ô-ji is dedicated. They are approximations of Sanskrit sounds and have no meaning in Japanese, nor do the worshippers, in using them, know their precise value.

Soon the preacher, gorgeous in red and white robes, made his appearance, following an acolyte who carried the sacred book called *Hokké* (upon which the sect of Nichiren is founded) on a tray covered with scarlet and gold brocade. Having bowed to the sacred picture which hung over the *tokonoma*—that portion of the Japanese room which is raised a few inches above the rest of the floor and which is regarded as the place of honor—his reverence took his seat at the table and adjusted his robes; then, tying up the muscles of his face into a knot, expressive of utter abstraction, he struck the bell upon the table three times, burned a little incense, and read a passage from the sacred book, which he reverently lifted to his head. The congregation joined in chorus, devout but unintelligent; for the Word, written in ancient Chinese, is as obscure to the ordinary Japanese worshipper as Latin liturgies are to a high-capped Norman peasant woman.

# JAPANESE SERMONS.

While his flock wrapped up copper coins in paper and threw them before the table as offerings, the priest next recited a passage alone, and the lay clerk irreverently entered into a loud dispute with one of the congregation concerning some payment or other. The preliminary ceremonies ended, a small shaved-headed boy brought in a cup of tea—to be refilled three times afterward—for his reverence’s refreshment; and he, relaxing his expression, gave a broad grin, cleared his throat, swallowed his tea, and beamed down upon us, as jolly and rosy a priest as ever wore a stole or scarf. His discourse, which was delivered in the most familiar and easy manner, was an extemporaneous talk on certain passages from the sacred books. Whenever he paused or made a point, the congregation broke in with a cry of “Nammiyô!”—a corruption of the first three words of the prayer cited above—to which they always managed to give an expression or intonation in harmony with the preacher’s meaning.

> “It is a matter of profound satisfaction to me,” began his reverence Nichirin, smiling blandly at his audience, “to see so many gentlemen and ladies gathered together here this day, in the faithfulness of their hearts, to do honor to the festival of Kishimojin.” <gloss>1</gloss>

> “Nammiyô! nammiyô!” self-deprecatingly, from the congregation.

> “I feel certain that your piety cannot fail to find favor with Kishimojin. Kishimojin always mourns over the tortures of mankind, who are living in a house of fire, and she always earnestly strives to find some means of delivering them.”

For instance, the prayer *Na Mu* is a prayer committing your bodies to the care of the gods; if, when you utter it, your hearts are true and single, surely your request will be granted. Now, this is not a mere statement made by Nichiren, the holy founder of this sect; it is the sacred teaching of Buddha himself and cannot be doubted.”

“Nammiyô! nammiyô!” with profound conviction.

“The heart of man is, by nature, upright and true; but there are seven passions <note>The seven passions are joy, anger, sadness, fear, love, hatred, and desire.</note> by which it is corrupted. Buddha is alarmed when he sees the fires by which the world is being consumed. These fires are the five lusts of this sinful world; and the five lusts are: the desire for beautiful sights, sweet sounds, fragrant smells, fine foods, and rich clothing. As soon as a man is endowed with a body, he is possessed by these lusts, which become his very heart; and, since it is a law that every man follows the dictates of his heart, in this way the body, the lusts of the flesh, the heart, and the dictates of the heart all blaze up in the consuming fire. ‘Alas for this miserable world!’ said the divine Buddha.”

“Nammiyô! nammiyô!” mournful, and with much head-shaking.

“There is nothing so foul under heaven as the human body. The body exudes grease, the eyes secrete discharge, the nose is full of mucus, and the mouth is full of drooling saliva; nor are these the most impure secretions of the body. What a mistake it is to look upon this impure body as clean and perfect! Unless we listen to the teachings of Buddha, how shall we be washed and purified?”

"The fate of man is uncertain and is always straying from the beaten path. Why go to look at the flowers and take delight in their beauty? What a terrible subject for thought this is! In the poems of the priest Saigiyo, it is written: 'Truly, I have been familiar with the flowers; yet they have withered and scattered, and we are parted. How sad!' The beauty of the convolvulus—how bright it is!—and yet in one short morning, it closes its petals and fades. In the book called *Rin Jo Bo Satsu* <gloss>One of the Buddhist classics.</gloss>, we are told how a certain king once went to take his pleasure in his garden and gladden his eyes with the beauty of his flowers. After a while, he fell asleep; and as he slumbered, the women of his retinue began pulling the flowers to pieces. When the king awoke, of all the glory of his flowers, there remained only a few torn and faded petals. Seeing this, the king said: 'The flowers pass away and die; so it is with mankind. We are born, we grow old, we sicken, and we die; we are as fleeting as a flash of lightning, as brief as the morning dew.' I do not know whether any of you here present ever turn your thoughts toward death; yet it is a rare thing for a man to live for a hundred years. How piteous it is that in this short and transient life, men should consume themselves in a fire of lust! And if we think to escape from this fire, how shall we succeed except by the teaching of the divine Buddha?"

“‘In truth, this is a thing the like of which no man has yet seen. Here am I, who know the way of the life and of the death even of the ants that creep. Truly, I thought that nothing could escape my knowledge; yet here lies one of your disciples, compared to whom no nobler being lives, and I am at fault. From this day forward I will enter your sect, praying only that I may receive your teaching.’

“Thus did this learned heretic become a disciple of Buddha. If even someone like him was converted, how much more should future generations of ordinary men feel that it is through Buddha alone that they can hope to overcome the sinful desires of the flesh! These desires are the passions which disturb our hearts: if we are free from these desires, our hearts will be bright and pure; and there is nothing, except the teaching of Buddha, which can ensure us this freedom. Following the commands of Buddha, and delivered by him from our desires, we may pass our lives in peace and happiness.”

# JAPANESE SERMONS.

"Nammiyô! nammiyô!" with triumphant exultation.

> "In the sacred books, we read of conversion from a state of sin to a state of salvation. Now, this salvation is not a million miles removed from us; nor do we need to die and be born again into another world in order to reach it. Whoever lays aside their carnal lusts and affections immediately and certainly becomes equal to Buddha. When we recite the prayer *Na Mu Miyô Hô Ren Go Kiyô*, we are praying to enter this state of peace and happiness. By what instruction, other than that of Nichiren, the holy founder of this sect, can we expect to attain this end? If we do attain it, there will be no difference between our state and that of Buddha and of Nichiren. With this view, we have learned from the pious founder of our sect that we must continually and thankfully repeat the prayer *Na Mu Miyô Hô Ren Go Kiyô*, turning our hearts away from lies and embracing the truth."

These were the main points of the sermon as they were recorded by my scribe. At its conclusion, the priest, looking about him and smiling—as if the solemn truths he had been teaching were nothing but a very good joke—was greeted by long and loud cries of "Nammiyô! nammiyô!" by the entire congregation. Then the lay clerk sat down again by the hanging drum; and the service ended as it had begun, with prayer in chorus, during which the priest retired, the sacred book being carried out before him by his acolyte.

Although occasionally, as in the above instance, sermons are delivered as part of a service on special days of the month, they are more frequently preached in courses, the delivery lasting about two weeks, during which two sermons are given each day. Frequently the preachers are itinerant priests who travel through the towns and villages, lecturing in the main hall of some temple or in the guest room of the resident priest.

There are many books of sermons published in Japan, all of which have some merit and much quaintness; none that I have seen, however, are in my opinion comparable to the "Kiu-ô Dô-wa," of which the following three sermons compose

the first volume. They are written by a priest belonging to the Shingaku sect—a sect professing to combine all that is excellent in Buddhist, Confucian, and Shinto teaching. It maintains the original goodness of the human heart and teaches that we only have to follow the dictates of the conscience implanted in us at our birth in order to steer on the right path. The texts are taken from Chinese classical books, in the same way that our preachers take theirs from the Bible. Jokes, stories which are sometimes untranslatable into our more fastidious language, and pointed applications to members of the congregation, enliven the discourses; it is a principle with the Japanese preacher that it is not necessary to bore his audience into virtue.

## SERMON I.

->(THE SERMONS OF KIU-Ô, VOL. I.)<-

Môshi<gloss>1</gloss> says, “Benevolence is the heart of man; righteousness is the path of man. How lamentable it is to leave the path and go astray, to cast away the heart and not know where to seek it!”

The text is taken from the first chapter of Kôshi (the commentator) on Môshi.

Now this quality, which we call benevolence, has been the subject of commentaries by many teachers; but as these commentaries have been difficult to understand, they are too hard for women and children to grasp. It is of this benevolence that I propose to speak, using examples and illustrations.

A long time ago, there lived in Kyoto a great physician named Imaôji—I forget his other name: he was a very famous man. Once upon a time, a man from a place called Kuramaguchi advertised a medicine for sale that he had compounded for cholera, and he got Imaôji to write an advertisement for him. Imaôji, instead of calling the medicine in the advertisement a specific for cholera, misspelled the word "cholera" to make it simpler. When the man who had employed him went and confronted him about this, and asked him why he had done so, he answered with a smile—

Truth itself loses its value if people do not understand it. What does it matter how I spelled the word cholera, so long as the effectiveness of the medicine remains intact?”

Now, was that not delightful? In the same way, the doctrines of the sages are mere gibberish to women and children who cannot understand them. Now, my sermons are not written for the learned; I address myself to farmers and tradesmen who, hard-pressed by their daily business, have no time for study, with the wish to make the teachings of the sages known to them. Carrying out the ideas of my teacher, I will make my meaning quite plain by bringing forward examples and quaint stories. Thus, by blending together the doctrines of Shintô, Buddhism, and other schools, we shall arrive at something near the true principle of things. Now, you really must not laugh if I introduce a light story now and then. Levity is not my object: I only want to explain things in a plain and easy manner.

Well, then, the quality we call benevolence is, in fact, a perfection; and it is this perfection that Môshi spoke of as the heart of man. With this perfect heart, by serving their parents, men attain filial piety; by serving their masters, they attain fidelity; and if they treat their wives, their brothers, and their friends in the same spirit, then the principles of the five relations of life will harmonize without difficulty. As for putting perfection into practice, parents have the special duties of parents; children have the special duties of children; husbands have the special duties of husbands; wives have the special duties of wives. It is when all these special duties are performed without fault that true benevolence is reached; and that, again, is the true heart of man.

I don’t mean to say that there are any such people here; still, there are plenty of them to be found—say, in the back streets of India, for instance. Please be so good as to mind what I have said.

# JAPANESE SERMONS.

...extravagant price for it. I repeat, follow the impulses of your hearts with all your strength. In the *Chin-yo*, the second of the books of Confucius, it is confirmed beyond a doubt that the impulses of nature are the true path to follow; therefore, you may set to work in this direction with your minds at ease.

Righteousness, then, is the true path, and righteousness is the avoidance of everything that is imperfect. If a man avoids what is imperfect, there is no need to point out how dearly he will be loved by all his fellows. This is why the ancients have defined righteousness as that which ought to be—that which is fitting. If a man is a retainer, it is good that he should perform his service to his lord with all his strength. If a woman is married, it is good that she should treat her parents-in-law with filial piety and her husband with reverence. For the rest, whatever is good—that is righteousness and the true path of man.

The duty of man has been compared by the wise men of old to a highway. If you want to go to Yedo or to Nagasaki, if you want to go out to the front of the house or to the back of the house, if you wish to go into the next room or into some closet or other, there is a right road to each of these places: if you do not follow the right road, but instead scramble over the roofs of houses and through ditches, crossing mountains and desert places, you will be utterly lost and bewildered. In the same way, if a man does what is not good, he is going astray from the highway. Filial piety in children, virtue in wives, truth among friends—but why list all these things, which are obvious?—all these are the right road and are good; but to grieve parents, to anger husbands, to hate and to breed hatred in others, these are all bad things—these are all the wrong road. To follow these is to plunge into rivers, to run onto thorns, and to jump into ditches, and it brings thousands upon tens of thousands of disasters. It is true that, if we do not pay close attention, we will not be able to follow the right road. Fortunately, we have heard through tradition the words of the learned Nakazawa Dôni; I will tell you about that in due time.

It happened that the learned Nakazawa once went to preach at Ikéda, in the province of Sesshiu, and stayed with a wealthy family of the lower class. The master of the house, who was especially fond of sermons, hosted the preacher hospitably and called for his daughter, a girl of about fourteen or fifteen years old, to wait on him at dinner. This young lady was not only extremely pretty but also had charming manners; she arranged bouquets of flowers, made tea, played the harp, and did her best to please the learned man by singing songs.

The preacher thanked her parents for all this and said,

“It must truly be a very difficult thing to educate a young lady to such a high standard as this.”

The parents, overcome by their pride, replied,

“Yes; when she is married, she will hardly bring shame upon her husband’s family. In addition to what she just did, she can weave garlands of flowers around torches, and we have had her taught to paint a little;”

And as they began to show a bit of vanity, the preacher said,

“I am sure this is something quite out of the ordinary. Of course, she knows how to rub the shoulders and lower back, and has learned the art of <term>shampooing</term>?”

The master of the house bristled at this and answered,

“I may be very poor, but I have not fallen so low as to let my daughter learn <term>shampooing</term>.”

The learned man smiled and replied, “I think you are making a mistake by losing your temper. No matter whether her family is rich or poor, when a woman is performing her duties in her husband’s house, she must look upon her husband’s parents as her own. If her honored father-in-law or mother-in-law falls ill, her being able to braid flowers, paint pictures, and make tea will be of no use in the sickroom. To <term>shampoo</term> her parents-in-law and nurse them affectionately, without employing either a <term>shampooer</term> or a servant girl, is the right path for a daughter-in-law. At this, the master of the house felt ashamed and, blushing, made many apologies, as I have heard. Certainly, the harp and guitar are very good things in their way; but attending to nursing their parents is the right path for children. Take this story to heart, and consider attentively where the right path lies. People who live near places of pleasure become at last so fond of pleasure that they teach their daughters nothing but how to play the harp and guitar, and train them in the manners and ways of singing-girls, but teach them next to nothing of their duties as daughters; and then very often they escape from their parents’ watchfulness and elope. Nor is this the fault of the girls themselves, but the fault of the education which they have received from their parents. I do not mean to say that the harp and guitar, and songs and dramas, are useless things. If you consider them attentively, all our songs encourage virtue and condemn vice. In the song called “The Four Sleeves,” for instance, there is the passage, “If people knew beforehand all the misery that it brings, there would be less going out with young ladies to look at the flowers at night.” Please give your attention to this piece of poetry. This is its meaning: When a young man and a young lady begin a flirtation without the consent of their parents, they think that it will all be very delightful, but find themselves very much deceived. If they knew what a sad and cruel world this is, they would not act as they do. The quotation is from a song of remorse. This sort of thing happens all too often in the world.

When a man marries a wife, he thinks how happy he will be and how pleasant it will be keeping house on his own account; but, before the bottom of the family kettle has been scorched black, he will be like a man learning to swim in a field, with his ideas all turned topsy-turvy, and, contrary to all his expectations, he will find the pleasures of housekeeping to be a complete delusion. He wondered if the Tai and the other fish were caught, and he felt quite anxious about them; however, at any rate, he was safe. As he looked a little more carefully, lo and behold! There he was in a fishmonger's shop, with a card marked "sixteen cash" on his back.

Isn't that a funny story? And so, in one fell swoop, all your boasted wealth of houses and warehouses, your cleverness and talent, and your rank and power are taken away. Poor shellfish! I think there are some people not unlike them to be found in China and India. How little the self is to be depended upon!
