## SERMON II.

->(THE SERMONS OF KIU-Ô, VOL. I.)<-

"If a man loses a bird or a dog, he knows how to reclaim it. If he loses his soul, he does not know how to reclaim it. The true path of learning has no other purpose than to teach us how to reclaim lost souls." This parable has been shared with us by Môshi <note>Môshi is the Japanese name for the Chinese philosopher Mencius.</note>. If a dog, a chicken, or a pet cat does not come home at the proper time, its master makes a great fuss about searching for it, wondering if it has been killed by a dog or a snake, or if someone has stolen it. Searching through the three houses across the street and his two next-door neighbors' houses, as if he were seeking a lost child, he cries, "Please, sir, has my tortoise-shell cat been with you? Has my pet chicken been here?" That is the way people run about in such circumstances. It is treated as a matter of the utmost importance.

And yet, to lose a dog or a pet chicken is not such a terrible loss after all. But the soul, which is called the lord of the body, is the master of our entire selves. If people part with this soul for the sake of other things, then they become deaf to the warnings of their parents, and the instructions of their superiors are to them like the blowing winds of heaven. Teaching them is like pouring water over a frog's face; they blink their eyes, and that is all. They say, "Yes, yes!" with their mouths, but their hearts are gone; seeing, they are blind, and hearing, they are deaf. Born whole and healthy, by their own actions they join the fraternity of cripples. Such are all

> "It is my parents' fault; it is my master's fault; it is my husband's fault; it is my elder brother's fault; it is Hachibei who is a rogue; it is O Matsu who is a bad woman."
They content themselves with looking at the faults of others, and do not examine their own consciences, nor search their own hearts. Is not this a cruel state of things? They set up a hue and cry for a lost dog or a pet chicken, but for this all-important soul of theirs they make no search. What mistaken people! For this reason the sages, mourning over such a state of things, have taught us what is the right path of man; and it is the receiving of this teaching that is called learning. The main object of learning is the examination and searching of our own hearts; therefore the text says,
> "The true path of learning has no other function than to teach us how to reclaim lost souls."
This is an exhaustive explanation of the functions of learning. That learning has no other object, we have this gracious pledge and guarantee from the sage. As for the mere study of the antiquities and records of China and Japan, and investigation into literature, these cannot be called learning, which is above all things an affair of the soul. All the commentaries and all the books of all the teachers in the world are but so many directories by which to find out the whereabouts of our own souls. This search after our own souls is that which I alluded to just now as the examination of our consciences. To disregard the examination of our consciences is a terrible thing, of which it is impossible to foresee the end; on the other hand, to practice it is most admirable, for by this means we can on the spot attain filial piety and fidelity to our masters. Virtue and vice are the goals to which the examination and non-examination of our consciences lead. As it has been rightly said, benevolence and malice are the two roads which man follows. Upon this subject I have a terrible and yet a very admirable story to tell you. Although I dare say you are very drowsy, I must beg you to listen to me.

In a certain part of the country, there was a well-to-do farmer whose marriage had brought him one son. He pampered this son excessively, as a cow licks its calf. Consequently, the child gradually became very sly; he used to pull the horses’ tails, blow smoke into the bulls' nostrils, and bully the neighbors’ children in petty ways, making them cry. From a peevish child, he grew to be a man who was unbearably disobedient to his parents. Taking pride in his slight physical advantage, he became a drunkard and a gambler, and he learned to wrestle at fairs. He would fight and quarrel over trifles, and he spent his time in vice and wild living. If his parents reasoned with him, he would raise his voice and abuse them, using foul language. “It’s all very well for you to scold me for being immoral and disobedient. But, tell me, who asked you to bring me into the world? You brought me into the world, and I have to thank you for its miseries; so now, if you hate immoral people, you had better put me back where I came from, and I shall be fine again.” This was the sort of insolent answer he would give his parents, who, at their wits’ end, began to grow old. And as he gradually became more and more of a bully, as unhappy as he made them, he was still their darling, and they could not find it in their hearts to turn him out of the house and disinherit him. So they let him follow his selfish path; and he went from bad to worse, knocking people down, breaking their arms, and causing great disturbances. There is no need to describe his parents’ feelings. Even his relatives and friends felt as if nails were being driven into their chests. He was a thoroughly wicked man.

Now, no one is born from their mother’s womb as wicked as this; but those who persist in selfishness lose their senses and gradually reach this level of wickedness. What a terrible thing is this throwing away of our hearts!

You see how bewildered parents must be by the love for their children, to be so merciful toward them. They care neither for the abuse of others, nor for their duties to their ancestors, nor for the wretched future in store for themselves. You see, the original heart of man is by nature bright virtue, but through our selfish pursuit of our own inclinations, the brilliance of our original virtue is hidden.

## SERMON III.

->(THE SERMONS OF KIU-Ô, VOL. I.)<-

MÔSHI has said, “There is the third finger. If a man’s third or nameless finger is bent so that he cannot straighten it, although his bent finger may cause him no pain, still if he hears of someone who can cure it, he will think nothing of undertaking a long journey from *Shin* to *So*¹ to consult him about this deformed finger; for he knows it is shameful to have a finger unlike those of other men. But he does not care at all if his heart is different from that of other men; and this is how men disregard the true order of things.”

Now this is the next chapter after the one about benevolence being the true heart of man, which I explained to you the other night. True learning has no other goal than that of reclaiming lost souls; and, in connection with this, Môshi has once again declared in a parable the supreme importance of the human heart.

The nameless finger is the one next to the little finger. The thumb is called the parent-finger; the first finger is called the index; the long one is called the middle finger; but the third finger has no name. It is true that it is sometimes called the finger for applying rouge; but that is only a name given to it by ladies, and it is not in general use. So, having no name, it is called the nameless finger. And why does it have no name? Well, because it is the least useful of all the fingers. When we clutch at or grasp things, we do so by the strength of the thumb and little finger. If

If a man scratches his head, he does it with his forefinger; if he wishes to test the heat of the wine¹ in the kettle, he uses his little finger. Thus, although each finger has its uses and duties, the nameless finger alone is of no use: it is not in our way if we have it, and we do not miss it if we lose it. Of the whole body, it is the humblest member: if it is crooked so that we cannot straighten it, it neither hurts nor itches; as Môshi says in the text, it causes no pain; even if we were without it, we should be no worse off. Therefore, even if it were bent, since it causes no pain, it would be better to leave it as it is. Yet if a person with such a crooked finger hears of a clever doctor who can set it straight, no matter how great the distance may be, he will go to consult this doctor. And why? Because he feels ashamed of having a finger slightly different from the rest of the world, and so he wants to be cured; he will think nothing of traveling from Shin to So—a distance of a thousand miles—for that purpose. To be sure, people are very sensitive and keenly aware of shame; and in this, they are quite right. The feeling of shame for what is wrong is the beginning of virtue. The sense of shame is innate in humanity; but there are two ways of perceiving shame. There are some people who feel shame regarding their bodies, but who are ignorant of shame concerning their hearts; and they make a terrible mistake. Nothing can be compared in importance to the heart. The heart is said to be the lord of the body, which it rules as a master rules his house. Should the lord, which is the heart, be ailing and his sickness neglected while his servants, which are only the limbs, are cared for? If the knee is cut, apply tinder to stop the bleeding; if the <term>moxa</term> should fester, apply a plaster; if a cold is caught, prepare medicine, garlic, gruel, and ginger wine! For a trifle, you will doctor and care for your bodies, and yet you take no care for your hearts. Although you are born of mankind, if your

...hearts resemble those of devils, of foxes, of snakes, or of crows, rather than the hearts of men, you pay no attention, caring for your bodies alone. How could you have fallen into such a mistake? It is a folly of long standing, too, for it was to this that Môshi pointed when he said that to be aware of a deformed finger and ignore the deformities of the soul was to disregard the true order of things. This is what it means not to distinguish between what is important and what is unimportant—to pick up a trifle and pass by something of value. The instinct of man prompts him to prefer the great to the small, the important to the unimportant.

If a man is invited out to a feast by his relatives or acquaintances, when the guests are assembled and the main part of the feast has disappeared, he looks all around him, with his eyes popping out of his head, and glares at his neighbors; and, comparing the little tidbits of roast fowl or fish served to them, he sees that they are about half an inch larger than those set before him. Then, his belly swelling with rage, he thinks,
> “What on earth can the host be doing? Master Tarubei is a guest, but so am I; what does the fellow mean by serving me such small portions? There must be some malice or ill will here.”
And so his mind becomes prejudiced against the host. Just be so good as to reflect upon this. Does a man show his spite by begrudging a bit of roast fowl or meat? And yet even in such trifles as these, men show how they try to obtain what is great and show their dislike for what is small. How can men be conscious of shame for a deformed finger, yet count it as no misfortune that their hearts are crooked? That is how they abandon the substance for the shadow.

Môshi severely censures the disregard of the true order of things. What mistaken and bewildered creatures men are! What does the old song say?
> “Hidden far among the mountains, the tree which seems to be rotten—if its core is still alive, it may yet be made to bear flowers.”
What does it matter if the hand or the foot is deformed? The heart is the important thing. If the heart is crooked, what does it matter if your skin is fair, your nose...

There is the scullery maid who has been washing out the pots at the kitchen sink, and the scullion Chokichi comes up and says to her, “You’ve got a lot of charcoal soot sticking to your nose,” and points out the ugly spot to her. The scullery maid is delighted to be told this and answers, “Really! Where is it?” Then she twists a towel around her finger and, bending her head until her mouth and forehead are almost on the same level, she squints at her nose and fiddles away with her fingers as if she were the famous Gotô¹ at work, carving the ornaments of a sword handle. “I say, Master Chokichi, is it off yet?” “Not a bit of it. See if I ever take the trouble to wash your dirty bedclothes for you again.” And she becomes a perfect devil, lacking only the horns.

In fact, if you help a person with anything involving a fault of the body, they take it very kindly and set about mending matters. If anyone helps another to rectify a fault of the heart, he has to deal with a man in the dark, who flies into a rage and does not care to improve. How out of tune all this is! And yet there are men who are bewildered to this point. Nor is this a special and extraordinary failing. This mistaken perception of the great and the small, of appearance and of substance, is common to us all—to you and to me.

Please give me your attention. The physical form strikes the eye, but the heart does not strike the eye. Therefore, that the heart should be distorted and turned awry causes no pain. This all results from the lack of sound judgment, and that is why we cannot afford to be careless.

The master of a certain house calls his servant Chokichi, who sits dozing in the kitchen. "Here, Chokichi! The guests are all gone; come and clear away the wine and fish in the back room."

Chokichi rubs his eyes and, with a sulky answer, goes into the back room; looking about him, he sees all the nice things displayed on the trays and in the bowls. But it’s no use trying to persuade his master that the little cuttlefish are spiders, for they are not the least like them. It’s no use hiding things—they are sure to come to light. So it is with the heart—its purposes will be revealed. If the heart is enraged, the dark veins stand out on the forehead; if the heart is grieved, tears rise to the eyes; if the heart is joyous, dimples appear in the cheeks; if the heart is merry, the face smiles. Thus, the face reflects the emotions of the heart. It is not because the eyes are filled with tears that the heart is sad, nor because the veins stand out on the forehead that the heart is enraged. It is the heart that leads the way in everything. All the important feelings of the heart are apparent in one's outward appearance. In the “Great Learning” of Kôshi <note>Confucius</note> it is written, “The truth of what is within appears upon the surface.” How then can the heart be something that can be hidden? So, before the disease has gained strength, I invite you to the study of the moral essays entitled *Shin-gaku* (the Learning of the Heart). If you once arrive at the possession of your heart as it was originally by nature, what an admirable thing that will be! While upon this subject, I may tell you a story which was related to me by a friend of mine. It is a story which the master of a certain money-changer’s shop was very fond of telling. An important part of a money-changer’s business is to distinguish between good and bad gold and silver. In the different establishments, the ways of teaching the apprentices this art vary; however, the plan adopted by the money-changer was as follows:—At first he would show them no bad silver, but would daily put before them good money only; when they had become thoroughly familiar with the sight of good money, if he stealthily put a little base coin among the good, he found that they would detect it immediately—they saw it as plainly as you see things when you throw light on a mirror. This faculty of detecting base money at a glance was the result of having learned thoroughly to understand good money. Having once been taught in this way, the apprentices would not make a mistake about a piece of base coin during their whole lives, as I have heard. I cannot vouch for the truth of this; but it is very certain that the principle, applied to moral instruction, is an excellent one—it is a most safe mode of study. However, I was further told that if, after having thus learned to distinguish good money, a man followed some other trade for six months or a year, and gave up handling money, he would become just like any other inexperienced person, unable to distinguish the good from the base.

Please reflect on this carefully. Once you make yourself familiar with the nature of the uncorrupted heart, from then on you will be immediately aware of the slightest tendency toward bias or selfishness. And why? Because the natural heart is enlightened. When a person has once learned what is perfect, they will never agree to accept what is imperfect; but if, after gaining this knowledge, they keep their natural heart at a distance again and gradually forget how to recognize what is perfect, they find themselves in the dark once more, no longer able to distinguish counterfeit money from the real thing. I urge you to be careful. If a person falls into bad habits, they can no longer perceive the difference between the good impulses of their natural heart and the evil impulses of their corrupt heart. Starting from this clouded heart, they can achieve none of their goals, and can only heave deep sighs again and again. A truly pitiful creature indeed! Then they lose all self-reliance; even though it would be better to keep quiet about it, if they are in the slightest trouble or distress, they go and confess the dishonesty of their heart to every person they meet. What a miserable state for a person to be in! For this reason, I urge you to learn the true silver of the heart thoroughly, so that you make no mistake about the counterfeit coins. I pray that you and I, throughout our whole lives, may never stray from the path of true principles.

Old and young, men and women, rich and poor, never stop grumbling from morning until night. All this is the result of a diseased heart. In short, for the sake of a very trivial whim or selfish pursuit, people will commit any wrong to achieve what is impossible. This is a lack of judgment, and it brings all sorts of trouble into the world. If once you gain possession of a perfect heart—knowing that what is impossible is impossible, and recognizing that what is difficult is difficult—you will not attempt to avoid trouble unfairly. What does the *Chin-Yo*¹ say? The wise man, whether his lot is cast among the rich or the poor, among barbarians or in sorrow, understands his position through his own instinct. If men do not understand this, they think that the causes of pain and pleasure lie in the body. # APPENDIX A.

## AN ACCOUNT OF THE HARA-KIRI.

### (FROM A RARE JAPANESE MS.)

SEPPUKU (*hara-kiri*) is the mode of suicide adopted among Samurai when they have no alternative but to die. There are some who commit suicide in this way of their own free will; there are others who, having committed a crime which does not place them beyond the limits of the privileges of the Samurai class, are ordered by their superiors to put an end to their own lives. It goes without saying that it is absolutely necessary for the principal, the witnesses, and the seconds who take part in the affair to be acquainted with all the ceremonies to be observed. A long time ago, a certain <term>Daimio</term> invited a number of people, well-versed in the various ceremonies, to call upon him to explain the different forms to be observed by the official witnesses who inspect and verify the head, etc., and then to instruct him in the ceremonies to be observed in the act of suicide; then he showed all these rites to his son and to all his retainers. Another person has said that, as the ceremonies to be gone through by the principal, witnesses, and seconds are all very important matters, men should familiarize themselves with such a terrible thing, so that, should the time come for them to take part in it, they may not be taken by surprise.

The witnesses go to see and certify the suicide. For

In former days, men used to keep these things in mind; but nowadays the fashion is to be ignorant of such ceremonies, and if upon rare occasions a criminal is handed over to a *Daimio*’s charge so that he may perform *hara-kiri*, it often happens, at the time of execution, that there is no one among all the prince’s retainers who is competent to act as a second. In such a case, a man has to be hired in a hurry from elsewhere to cut off the head of the criminal, and for that day he changes his name and becomes a retainer of the prince—either of the middle or lowest class—and the task is entrusted to him. Thus the difficulty is overcome, nor is this considered to be a disgrace. It is a great breach of etiquette if the second, who is a most important official, commits any mistake (such as failing to strike off the head with a single blow) in the presence of the witnesses sent by the Government. On this account, a skilled person must be employed; and, to hide the incompetence of his own people, a prince must perform the ceremony in this irregular manner. Every Samurai should be able to cut off a man’s head; therefore, to have to employ a stranger to act as a second is to invite the charge of ignorance of the martial arts and is a bitter humiliation. However, young men, relying on their youthful enthusiasm, are prone to be careless and are certain to make a mistake. There are some people who, while not lacking in skill on ordinary occasions, lose their composure in public and cannot do themselves justice. It is all the more important, therefore, as the act occurs but rarely, that men who are liable to be called upon to be either principals, seconds, or witnesses in the *hara-kiri* should be constantly examined in their skill as swordsmen and should be familiar with all the rites, so that when the time comes they may not lose their composure.

At that time the country was in a state of utter confusion; and there were men who, although fighting, were guilty of neither high treason nor infidelity to their feudal lords, but who were taken prisoner by the chances of war. To drag out such men, bound as criminals, and cut off their heads was intolerably cruel; accordingly, men devised a ceremonious mode of suicide by disembowelling in order to comfort the departed spirit. Even now, when it becomes necessary to put to death a man who has been guilty of some act not unworthy of a Samurai, witnesses are sent to the house at the time of the execution; and the criminal, having bathed and put on new clothes, puts an end to himself in obedience to the commands of his superiors, but does not forfeit his rank as a Samurai on that account. This is a law for which, in all truth, men should be grateful.

### ON THE PREPARATION OF THE PLACE OF EXECUTION.

In the old days, the ceremony of *hara-kiri* used to be performed in a temple. In the third year of the period called Kan-ei (A.D. 1626), a certain person who had been guilty of treason was ordered to disembowel himself on the fourteenth day of the first month, in the temple of Kichijōji at Komagome in Yedo. Eighteen years later, the retainer of a certain Daimyo, after having a dispute with a sailor belonging to an Osaka coasting ship, killed the sailor; and, an investigation having been made into the matter by the Governor of Osaka, the retainer was ordered to perform *hara-kiri* on the twentieth day of the sixth month, in the temple called Sokusanji in Osaka. During the Shoho period (the middle of the seventeenth century), a certain man who was guilty of heinous misconduct performed *hara-kiri* in the

In modern times, the ceremony has taken place at night, either in the palace or in the garden of a Daimyo to whom the condemned man has been entrusted. Whether it takes place in the palace or in the garden depends upon the rank of the individual. Daimyos and Hatamotos, as a matter of course, as well as the higher retainers of the Shogun, disembowel themselves in the palace; retainers of lower rank should do so in the garden. In the case of vassals of feudal lords, depending on the rank of their families, those who are above the grade of captains and carry the baton¹ should perform *hara-kiri* in the palace; all others in the garden. If, when the time comes, the persons involved in the ceremony have any doubt regarding the proper rules to be followed, they should consult competent persons and settle the matter. Nowadays, when *hara-kiri* is performed inside a palace, a temporary site is prepared specifically for that purpose, either in the garden or in some unoccupied spot. However, if the condemned man is to die on the day he is placed in custody, or on the next day, the ceremony—having to take place so quickly—is performed in the reception room. Still, even if there is a delay between the time the prisoner is placed in custody and the execution, it is better for the ceremony to take place in a proper room in the house than in a place built specifically for the occasion. If it is heard that a man has created a special site solely for fear of dirtying his house, he will be criticized for it. It certainly can be no disgrace to the house of a soldier that he was ordered to perform the final rites for a Samurai who died by *hara-kiri*. To slay an enemy for whom he has cause for hatred, and then to kill himself, is the duty of a noble Samurai; and it is sheer nonsense to view the place where he has disemboweled himself as polluted. At the beginning of the eighteenth century, seventeen of the retainers of Asano Takumi no Kami performed *hara-kiri* in the garden of a palace at Shirokané, in Yedo. When it was over, the palace staff called upon the priests of a sect named Shugenja to come and purify the place; but when the lord of the palace heard this, he ordered the place to be left as it was, for what need was there to purify a place where faithful Samurai had died by their own hand? However, in other palaces to which the rest of the retainers of Takumi no Kami were entrusted, it is said that the execution sites were purified. But the people of that day praised Kumamoto Ko (the Prince of Higo), to whom the palace at Shirokané

In modern times, the place for *hara-kiri* is eighteen feet square in all cases; in the center is a place to sit upon, and the condemned man is made to sit facing the witnesses; at other times he is placed with his side to the witnesses: this is according to the nature of the spot. Although the ceremony is performed in other ways as well, it is still more convenient to follow the manner indicated.

If the execution takes place in a room, a cloth of five widths of white cotton or a quilt should be laid down, and it is also said that two mats should be prepared; however, as there are already mats in the room, there is no need for special mats: two red rugs should be spread over everything, sewn together, one on top of the other; for if the white cotton cloth is used alone, the blood will soak through onto the mats; therefore, it is right the rugs should be spread. The reason for this is that some men in that position suffer from a rush of blood to the head due to nervousness, so their sandals might slip off their feet without them being aware of the loss; and as this would have a very bad appearance, it is better to spread matting. Care must be taken so that, in spreading the matting, no place is left where two mats join against which the foot might trip. The white screens and other things are prepared as has been directed above. If any reduction is made to the ceremony, it must be done as well as circumstances will permit. > “The house in which we live is very small and inconvenient in all respects. We have ordered the guard to treat our prisoner with all respect; but our retainers who are placed on guard are much inconvenienced for want of space; besides, in the event of fire breaking out or any extraordinary event taking place, the place is so small that it would be difficult to get out. We are thinking, therefore, of adding an apartment to the original building, so that the guard may be able at all times to go in and out freely, and that if, in case of fire or otherwise, we should have to leave the house, we may do so easily. We beg to consult you upon this point.”

If the principal palace <note>The principal <term>yashikis</term> (palaces) of the nobles are mostly located immediately around the <term>Shogun</term>'s castle, in the enclosure known as the official quarter. When a retainer is suddenly ordered to perform <term>hara-kiri</term> during a journey, a temple or shrine should be hired for the occasion. On these hurried occasions, coarse mats, faced with finer matting or common mats, may be used. If the prisoner is of a rank to have an armor-bearer, a carpet of skin should be spread, if one is easily available. The straps of the skin (which are at the head) should, according to old custom, be to the front, so that the fur points backward. In the old days, when the ceremony took place in a garden, a carpet of skin was spread. Hiring a temple for the purpose of having a man perform <term>hara-kiri</term> was a frequent occurrence; it is doubtful whether this is permitted at the present time. This sort of question should be referred beforehand to a competent person, so that the course to be adopted may be clearly understood.

In the <term>Kambun</term> period (A.D. 1661—1673), a <term>Prince Sakai</term>, traveling through the <term>Bishiu</term> territory, hired a temple or shrine for one of his retainers to disembowel himself in; and so the affair was concluded.

### ON THE CEREMONIES OBSERVED AT THE <term>HARA-KIRI</term> OF A PERSON GIVEN IN CHARGE TO A <term>DAIMIO</term>.

When a man has been ordered by the Government to perform <term>hara-kiri</term>, the public censors, who have been appointed to act as witnesses, write to the prince who has the prisoner in his charge to inform him that they will go to his palace on public business. This message is written directly to the chief official and is sent by an assistant censor; a suitable answer is returned to it. Before the ceremony, the witnesses send an assistant censor to inspect the site and look at a plan of the house, and to take a list of the names of the persons who are to be present; he also has an interview with the *<term>kaishaku</term>*, or seconds, and examines them on the way they will perform the ceremonies. When all the preparations have been made, he goes to fetch the censors; and they all proceed together to the place of execution, dressed in their ceremonial hempen-cloth robes. The retainers of the palace are gathered to bow in the entrance courtyard; and the lord, to whom the prisoner has been entrusted, goes as far as the front porch to meet the censors and conducts them to the front reception room. The chief censor then announces to the lord of the palace that he has come to read out the sentence of the individual who has been condemned to perform *<term>hara-kiri</term>*, and that the second censor has come to witness the execution of the sentence. The lord of the palace then inquires whether he is expected to attend the execution in person, and, if any of the relatives or family of the prisoner should ask to receive his remains, whether their request should be granted; after this, he announces that he will order everything to be made ready and leaves the room. Tea, a charcoal brazier for smoking, and sweets are set before the censors; but they decline to accept any hospitality until their business has been concluded. The minor officials follow the same rule. If the censors express a wish to see the place of execution, the retainers of the palace show the way, and their lord accompanies them.

From the time the chief censor enters the house until he leaves it, no one is allowed to enter the premises. The servants on guard at the entrance porch should wear their ceremonial hempen dresses. The blood-stained ground was sprinkled with sand and swept clean; fresh mats were laid down, and the place prepared anew, after which the next man was summoned to come forward.

### ON CERTAIN THINGS TO BE BORNE IN MIND BY THE WITNESSES.

When a clansman is ordered by his feudal lord to perform <term>*hara-kiri*</term>, the sentence must be read out by the censor of the clan, who also acts as a witness. He should take his place in front of the prisoner at a distance of twelve feet; according to some books, the distance should be eighteen feet, and he should sit at an angle, not directly facing the prisoner; he should lay his sword down by his side, but, if he pleases, he may wear it in his belt; he must read the sentence distinctly. If the sentence is a long document, starting to read in a very loud voice and afterwards dropping into a whisper appears faint-hearted; but to read it throughout in a low voice is even worse: it should be delivered clearly from begin—

...ning to end. It is the duty of the chief witness to set an example of courage for the other people who are to take part in the execution. When the second has finished his task, he carries the head to the chief witness, who, after inspecting it, must declare that he has identified it; he should then take his sword and leave his position. It is sufficient, however, for the head to be struck off without being carried to the chief witness; in that case, the second receives his instructions beforehand. Upon rising, the chief witness should step out with his left foot and turn to the left. If the ceremony takes place outdoors, the chief witness, wearing his sword and dagger, should sit upon a box; he must wear his ritual hempen dress; he may hitch his trousers up slightly; depending on his rank, he may wear his full dress—that is, "wings" <note>the kamishimo, or formal winged vest</note> over his formal clothing. It is the responsibility of the chief witness to instruct the seconds and others in the duties they must perform, and also to plan in advance for the possibility of any mishap occurring.

If any other person should enter while the various people involved in the ceremony are brushing up on their military knowledge and preparing for the event, they should immediately change the subject. People of the rank of Samurai should be familiar with all the details of *hara-kiri*; to be seen discussing what should be done in case anything went wrong, and so forth, would give the appearance of ignorance. However, if a close friend should visit the place, he may be consulted on the whole affair rather than having any awkward concealment.

When the sentence has been read, it is likely that the condemned man will have some last words to say to the chief witness. Whether or not these words are accepted depends on their nature. If he speaks in a confused or bewildered manner, no attention is paid to him; his second should lead him away, either on his own initiative or at a signal from the chief witness.

> "Sir, I thank you for your careful consideration, but I have nothing that I wish to say. Or he may say, "Sirs, I have nothing to say; yet, since you are so kind as to think of me, I should be obliged if you would deliver such and such a message to a certain person."

This is the proper and appropriate sort of speech for the occasion. If the prisoner entrusts them with any message, the retainers should receive it in such a manner as to set his mind at rest. Should he ask for writing materials in order to write a letter, as this is forbidden by the law, they should tell him so, and not grant his request. Still, they must feel that it is painful to refuse the request of a dying man and must do their best to assist him. They must show every possible kindness and civility, as was done in the Genroku <note>1688–1704</note> period, in the case of the Ronin <note>Masterless samurai</note> of Asano Takumi no Kami. The Prince of Higo, after the sentence had been read, caused paper and writing materials to be taken to their room. If the prisoner is light-headed from excitement, it is no use furnishing him with writing materials. It must depend upon circumstances; but when a man has murdered another, having made up his mind to abide by the consequences, then that man's execution should be carried through with all honor. When a man kills another on the spot in a fit of uncontrollable passion, and then is bewildered and dazed by his own act, the same pains need not be taken to conduct matters so punctiliously. After the Ronin of Asano Takumi no Kami had heard their sentence in the palace of Matsudaira Oki no Kami, that Daimyo went in person to take leave of them. Calling Oishi Chikara,¹ the son of their leader, to him, he said, “I have heard that your mother is at home in your own province; I can well imagine how she will grieve when she hears of your death and that of your father. If you have any message that you wish to leave for her, tell me without standing on ceremony, and I will deliver it without delay.” For a while, Chikara kept his head bowed toward the ground; at last, he drew back slightly and, lifting his head, said, “I humbly thank your lordship for what you have been pleased to say. My father warned me from the beginning that our crime was so great that, even if we were pardoned by a gracious judgment on one count, I must not forget that there would be a hundred million other counts against us for which we must commit suicide; and that if I disregarded his words, his hatred would pursue me after death. My father impressed this upon me at the temple called Sengakuji, and again when I was separated from him to be taken to the palace of Prince Sengoku. Now my father and I have been condemned to perform *hara-kiri*, according to the desire of our hearts. Still, I cannot help but think of my mother. When we parted at Kyoto, she told me that our separation would be long, and she commanded me not to act like a coward when I thought of her. As I took a final leave of her then, I have no message to send to her now.” When he spoke this way, Oki no Kami and all his retainers, who were lined up around him, were moved to tears in admiration of his heroism.

Although it is proper for the condemned man to bathe and partake of wine and food, these details should be cur-

->CONCERNING SECONDS (<term>KAISHAKU</term>).<-

When the condemned man is someone who has been handed over for execution, six attendants are employed; when the execution is within the clan, then two or three attendants will suffice; the number, however, must depend upon the rank of the principal. Men of great nerve and strength must be selected for the office; they must wear their formal hempen dress and tuck up their trousers; they must on no account wear either a sword or a dagger, but have a small <term>poniard</term> hidden in their robes: these are the officers who attend to the condemned man when he changes his clothes, and who sit by him on his right and left to guard him while the sentence is being read. In the event of any mistake occurring (such as the prisoner attempting to escape), they knock him down; and should he be unable to stand or to walk, they help to support him. The attendants accompanying the principal to the place of execution, if they are six in number, four of them take their seats some distance away and mount guard, while the other two should sit close behind the principal. They must understand that should there be any mistake, they must throw the condemned man down and, holding him down, cut off his head with their <term>poniard</term>, or

They must help him take off his upper garments and bare his body. In recent times, however, there have been cases where the upper garments have not been removed; this depends upon the circumstances. Setting up the white screen and laying the corpse in the coffin are duties which, although they may be performed by other officers, originally fell to the six attendants. When a common man is executed, he is bound with cords and forced to take his place; but a <term>Samurai</term> wears his ceremonial dress, is presented with a dagger, and dies in this manner. There should be no worry that such a man might attempt to escape; nonetheless, as there is no knowing what these six attendants might be called upon to do, men should be selected who thoroughly understand their business.

   The seconds are three in number—the chief second, the assistant second, and the inferior second. When the execution is carried out with proper solemnity, three men are employed; yet a second and an assistant second are sufficient. If three men serve as seconds, their several duties are as follows:
   The chief second strikes off the head; that is his duty. He is the most important officer in an execution by *hara-kiri*. The assistant second brings forward the tray on which the dirk is placed; that is his duty. He must perform his part in such a way that the principal second is not hindered in his work. The assistant second is the officer of second importance in the execution. The third, or inferior second, carries the head to the chief witness for identification; and in the event of something suddenly occurring to hinder either of the other two seconds, he should keep in mind that he must be ready to act as a substitute. His is an office of great importance, and a suitable person must be selected to fill it.

When a man is appointed to act as second to another, what shall be said of him if he accepts the office with a smiling face? Yet, he must not put on a look of distress. It is appropriate to try to excuse oneself from performing the duty. There is no heroism in cutting off a man's head well, and it is a disgrace to do it in a bungling manner; yet, a man must not claim a lack of skill as a pretext for evading the office, for it is an unworthy thing for a <term>Samurai</term> to lack the skill required to behead a man. If there are any who advocate for employing young men as seconds, it should instead be said that their hands are inexperienced. To play the coward and hand over the office to another man is out of the question. When a man is called upon to perform the office, he should express his readiness to use his sword (the dirk may be used, but the sword is the proper weapon). Regarding the sword, the second should borrow that of the principal; if there is any objection to this, he should receive a sword from his lord; he should not use his own sword. When the assistant seconds have been appointed, the three should consult together about the details of the place of execution after they have been carefully instructed in all the ceremonies by their superiors; and having made a careful inquiry, should anything be wrong, they should appeal to their superiors for instruction. The seconds wear their ceremonial dress when the criminal is a man placed in their charge by the Government; when he is a member of their own clan, they need only wear the trousers of the <term>Samurai</term>. In the old days, it is said that they were dressed in the same way as the principal; and some authorities assert that at the *hara-kiri* of a high-ranking nobleman, the seconds should wear white clothes, and the handle of the sword should be wrapped in white silk. The seconds should address the principal and say, “Sir, we have been appointed to act as your seconds; we pray you to set your mind at rest,” and so forth; but this must depend upon the rank of the criminal. At this time, too, if the principal has any last wish to express, the second should receive it and should treat him with every consideration in order to relieve his anxiety. If the second has been selected by the principal on account of an old friendship between them, or if the latter, during the time that he has been in charge, has asked some special retainer of the palace to act as his second in the event of his being condemned to death, the person so selected should thank the principal for choosing such an unworthy person and promise to ask his lord to allow him to act as second: so he should answer and comfort him, and having reported the matter to his lord, should act as second. He should take that opportunity to borrow the principal’s sword in terms such as the following: “As I am to have the honor of being your second, I would gladly borrow your sword for the occasion. It may be a consolation to you to die by your own sword, with which you are familiar.” If, however, the principal declines and prefers to be executed with the second’s sword, his wish must be complied with. Although this is the rule, and although every <term>Samurai</term> should wear a sword fit to cut off a man’s head, still, if the principal has asked to be executed with the second’s own sword, it must be done as he desires.

Some say that the <term>principal</term> should take the tray, raise it respectfully to his head, and set it down; and that this is the moment to strike. There are three rules for the timing of cutting off the head: the first is when the <term>dirk</term> is laid on the tray; the second is when the <term>principal</term> looks at the left side of his belly before inserting the <term>dirk</term>; the third is when he inserts the <term>dirk</term>. If these three moments are allowed to pass, it becomes a difficult matter to cut off the head; so says tradition. Although all four ways are approved, the first is considered too soon; the last three are right and proper. In short, the blow should be struck without delay. 

If he has struck off the head with one blow without failure, the <term>second</term>—taking care not to raise his sword but holding it point downward—should retire backward a little and wipe his weapon while kneeling. He should have plenty of white paper ready in his belt or inside his robe to wipe away the blood and polish his sword. Having replaced his sword in its scabbard, he should readjust his upper garments and take his seat to the rear. When the head has fallen, the junior <term>second</term> should enter and, taking up the head, present it to the witness for inspection. When he has identified it, the ceremony is concluded. If there is no assistant or junior <term>second</term>, the <term>second</term>—as soon as he has cut off the head—should carry his sword reversed in his left hand and take the head in his right hand, holding it by the topknot of hair. He should advance toward the witness, passing on the right side of the corpse, and show the right profile of the head to the witness, resting the chin of the head upon the hilt of his sword and kneeling on his left knee. **NOTE.**—<note>To lay down thick paper and place the head on it shows a desire to show respect to the head; to place it on the edge of the sword is insulting. The course followed must depend upon the rank of the person. There are some who say that the perfect way for the <term>second</term> to cut off the head is not to cut completely through the neck with one blow, but to leave a small amount uncut; then, as the head hangs by the skin, to seize the <term>top-knot</term> and slice it off, and then submit it for <term>head inspection</term>. According to the old authorities, this is the proper and respectful manner. After the head is cut off, the eyes are prone to blink and the mouth to move and bite the pebbles and sand. Since this is unpleasant to see during such an important occasion among <term>Samurai</term>, and is considered a shameful thing, it is held to be best not to let the head fall, but to hold back a little when delivering the blow. Three methods of carrying the sword are recognized among those skilled in **swordsmanship**. If the rank of the **principal** be high, the sword is raised aloft; if the **principal** and **second** are of equal rank, the sword is carried at the center of the body; if the **principal** be of inferior rank, the sword is allowed to hang downward. The proper position for the **second** to strike from is kneeling on one knee, but there is no harm in his standing up: others say that, if the execution takes place inside the house, the **second** should kneel; if in the garden, he should stand. These are not points upon which to insist obstinately: a man should strike in whatever position is most convenient to him.

The chief duty for the **assistant second** to bear in mind is the bringing in of the tray with the <term>dirk</term>, which should be produced very quietly when the **principal** takes his place: it should be placed so that the condemned man may have to stretch his hand well out in order to reach it. <note>It should be placed about three feet away from him.</note> The **assistant second** then returns to his own place; but if the condemned man shows any signs of agitation, the **assistant second** must lend his assistance, so that the head may be properly cut off. It once happened that the condemned man, having received the tray from the **assistant second**, held it up for a long time without putting it down, until those near him had over and over again urged him to set it down. It also happens that after the tray has been set down, and the **assistant second** has retired, the condemned man does not put out his hand to take it; then the **assistant second** must urge him to take it. If the prisoner is an unruly or violent man, a fan should be placed upon the tray instead of a dirk; if he objects to this, he should be told in response that the substitution of the fan is an ancient custom. If the condemned man appears inclined to be turbulent, the seconds—without showing any sign of alarm—should hurry to his side and, urging him to get ready, quickly cause him to make all his preparations with speed and to sit down in his place. The chief second, then drawing his sword, should get ready to strike and, ordering him to proceed as fast as possible with the ceremony of receiving the tray, should perform his duty without appearing to be afraid.

A certain Prince Katô, having condemned one of his councilors to death, attended the ceremony from behind a curtain of bamboo slats. The councilor, whose name was Katayama, was bound, and during that time glared fiercely at the curtain and showed no signs of fear. The chief second was a man named Jihei, who had always been accustomed to treating Katayama with great respect. So Jihei, sword in hand, said to Katayama, "Sir, your last moment has arrived: be so good as to turn your cheek so that your head may be straight." When Katayama heard this, he replied, "Fellow, you are insolent"; and as he was looking around, Jihei struck the fatal blow. When the head has been struck off, it becomes the duty of the junior second to pick it up by the top-knot and, placing it upon some thick paper laid over the palm of his hand, to carry it for inspection by the witness. This ceremony has been explained above. If the head is bald, he should pierce the left ear with the stiletto carried in the scabbard of his dirk, and so carry it to be identified. When the identification of the head is concluded, the junior second’s duty is to place it in a bucket.

If anything should occur to hinder the chief second, the assistant second must take his place. It happened on one occasion that before the execution took place, the chief second lost his nerve, yet he cut off the head without any difficulty; but when it came to picking up the head for inspection, his nervousness so far got the better of him that it was extremely inconvenient. This is something against which persons acting as seconds have to guard.

As a supplement to the elaborate statement above regarding the ceremonies proper to be observed at the *hara-kiri*, I may here describe an instance of such an execution which I was sent officially to witness. The condemned man was Taki Zenzaburô, an officer of the Prince of Bizen, who gave the order to fire upon the foreign settlement at Hiogo in the month of February 1868—an attack to which I have alluded in the introduction to the story of the Eta Maiden and the Hatamoto. Up to that time, no foreigner had witnessed such an execution, which was rather looked upon as a traveler’s myth.

headquarters of the Satsuma troops at Hiogo. A witness was sent from each of the foreign legations. We were seven foreigners in all.

We were conducted to the temple by officers of the Princes of Satsuma and Choshiu. Although the ceremony was to be conducted in the most private manner, the casual remarks which we overheard in the streets, and a crowd lining the principal entrance to the temple, showed that it was a matter of no little interest to the public. The courtyard of the temple presented a most picturesque sight; it was crowded with soldiers standing about in groups around large fires, which threw a dim flickering light over the heavy eaves and quaint gable-ends of the sacred buildings. We were shown into an inner room, where we were to wait until the preparation for the ceremony was completed; in the next room to us were the high Japanese officers. After a long interval, which seemed doubly long because of the silence which prevailed, Itô Shunské, the provisional Governor of Hiogo, came and took down our names, and informed us that seven *<term>kenshi</term>*, sheriffs or witnesses, would attend on the part of the Japanese. He and another officer represented the Mikado; two captains of Satsuma’s infantry, and two of Choshiu’s, with a representative of the Prince of Bizen, the clan of the condemned man, completed the number, which was probably arranged in order to match that of the foreigners. Itô Shunské further inquired whether we wished to put any questions to the prisoner. We replied in the negative.

A further delay then ensued, after which we were invited to follow the Japanese witnesses into the *<term>hondo</term>* or main hall of the temple, where the ceremony was to be performed. It was an imposing scene. A large hall with a high roof supported by dark pillars of wood. From the ceiling hung a profusion of those huge gilt lamps and ornaments peculiar to Buddhist temples. In front of the high altar, where the floor, covered with beautiful white mats, is raised some three or four inches from the ground, was laid a rug of scarlet felt. After an interval of a few minutes of anxious suspense, Taki Zenzaburô, a stalwart man of thirty-two years of age with a noble air, walked into the hall dressed in his ceremonial robes, featuring the peculiar hempen-cloth wings which are worn on great occasions. He was accompanied by a *kaishaku* and three officers, who wore the *jimbaori*, or war surcoat, with gold-tissue facings. The word *kaishaku*, it should be noted, is a term for which our word "executioner" is not an equivalent. The office is that of a gentleman: in many cases, it is performed by a kinsman or friend of the condemned, and the relationship between them is more like that of a principal and his second than that of a victim and an executioner. In this instance, the *kaishaku* was a pupil of Taki Zenzaburô and was selected by Taki’s friends from among their own number for his skill in swordsmanship.

With the *kaishaku* at his left side, Taki Zenzaburô advanced slowly toward the Japanese witnesses, and the two bowed before them; then, drawing near to the foreigners, they saluted us in the same way, perhaps even with more deference. In each case, the salutation was ceremoniously returned. Slowly and with great dignity, the condemned man mounted onto the raised floor, prostrated himself twice before the high altar, and seated<gloss>1</gloss> himself on the felt carpet with his back to the high altar, the *kaishaku* crouching at his left side. One of the three attendant officers then came forward, bearing the kind of stand used in temples for offerings, on which, wrapped in paper, lay the *wakizashi*—the short sword or dagger of the Japanese, nine and a half inches in length, with a point and an edge as sharp as a razor’s. This he handed, while prostrating himself, to the condemned man, who received it

After another profound bow, Taki Zenzaburô, in a voice which betrayed just as much emotion and hesitation as might be expected from a man who is making a painful confession, but with no sign of either in his face or manner, spoke as follows:—

“I, and I alone, unjustifiably gave the order to fire on the foreigners at Kôbé, and again as they tried to escape. For this crime I disembowel myself, and I beg you who are present to do me the honor of witnessing the act.”

Bowing once more, the speaker allowed his upper garments to slip down to his belt, and remained naked to the waist. Carefully, according to custom, he tucked his sleeves under his knees to prevent himself from falling backwards; for a noble Japanese gentleman should die falling forwards. Deliberately, with a steady hand, he took the dirk that lay before him; he looked at it wistfully, almost affectionately; for a moment he seemed to collect his thoughts for the last time, and then stabbing himself deeply below the waist on the left-hand side, he drew the dirk slowly across to the right side, and, turning it in the wound, gave a slight cut upwards. During this sickeningly painful operation he never moved a muscle of his face. When he drew out the dirk, he leaned forward and stretched out his neck; an expression of pain for the first time crossed his face, but he uttered no sound. At that moment the *<term>kaishaku</term>*, who, still crouching by his side, had been keenly watching his every movement, sprang to his feet, poised his sword for a second in the air; there was a flash, a heavy, ugly thud, a crashing fall; with one blow the head had been severed from the body.

A dead silence followed, broken only by the hideous noise of the blood throbbing out of the inert heap before us, which but a moment before had been a brave and chivalrous man. It was horrible.

The *<term>kaishaku</term>* made a low bow, wiped his sword with a piece of paper which he had ready for the purpose, and retired.

The two representatives of the Mikado then left their places and, crossing over to where the foreign witnesses sat, called upon us to witness that the sentence of death upon Taki Zenzaburô had been faithfully carried out. The ceremony being over, we left the temple.

The ceremony, which was made even more solemn by the location and the hour, was characterized throughout by that extreme dignity and formality which are the hallmarks of the proceedings of Japanese gentlemen of rank; and it is important to note this fact, because it carries with it the conviction that the dead man was indeed the officer who had committed the crime, and not a substitute. While deeply moved by the terrible scene, it was also impossible not to be filled with admiration for the firm and courageous bearing of the condemned man, and for the composure with which the *kaishaku* performed his last duty to his master. Nothing could more strongly demonstrate the power of upbringing. The Samurai, or gentleman of the military class, learns from his earliest years to view the *hara-kiri* as a ceremony in which he may one day be called upon to play a part as either the principal or the second. In traditional families, which hold to the traditions of ancient chivalry, the child is instructed in the rite and made familiar with the idea as an honorable atonement for a crime or the erasing of disgrace. If the hour comes, he is prepared for it and bravely faces an ordeal which early training has stripped of half its horrors. In what other country in the world does a man learn that the last tribute of affection which he may have to pay to his best friend may be to serve as his executioner?

The opinion has been expressed that it would have been politic for the foreign representatives to have interceded for the life of Taki Zenzaburô at the last moment. The question is believed to have been debated among the representatives themselves. My own belief is that mercy, although it might have produced the desired effect among the more civilized clans, would have been mistaken for weakness and fear by those wilder people who do not yet have a personal knowledge of foreigners. The offense—an attack upon the flags and subjects of all the Treaty Powers, which only a lack of skill, not of will, prevented from ending in a universal massacre—was the gravest that has been committed against foreigners since they began residing in Japan. Death was undoubtedly deserved, and the form chosen was, in Japanese eyes, merciful and yet judicial. The crime might have involved a war and cost hundreds of lives; it was wiped out by one death. I believe that, in the interest of Japan as well as in our own, the course pursued was wise, and it was very satisfactory to me to find that one of the ablest Japanese ministers, with whom I had a discussion upon the subject, completely agreed with my opinion.

The *kaishaku* on the right side picks up the head and shows it to the sheriff. The body is given to the relatives for burial. In most cases, the property of the deceased is confiscated.

3rd. *Self-immolation of a Daimio due to disgrace.*—When a Daimio had been guilty of treason or had offended the Tycoon, since the family was disgraced and an apology could neither be offered nor accepted, the offending Daimio was condemned to *hara-kiri*. Calling his councillors around him, he entrusted them with his last will and testament to be delivered to the Tycoon. Then, dressing himself in his court attire, he disemboweled himself and cut his own throat. His councillors then reported the matter to the Government, and a coroner was sent to investigate it. To him, the retainers handed their lord's last will and testament, and he took it to the Gorôjiu (First Council), who passed it on to the Tycoon. If the offense was heinous, such as would involve the ruin of the entire family, through the clemency of the Tycoon, half the property might be confiscated and half returned to the heir; if the offense was minor, the heir inherited the property intact, and the family did not suffer.

In all cases where the accused disembowels himself of his own accord without being condemned or investigated, since he is no longer able to defend himself, the offense is considered unproven and the property is not confiscated. In the year 1869, a motion was brought forward in the Japanese parliament by one Ono Seigorô, clerk of the house, advocating for the abolition of the practice of *hara-kiri*. Two hundred members out of a house of 209 voted against the motion, which was supported by only three speakers; six members did not vote for either side. "pillar of the constitution," "a valuable institution, tending to the honor of the nobles, and based on a compassionate feeling toward the official caste," "a pillar of religion and a spur to virtue." The whole debate (which is well worth reading, and an able translation of which by Mr. Aston has appeared in a recent Blue Book) shows the affection with which the Japanese cling to the traditions of a chivalrous past. It is worth noting that the proposer, Ono Seigorô, who on more than one occasion made himself conspicuous by introducing motions based upon an admiration of our Western civilization, was murdered not long after this debate took place.

There are many stories on record of extraordinary heroism being displayed in *hara-kiri*. The case of a young man, only twenty years old, of the Choshiu clan, which was told to me the other day by an eyewitness, deserves mention as a marvelous instance of determination. Not content with giving himself the one necessary cut, he slashed himself three times horizontally and twice vertically. Then he stabbed himself in the throat until the dagger protruded on the other side, with its sharp edge to the front; setting his teeth in one supreme effort, he drove the knife forward with both hands through his throat, and fell dead.

One more story and I am done. During the revolution, when the Tycoon, beaten on every side, fled ignominiously to Yedo, he is said to have decided to fight no more, but to yield everything. A member of his second council went to him and said, "Sir, the only way for you now to restore the honor of the Tokugawa family is to disembowel yourself; and to prove to you that I am sincere and selfless in what I say, I am here ready to disembowel myself with you." The Tycoon flew into a great rage, saying that he would listen to no such nonsense, and left the room. His faithful retainer, to prove his honesty, retired to another part of the castle, and solemnly performed *hara-kiri*.

# APPENDIX B.

## THE MARRIAGE CEREMONY.

->(FROM THE “SHO-REI HIKKI”—RECORD OF CEREMONIES.)<-

The ceremonies observed at marriages are varied, and it is not proper for a man, by exceeding the limits of his social status, to violate the established rules. When the middleman has arranged the preliminaries of the marriage between the two parties, he carries the complimentary gift, which is given at the time of betrothal, from the future bridegroom to his intended bride; and if this gift is accepted, the lady’s family can no longer withdraw their promise. This is the beginning of the contract. The usual betrothal gifts are as follows: Persons of the higher classes send a robe of white silk; a piece of gold embroidery for a girdle; a piece of silk fabric; a piece of white silk with a lozenge pattern, and other silk fabrics (these are arranged in a stack of three layers); fourteen barrels of wine, and seven types of condiments. Persons of the middle class send a piece of white silk fabric; a piece of gold embroidery for a girdle; a piece of white silk with a lozenge pattern, and other silk fabrics (these are arranged in a stack of two layers); ten barrels of wine, and five types of condiments. The lower classes send a robe of white silk and a robe of colored silk in a single-layered stack, together with six barrels of wine and three types of condiments. To the future father-in-law, a sword is sent with a scabbard for slinging, such as is worn in wartime, together with a list of the gifts; to the mother-in-

The future father-in-law sends a present of equal value in return to his son-in-law, but the bride-to-be sends no return present to her future husband; the present from the father-in-law must by no means be omitted, but depending on his position, if he is poor, he need only send wine and condiments.

In sending the presents, care must be taken not to fold the silk robe. The two silk robes that are sent on the marriage night must be placed with the collars stitched together in a particular fashion.

The ceremonies for sending the litter to fetch the bride on the wedding night are as follows. In families of good social standing, one of the principal retainers from each side is appointed to accompany the bride and to receive her. Matting is spread before the entrance door, upon which the bride's litter is placed, while the two principal retainers congratulate one another, and the officers of the bridegroom receive the litter. If a bucket containing clams to make the wedding broth has been sent with the bride, it is carried and received by a person of distinction. Close by the entrance door, a fire is lit on the right hand and on the left. These fires are called garden-torches. In front of the corridor along which the litter passes, on the right hand and on the left, two men and two women, in pairs, place two mortars, right and left, in which they pound rice; as the litter passes, the pounded rice from the left-hand side is moved across to the right, and the two are mixed together into one. The candle on the left is passed over to the right, and, once the two wicks are brought together, the candles are extinguished. These last three ceremonies are only performed at the weddings of people of high rank; they are not observed at the weddings of ordinary people. The bride takes several gifts with her to her husband’s house: two silk robes sewn together in a specific manner, a ceremonial dress with wings made of hemp cloth, an upper girdle and an under girdle, a fan, either five or seven pocket-books, and a sword. These seven presents are placed on a long tray, and their value depends on the family's financial means.

The bride’s dress is a white silk robe with a diamond pattern, worn over an under-robe also made of white silk. Over her head, she wears a veil of white silk which she allows to fall around her like a mantle when she sits down.

The bride’s furniture and personal effects are all organized for her by female attendants from her own house on a day before the wedding; the bridegroom’s effects are likewise arranged by the women of his own house.

When the bride meets her husband in the room where the relatives are gathered, she takes the seat of honor for this one occasion. Her husband sits in a lower place, not directly opposite her but diagonally, discreetly avoiding her gaze.

Then two handmaids, who act as wine pourers, bring the kettles and place them in the lower part of the room. The two wine bottles have a male and female butterfly, made of paper, attached to them respectively. The female butterfly is laid on its back, and the wine is poured from the bottle into the kettle. The male butterfly is then taken and laid on the female butterfly, and the wine from the bottle is poured into the same kettle; the entire mixture is then transferred with due ceremony to another kettle of a different shape, which the wine pourers place in front of themselves. Small, low dining tables are laid—one for each person—before the bride and bridegroom, and before the bride’s ladies-in-waiting. The woman assigned to pour the wine takes the three wine cups and stacks them one on top of the other before the bridegroom, who drinks two sips¹ from the top cup and pours a little wine from the full kettle into the empty kettle. The pouring together of the wine on the wedding night is symbolic of the union being formed. The bridegroom then pours a third cup of wine and drinks it, and the cup is carried by the ladies to the bride, who drinks three cups and pours a little wine from one kettle into the other, just as the bridegroom did. A cup is then set down and placed on the other two, and they are carried back to

### RITES AND CEREMONIES.

...one course of five dishes and one of three dishes, or else two courses of five dishes and one of three dishes, according to the wealth of the family. The ceremonies described above are those appropriate only for families of the highest rank and are by no means suitable for the lower classes, who must not overstep the proper boundaries of their social position.

There is a popular tradition that, in the ceremony of drinking wine on the wedding night, the bride should drink first and then hand the cup to the bridegroom; but although some authorities on ceremonies favor this course, it is undoubtedly a very great mistake. In the *Record of Rites* by Confucius, it is written: “The man stands in importance before the woman; it is the right of the strong over the weak. Heaven ranks above the earth; the prince ranks above his minister. This law of honor is one.” Again, in the *Book of History* by Confucius, it is written: “The hen that crows in the morning brings misfortune.” In our own literature, in the *Jusho* (*Book of the Gods*): “When the goddesses saw the gods for the first time, they were the first to cry out, ‘Oh! What beautiful males!’ But the gods were greatly displeased and said, ‘We, who are so strong and powerful, should by rights have been the first to speak; why is it that, on the contrary, these females speak first? This is indeed unrefined.’” Again, it is written: “When the gods brought forth the cripple Hiruko, the Lord of Heaven said in response that his misfortune was a punishment upon the goddesses who had presumed to speak first.” The same rule, therefore, exists in both China and Japan, and it is held to be unlucky for the wife to take precedence; with this warning, people should be careful not to commit a breach of etiquette, even though it may be sanctioned by the common people.

At the weddings of the lower classes, the bride and her ladies and friends have a feast, but the bridegroom has no feast; and when the bride’s feast is over, the bridegroom is called in and presented with the bride’s wine cup. However, as the forms observed are very unrefined, it is not worth pointing out the rules that guide them. As this night is

If the parents of the bridegroom are deceased, instead of the ceremony described above, he leads his bride to make her obeisances before the tablets on which their names are inscribed.

In the old days, after the ceremonies recorded above had been completed, the bridegroom used to pay a ceremonial visit to the bride's parents; but at the present time, the visit is paid before the wedding, and although the forms observed on the occasion resemble those of ancient times, they are still different, and it would be better if we resumed the old fashion. The two trays which had been used at the wedding feast, loaded with fowl, fish, and neatly arranged condiments, used to be put into a long box and sent to the father-in-law's house. Five hundred and eighty rice cakes in lacquer boxes were also sent. The modern practice of sending the rice cakes in a bucket is quite contrary to etiquette; no matter how many lacquer boxes may be required for the purpose, they are the proper utensils for sending the cakes in. The *kaioké*² is placed on the raised floor; but if there is no raised floor, it is placed in a closet with the door open, so that it may be clearly seen. The books are arranged on a bookshelf or in a cabinet; if there is neither a shelf nor a cabinet, they are placed on the raised floor. The bride’s clothes are set out on a clothes-rack: in families of high rank, seven robes are hung on the rack; five of these are removed and replaced by others, and then three more are removed and replaced by others. There are either two or three clothes-racks, and the towel-rack is placed in a position of greater honor than the clothes-racks.

->NOTE.<-

The author of the *Sho-rei Hikki* makes no reference to the custom of shaving the eyebrows and blackening the teeth of married women as a sign of loyalty to their husbands. In the upper classes, young ladies usually blacken their teeth before leaving their father’s house to enter that of their husbands, and they complete the ceremony by shaving their eyebrows immediately after the wedding, or, at any rate, no later than the occasion of their first pregnancy.

The origin of this fashion is lost in antiquity. As proof that it existed before the eleventh century A.D., a curious book called *Teijô Zakki*, or the *Miscellaneous Writings of Teijô*, cites the diary of <term>Murasaki Shikibu</term>, the daughter of one <term>Tamésoki</term>, a retainer of the house of <term>Echizen</term>, a lady of the court and a famous poet, and the author of a book called <term>Genji-mono-gatari</term> and other works. In her diary, it is written that on the last night of the fifth year of the <term>Kankô</term> period (A.D. 1008), so that she might appear at her best on New Year’s Day, she retired to the privacy of her own apartment and corrected the flaws in her appearance by re-blackening her teeth and otherwise decorating herself. Reference is also made to the custom in the <term>Yeiga-mono-gatari</term>, an ancient book by the same author.

The Emperor and the nobles of his court are also in the habit of blackening their teeth, but the custom is gradually dying out for them. It is said to have originated with one <term>Hanazono Arishito</term>, who held the high rank of <term>Sa-Daijin</term>, or “Minister of the Left,” at the beginning of the twelfth century, during the reign of <term>Emperor Toba</term>. Being a man of refined and sensual tastes, this minister plucked out his eyebrows, shaved his beard, blackened his teeth, powdered his face white, and rouged his lips in order to

make himself look as much like a woman as possible. In the middle of the twelfth century, the court nobles who went to war all blackened their teeth; and from that time on, the practice became a fashion of the court. The followers of the chiefs of the Hôjô dynasty also blackened their teeth as a symbol of their loyalty; and this was called the Odawara fashion, named after the family's castle town. Thus, a custom that had its origin in a love of luxury and pleasure came to be mistaken for the sign of a good and faithful spirit.

The fashion of blackening the teeth causes significant trouble for its followers, for the color must be renewed every day, or at least every other day. Strange and repulsive as the custom appears at first, the eye soon learns to look without dislike upon a well-blackened and polished set of teeth; but when the color begins to wear away and turns to a dull grey, streaked with black, the mouth certainly becomes most hideous. Although no one who reads this is likely to put a recipe for blackening the teeth to a practical test, I include one provided to me by a fashionable chemist and druggist in Yedo:

> “Take three pints of water and, after warming it, add half a teacup of wine. Put a quantity of red-hot iron into this mixture; let it stand for five or six days, until a scum forms on the top of the mixture. This should then be poured into a small teacup and placed near a fire. When it is warm, powdered gall-nuts and iron filings should be added to it, and the whole should be warmed again. The liquid is then painted onto the teeth using a soft feather brush, along with more powdered gall-nuts and iron; after several applications, the desired color will be achieved.”

The process is said to preserve the teeth, and I have known men who were habitual sufferers of toothaches to prefer the martyrdom of ugliness to that of pain, and apply the black coloring when the bouts of pain were severe. One man told me that he experienced immediate relief from the application, and that as long as he blackened his teeth, he was quite free from pain.

## ON THE BIRTH AND REARING OF CHILDREN.

->(FROM THE "SHO-REI HIKKI.")<-

In the fifth month of a woman’s pregnancy, a very auspicious day is selected for the ceremony of putting on a girdle, which is made of white and red silk, folded, and is eight feet long. The husband produces it from the left sleeve of his robe; and the wife receives it in the right sleeve of her robe and puts it on for the first time. This ceremony is performed only once. When the child is born, the white part of the girdle is dyed sky-blue with a unique mark on it and is made into clothes for the child. These, however, are not the first clothes that the infant wears. The dyer is presented with wine and condiments when the girdle is entrusted to him. It is also customary to ask a matron, who has herself had an easy labor, for the girdle that she wore during her pregnancy; and this lady is called the "girdle-mother." The borrowed girdle is tied on along with the one given by the husband, and the girdle-mother exchanges gifts at this time.

The furniture of the birthing room is as follows: — Two tubs for placing undergarments in; two tubs to hold the placenta; a piece of furniture like an armchair without legs for the mother to lean against;<note>Women in Japan give birth in a kneeling position, and after the birth of the child, they remain day and night in a squatting position, leaning back against a support for twenty-one days, after which they are allowed to lie down.
