When the child is taken out of the warm water, its body must be dried with a kerchief of fine, unhemmed cotton.

On the seventy-fifth or one hundred and twentieth day after its birth, the baby stops wearing its baby linen, and this day is kept as a holiday. Although it is the general practice to dress children in various kinds of silk, this is very wrong; as the two principles of life are thereby injured, the child contracts disease. For this reason, the ancients strictly forbade the practice. In modern times, the child is dressed up in beautiful clothes; however, putting a cap on its head, thinking to show it affection when, on the contrary, it is harmful to the child, should be avoided. It would be an excellent thing if rich people, out of care for the health of their children, would put a stop to a practice to which fashion clings.

On the one hundred and twentieth day after their birth, children, whether male or female, are weaned.<note>This is only a nominal weaning. Japanese children are not really weaned until much later than is ordinary in Europe; and it is by no means uncommon to see a mother in the poorer classes nursing a large child of five to seven years old. One reason given for this practice is that by this means the danger of having to provide for large families is lessened.</note> This day is fixed, and there is no need to choose a lucky day. If the child is a boy, it is fed by a gentleman of the family; if a girl, by a lady. The ceremony is as follows: The child is brought out and given to the weaning father or sponsor. He takes it on his left knee. A small table is prepared. The sponsor who is to feed the child, taking some rice which has

When the child has been made to pretend to drink two cups, it receives a gift from its sponsor, after which the child is supposed to drink a third time. Dried fish is then brought in, and the baby, having "drunk" three times, passes the cup to its sponsor, who also drinks three times. More fish of a different kind is served. The drinking is repeated, and the weaning-father receives a gift from the child. The guardian, according to the rules of etiquette, should remain near the child. A feast should be prepared according to the family's means. If the child is a girl, a weaning-mother performs this ceremony, and suitable gifts must be offered by both parties. The wine-drinking ritual is conducted as described above.

On the fifteenth day of the eleventh month of the child’s third year—whether the child is a boy or a girl—its hair is allowed to grow. (Until this time, the entire head has been shaved; now, three patches are allowed to grow: one on each side and one at the back of the head.) For this occasion, a sponsor is also chosen. A large tray must be prepared with seven items: a comb, scissors, paper string, a piece of string for tying the hair in a knot, cotton wool, the piece of dried fish or seaweed that typically accompanies gifts, and seven rice straws.<note>For a few days before the ceremony, the child’s head is not shaved.</note>

The child is positioned facing the direction of the compass that is auspicious for that year. If the child is a boy, the sponsor takes the scissors and makes three snips at the hair on the left temple, three on the right, and three in the center.

He then takes the piece of cotton wool and spreads it over the child's head, from the forehead, so as to make it hang down behind his neck, and he places the bit of dried fish or seaweed and the seven straws at the bottom of the piece of cotton wool, attaching them to the wool, and ties them in two loops, like a man's hair, with a piece of paper string; he then makes a woman's knot with two pieces of string. The ceremony of drinking wine is the same as that performed at the weaning. If the child is a girl, a lady acts as sponsor; the hair-cutting is begun from the right temple instead of from the left. There is no difference in the rest of the ceremony.

On the fifth day of the eleventh month of the child's fourth year, he is invested with the *hakama*, or loose trousers worn by the Samurai. On this occasion again, a sponsor is called in. The child receives from the sponsor a dress of ceremony, on which are embroidered storks and tortoises (emblems of longevity—the stork is said to live a thousand years, the tortoise ten thousand), fir-trees (which, being evergreen and not changing their color, are emblematic of an unchangingly virtuous heart), and bamboos (emblematic of an upright and straight mind). The child is placed upright on a checkerboard, facing the auspicious point of the compass, and invested with the dress of ceremony. It also receives a sham sword and dirk. The usual ceremony of drinking wine is observed.

<note>To understand the following ceremony, it is necessary to remember that a child at three years of age is allowed to grow its hair in three patches. By degrees the hair is allowed to grow, with only the crown being shaved and a forelock left. At ten or eleven years of age, the boy's head is dressed like a man's, with the exception of this forelock.</note>

The ceremony of cutting off the forelock used to include the ceremony of putting on the noble's cap in the old days; but as this has gone out of fashion, there is no need to discuss it.

<meta>This page continues the description of Japanese childhood rituals, transitioning from the early childhood hair-growing and hakama investment to the formal coming-of-age ceremony (Genpuku) performed at age fifteen.</meta>

<header>RITES AND CEREMONIES. 379</header>

Any time after the youth has reached the age of fifteen, depending on the intelligence and ability he shows, a lucky day is chosen for this most important ceremony, after which the boy takes his place among adult men. A person of virtuous character is chosen as a sponsor or "cap-father." Although the man's real name (the name known only to his intimate relatives and friends, not the one he usually goes by in society) is usually determined before this date, if it has not been, he receives his real name from his sponsor on this day. In the old days, there used to be an earlier ceremony of cutting the hair off the forehead in a straight line so as to make two angles: up to this time, the youth wore long sleeves like a woman, and from that day forward, he wore short sleeves. This was called the "half cutting." The poorer classes have a habit of shortening the sleeves before this period, but that is contrary to all rules and is a bad custom.

A common tray is brought out, on which is placed an earthenware wine cup. The sponsor drinks three times and hands the cup to the young man, who, having also drunk three times, gives the cup back to the sponsor; the sponsor drinks three times again and then proceeds to tie up the young man's hair.

There are three ways of tying the hair, and there is also a particular fashion of letting the forelock grow long; when this is the case, the forelock is only clipped. (This is especially the fashion among the nobles of the Mikado's court.) This applies only to persons who wear the court cap, and not to gentlemen of lower rank. Still, these latter individuals, if they wish to go through the ceremony in its entirety, may do so without impropriety. Gentlemen of the Samurai or military class cut off the whole of the forelock. The sponsor either ties up the hair of the young man, or else, placing the forelock on a willow board, cuts it off with a knife; or, among persons of very high rank, he only pretends to do so and goes into another room while the real cutting is going on, and then returns to the same room. The sponsor then, without letting the young man see what he is

But this is incorrect. The locks should be well wrapped in paper and kept in the house until the man’s death to serve as a reminder of the favors a man receives from his father and mother during his childhood; when he dies, they should be placed in his coffin and buried with him. The wine-drinking and presents follow the customs described before.

In the *Shorei Hikki*, the book from which the above was translated, there is no mention of the naming ceremony for the child; the following is a translation from a Japanese manuscript:

> “On the seventh day after its birth, the child receives its name; the ceremony is called the 'Congratulations of the Seventh Night.' On this day, one of the family's relatives who holds an exalted position, due to either rank or virtue, selects a name for the child. The child keeps this name until the time of the cutting of the forelock, when he takes the name he will bear as a man. This second name is called *Yeboshina*,<note>From *Yeboshi*, a court cap, and *Na*, a name.</note> the cap-name, which is composed of syllables taken from an old family name and from the name of the sponsor. If the sponsor later changes his name, his namesake must also change his name. For instance, the famous warrior Minamoto no Yoshitsuné was called Ushiwakamaru as a child; when he grew up to be a man, he was called Kurô; and his real name was Yoshitsuné.”

# FUNERAL RITES.

->(FROM THE "SHOREI HIKKEI.")<-

On the death of a parent, the mourning clothes worn are made of coarse hempen cloth, and throughout the entire period of mourning, these must be worn night and day. As the burial of one's parents is the most important ceremony a man must go through during his whole life, when the occasion arrives, he must employ someone to teach him the usual and proper rites to ensure there is no confusion. Above all else, the cremation of the dead is to be condemned; they should be buried without being burned.<note>On the subject of cremating the dead, see a note to the story of Chôbei of Bandzuin.</note> The ceremonies to be observed at a funeral should, by right, be learned before there is an occasion to put them into practice. If a man has no father or mother, he is certain to have to bury other relatives; therefore, he should not neglect this study. There are some authorities who select lucky days, hours, and places for burying the dead, but this is wrong; and when they speak of curses being brought upon descendants by not observing these auspicious seasons and locations, they are making a great mistake. It is a matter of course that an auspicious day must be chosen to avoid wind and rain, so that men may bury their dead without their minds being distracted; and it is important to choose a suitable cemetery, lest in later days the tomb should be damaged by rain, or by people walking over it, or by the place being turned

<summary>This page introduces Japanese funeral customs from the "Shorei Hikkei," emphasizing the use of hempen mourning clothes and the preference for burial over cremation. It also argues against superstitious practices regarding "lucky" burial dates, favoring practical concerns like weather and the long-term stability of the gravesite.</summary>

## TALES OF OLD JAPAN.

into a field, or built upon. When invited to a friend’s or neighbor’s funeral, a man should avoid wearing smart clothes and ceremonial dress; and when he follows the coffin, he should not speak in a loud voice to the person next to him, for that is very rude. Even if he has reason to do so, he should avoid entering wine shops or tea houses on his return from the funeral.

The list of persons present at a funeral should be written on slips of paper and firmly bound together. It may be written like any other list, except that it must not be written starting from the right hand, as is usually the case, but from the left hand (as is the case in European books).

On the day of burial, during the funeral service, incense is burned in the temple before the tablet on which is inscribed the name under which the dead person enters salvation.<note>After death, a person receives a new name. For instance, the famous Prince Tokugawa Iyéyasu entered salvation as Gongen Sama. This name is called *okurina*, or the posthumous name.</note> Those offering the incense, having washed their hands, enter the room where the tablet is displayed one by one. They advance halfway to the tablet, facing it; taking incense wrapped in paper from the front of their robes, they hold it in their left hands, and, taking a pinch with the right hand, they place the packet in their left sleeve. If the table on which the tablet is placed is high, the person offering incense half-raises himself from his crouching position; if the table is low, he remains crouching to burn the incense. After this, he takes three steps backward with bows and gestures of respect, and retires six feet, where he again crouches down to watch the incense-burning. He then bows to the priests who are sitting in a row with their chief at their head, after which he rises and leaves the room. Until the time of burning the incense, no notice is taken of the priest. At the ceremony of burning incense before the grave, the priests are not saluted. The packet of incense is made of fine paper folded in three in both directions.

--- Page 462 ---
<meta>This page serves as a concluding note to the discussion on rites and ceremonies, specifically addressing why funeral rites were only briefly covered and commenting on the state of Buddhism in Japan at the time of writing.</meta>

RITES AND CEREMONIES.

## NOTE.

The reason why the author of the “Shorei Hikki” has treated the funeral ceremonies so briefly is probably because these rites, being always entrusted to the Buddhist priesthood, vary according to the sect of the priest; and, as there are no fewer than fifteen sects of Buddhism in Japan, it would be a lengthy matter to go into the ceremonies practiced by each. Should Buddhism be swept out of Japan, as seems likely to be the case, people will probably return to the old rites that existed before its introduction in the sixth century of our era. What those rites were, I have been unable to learn.

->THE END.<-

->LONDON : R. CLAY, SONS, AND TAYLOR, PRINTERS, BREAD STREET HILL.<-

<summary>The author explains that funeral rites were only briefly described because they vary across the fifteen different Buddhist sects in Japan. He also speculates that if Buddhism were to decline in Japan, the people might return to ancient, unknown pre-Buddhist traditions.</summary>
